This research paper delves into the properties of an ensemble of random matrices that combines elements of the Gaussian Orthogonal Ensemble (GOE) and the Gaussian Unitary Ensemble (GUE). A key distinguishing feature of this particular matrix ensemble is the incorporation of a complex logarithmic potential that restricts matrix elements off the real diagonal, resulting in a distribution that inherits characteristics from both the GOE and GUE. To investigate this mixed ensemble, we examine the correlations between eigenvalues and eigenvectors, as well as eigenvalues and their corresponding properties. Specifically, we analyze the distribution of eigenvalues, their fluctuations, and the distribution of their spacings. Furthermore, we investigate the correlations between eigenvalues and eigenvectors, as well as the distribution of the logarithm of eigenvalues. To this end, we develop a detailed analysis of the determinants of various products of different types of matrix kernels, which are crucial for our calculations. These determinants are then used to derive the main results of the study, including the main term of the Tracy-Widom distribution, the correlation functions of eigenvalues, and the distribution of the logarithm of eigenvalues.

This research investigates the presence of quantum connections between distinct qutrit particles and their surroundings by employing a quantum model that simulates interactions at the molecular level.  The study utilizes a quantum system consisting of a linear chain of three molecules, with each molecule comprising three interacting spin systems and interacting with its neighboring molecules.  We examine the quantum connections between the central molecule and its neighbors by analyzing the behavior of entanglement and other quantum correlation measures between the central molecule and its surroundings.  We also investigate the effects of local and non-local interactions on these quantum connections.  The findings of this study reveal that the central molecule exhibits quantum connections with its surroundings under certain conditions, with the specific type of interaction depending on the strength of molecular interactions and the distance between the molecules.  The study also demonstrates that the quantum connections between the central molecule and its surroundings can be strengthened or disrupted by modifying the molecular environment, with the latter approach offering a novel method for controlling and manipulating quantum connections.  The results of this study provide new insights into the behavior of quantum systems and have the potential to inform the development of quantum technologies.

We introduce a departure from Bell's theorem rooted in the concept of spatial locality, which is broader than spatial separability implied by Bell's inequality. Our results indicate that all quantum systems conform to this locality principle. However, this cannot be reconciled with a theoretical framework in which quantum systems can be broken down into smaller, spatially discrete components. Instead, this discrepancy can be resolved if either the locality principle or the idea of decomposable subsystems is relaxed. Our research reveals that replacing spatial locality with a concept of causal locality, where information cannot be exchanged across space and time without a physical connection, can restore compatibility with the principle of decomposability.

We introduce StyleGAN-V, a groundbreaking generative model that creates an endless variety of high-quality videos. This innovative deep learning framework builds upon the success of StyleGAN-ADA, its precursor, and achieves this by generating video sequences through a series of frames, each produced by a specially designed neural network. This approach is made possible by the utilization of a unique latent space that can be easily traversed. Not only does StyleGAN-V excel in creating a multitude of images, but it also produces a range of video sequences with diverse styles at a significantly reduced computational cost similar to StyleGAN-ADA in terms of training data. Leveraging the model's capabilities, we have developed a user-friendly interface that enables users to manipulate video appearance in real-time. We demonstrate StyleGAN-V's versatility by showcasing its ability to generate high-quality videos across various scales, from small 4x4 frames to longer sequences of 128 frames. Moreover, we have successfully integrated this framework with the StyleGAN-ADA framework, allowing us to generate high-quality videos using the latent codes of StyleGAN-ADA. We have made StyleGAN-V publicly available at https://github.com/NVlabs/StyleGAN-V.

Our research involves examining how the degrees of modular forms change under the action of the eta correspondence, with a significant aspect being the computation of degree fluctuations in the theta correspondence.  To achieve this, we leverage the idea that the theta correspondence can be viewed as a composition of the Ramanujan-Petersson conjecture-verified eta correspondence and square map, allowing us to adapt and expand existing results on the theta correspondence to also cover the eta correspondence.  Furthermore, we demonstrate that the degree fluctuations of the eta correspondence exhibit the same properties as those of the theta correspondence in terms of cusp forms, with an additional finding that the degree of Eisenstein series eta(q) is zero.

Personal dosimetry is crucial for professionals in medical imaging, nuclear, and occupational settings, enabling them to monitor radiation exposure through dosimeter analysis. Dosimeters measuring the full dose history are beneficial, but currently, only the total dose can be calculated using conventional methods. To assess the exact exposure date and dose received, the exposure history must be reconstructed, typically achieved through thermoluminescence dosimetry (TLD) by analyzing the residual signal of multiple dosimeters. This paper presents a novel approach utilizing deep learning to reconstruct the full dose history from multiple dosimeters. By training a neural network on simulated data, the method enables accurate estimation of the exact exposure date and dose received, even when dosimeters are exposed to varying radiation patterns. This approach enhances traditional methods by leveraging the unique signal of each dosimeter for improved results. Experimental validation using actual TLD measurements confirms the effectiveness of the proposed deep learning technique, demonstrating its potential to reconstruct the full dose history and estimate the exact exposure date and dose received with high accuracy.

We verify the existence of nontrivial solutions for equations describing certain types of singular elliptic problems within the context of Sobolev-Orlicz spaces on a complete manifold. The potential energy function exhibits a peculiar property where its growth depends on two variable exponents p( x) and q( x) that fluctuate. Assuming that the weight function is non-negative and has a specific level of integrability, we establish a rigorous existence result for these types of problems. The proof relies on a highly innovative approach to regular perturbation theory, specifically addressing the effect of singular coefficients on a family of nonlinear problems. The key challenge lies in adapting this approach to handle the singular coefficients and derive a uniform ( x,y)-estimation for the linearized operator, a crucial condition for the presence of nontrivial solutions.

A computer algorithm was developed to convert 3D images captured using cone beam computed tomography into more detailed three-dimensional images that can be used alongside radiation therapy treatment plans. This algorithm was tested with images taken at two different energy levels and found to successfully produce images that match the quality of the original images. Further testing involved comparing the algorithm's images with those generated by a computer program designed to simulate radiation therapy scans and found that the results were similar, indicating that the algorithm is effective at replicating the characteristics of the original images.

In recent years, LIME (Language Interpretable Mapping) has become a widely accepted method for generating local explanations in complex ML models. However, our research reveals that LIME's explanations can be misleading due to the random nature of its process. We introduce S-LIME, an enhanced approach to LIME, utilizing a unique resampling technique to ensure accurate, reliable, and stable explanations. Experimental results demonstrate that S-LIME outperforms LIME, maintaining consistency regardless of the dataset or model used.

In real-world applications, categorization is a fundamental skill that enables individuals to navigate their environment. However, the accuracy of their categorization can be compromised by preconceived notions and a lack of motivation. To address this issue, we developed an innovative method that integrates Bayesian probability theory and Justification Feedback to create an engaging and effective categorization training system. The system, which is based on a hierarchical Bayesian model, allows learners to refine their categorization skills and provides them with a sense of agency by showcasing their progress. Our research involved designing an interactive game, called Bayes Digg, and conducting experiments on 103 undergraduate students to test the efficacy of our method. The results indicate that our Bayes Digg system is a successful tool for enhancing categorization skills, and significantly, it outperformed traditional methods that lack the Bayesian-based justification feedback.

TbInO$_3$ is a promising spin-liquid candidate with a unique triangular-lattice structure and J$_{\text{eff}}$ = 1/2 ground state. Our study focuses on the crystal-field excitations of TbInO$_3$ using polarized inelastic neutron scattering, yielding detailed crystal-field levels and coupling constants. The obtained results are consistent with theoretical predictions and provide insight into the material's properties. The observed spin-liquid excitations exhibit distinct patterns, while thermal coherence effects are supported by data analysis. The material's properties are well-reproduced within the framework of crystal-field theory, allowing us to estimate the single-ion parameters. The material's properties are also consistent with theoretical predictions for a broader class of triangular-lattice materials.

We apply the broader concept of anisotropic curvature to a comprehensive definition that encompasses the power-of-mean-curvature function from literature. By utilizing a novel variational method based on convex optimization, we analyze and establish the existence, uniqueness, and long-term stability of evolving surfaces governed by this anisotropic curvature model. Our approach allows for a range of exponents (greater than zero and less than infinity) for which the model is applicable. Key benefits of this method include the ability to handle complex anisotropic curvature functions and the absence of reliance on specific curvature properties such as concavity or convexity. Additionally, this method accommodates initial data that deviate from surfaces with minimal curvature.

This research introduces a pioneering approach to directly train convolutional neural networks in the spectrum domain, eliminating the need for time domain training and subsequent frequency domain inference. The proposed spectrum domain method enables end-to-end training and allows for direct generation of convolutional neural network weights in the spectrum domain, thus simplifying the process of spectrum domain training and eliminating the need for time domain and frequency domain equivalents of these weights. The approach is experimentally demonstrated to yield a notable 2.54 dB improvement in signal-to-noise ratio for a given convolutional neural network architecture across a range of signal-to-noise ratios, with results validated through a practical application of spectrum sensing in cognitive radio systems.

The primary goal of the image grouping task is to categorize images into a common group based on their semantic and visual similarities. Recent research has shown that deep learning models excel in image grouping, especially when using convolutional neural networks (CNNs). To further enhance this capability, a new framework called DeepCluE has been proposed, which incorporates multiple deep learning layers to extract the necessary information. Firstly, a CNN is used to extract basic image features, which are then used to train a set of random forest classifiers in the second layer. These classifiers are then utilized to generate a matrix containing similarity scores between images, which is subsequently fed into a third-layer autoencoder for further processing. This autoencoder then produces a compact numerical representation for each image, which is used by the fourth layer's random forest classifier to make a final grouping decision. Experimental results on three datasets demonstrate the DeepCluE framework's superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.

The concept of stakeholder influence within global value chains has gained significant attention in the fields of risk and corporate social responsibility. This study introduces a novel approach to identifying key stakeholders and monitoring their concerns, which can significantly impact a company's risk profile. We utilize a unique blend of social network analysis, news media analysis, and open research data to identify influential stakeholders and track their viewpoints. The proposed method consists of three stages: first, we build a knowledge network of influential stakeholders and risk-relevant themes; next, we monitor news outlets for mentions of these stakeholders and themes; finally, we analyze the news articles to inform insights for risk management. The approach is tested using a case study of the global automotive industry, focusing on key stakeholders and risk associated with supply chain management. The resulting system dynamically updates a knowledge graph showcasing the stakeholder's network, risk themes, and corresponding news articles.

Machine learning's classification involves categorizing data into distinct, mutually exclusive groups. In contrast, data science often groups items that share a common purpose, like customers who buy the same products or communications that contain similar content. These tasks are typically performed by humans, but we aim to automate this process using TDA to identify meaningful clusters within datasets. Our approach utilizes persistent homology to evaluate the effectiveness of various categorization methods, including both supervised and unsupervised techniques. We demonstrate that a simple density-based clustering algorithm based on persistent homology outperforms more advanced methods like k-means and hierarchical clustering, often producing more intuitive and useful groupings.

This research explores an alternative approach to simulating the effects of a two-player game that involves strategic interactions between the players' attempts to approximate truth and falsehood. The study introduces a new concept called 'contrasimilarity', which measures the similarity between the players' information states. The analysis reveals that under specific conditions, the equilibrium of this game corresponds to the maximally similar state. The study extends this analysis to a broader class of games and proposes a new game that ensures the equilibrium is a non-increasing sequence of states. The proposed game can be implemented through a simple iterative process.

We utilize the M-theoretic frame-work to re-examine the string 2-group, beginning with its root system, and then considering the implications of world-volume attachments to NS5-branes on the 6-dimensional world-volume. These world-volume attachments lead to the emergence of three-dimensional operators that are dual to the 2-form NS field, and enable the introduction of a string 2-form, $B_{\text{string}}$, in addition to the Kalb-Ramond 2-form. By integrating the string 2-form with the low-energy effective action, we can incorporate the self-dual 2-form world-volume operator into its action.

The formation of unusual ion-acoustic pulses in a double pair plasma with non-extensive electrons is investigated using a nonlinear, quasi-one-dimensional, electrostatic model. It is discovered that the parameters of the plasma, including temperature, density, and electron charge, significantly impact the properties of the resulting pulses. Additionally, increasing the non-extensive electron characteristic parameter enhances the rogue pulse's amplitude and compresses its width. The results also reveal the impact of ion charge and mass on the pulse's properties. A double pair plasma can produce both solitary and periodic waves, and it is found that varying the ion charge can alter the properties of these waves. Ultimately, this research demonstrates the potential of rogue pulses in a double pair plasma in fields like space and laboratory plasma research.

A novel approach has been developed to model the Alfvén wave parametric decay instability using a hybrid method that combines kinetic theory with a hybrid model. This instability is predicted to significantly impact fusion reactors' stability and plasma heating. Our hybrid model includes kinetic ion dynamics and a fluid-based electron model, and it employs a fully-implicit scheme for efficient numerical solution. To validate the model, we compared its results with kinetic simulations for a specific case of AWPII, and it showed consistent outcomes. Furthermore, we examined the effects of varying parameters such as ion temperature, electron temperature, and ion species on the instability. Our research findings are expected to contribute to the development of improved theoretical models for enhancing the stability of fusion reactors.

We investigate the gravitational instability in molecular thread-nebulae, which are considered a common form of molecular clouds. Given the presence of a magnetic field, the presence of ambipolar diffusion significantly alters the effective viscosity of the medium. A thin thread-like molecular cloud with a uniform magnetic field will experience gravitational instability if its length exceeds 0.1 parsecs, provided the gas density is 1000 cm-3 or higher. This critical length decreases with magnetic field strength, including scenarios with perpendicular and parallel field orientations. Notably, the instability growth rate is influenced by the magnetic field orientation and the presence of ambipolar diffusion, which can lead to an estimated cloud fragmentation time of approximately 0.1-10 million years. This timeframe is comparable to the cloud's dynamical time, which may explain why many thread-like filaments lack substructure.

The article investigates the impact of frequent measurements on a quantum system interacting strongly with a harmonic resonator, where the system is modeled by a dissipatively driven Josephson junction. It examines the dynamics of this system, particularly the transition probability from the ground state to an excited state, using perturbation theory to analyze both weak and strong coupling scenarios. The study reveals that, in the case of frequent measurements, transitions are suppressed in systems interacting with coherent vibrations but enhanced by noise vibrations, a phenomenon contrary to the classical Zeno effect. It also shows that, in systems initially excited, the transition probability is reduced by noise vibrations while increased by coherent vibrations, exhibiting the anti-Zeno effect.

We investigate how the Heisenberg model with Dzyaloshinsky-Moriya interactions responds in an inhomogeneous external field, specifically examining the properties of the resulting system. By applying the cluster variation method, we calculate the magnetization and magnon excitation spectrum within a mean-field approximation. Our analysis reveals that the magnetization and magnon spectra converge at high temperatures, validating the chosen model against established theoretical and experimental findings. Notably, we demonstrate that the introduction of an external field reduces symmetry, leading to the presence of two distinct types of magnon modes within the cubic lattice.

This study introduces a groundbreaking approach to path planning for a swarm of quadrotors, focusing on ensuring their safe and efficient navigation of the internet. A novel algorithm, the Viability Guarantee method, has been developed to calculate safe trajectories while accounting for the vehicles' limited communication and travel times. The algorithm, based on the concept of the bag-of-triggers programming system, allows for more flexible planning and real-time adjustments without restricting the vehicles' navigation capabilities. In contrast to existing models, the new approach enables the quadrotors to maintain constant velocity while minimizing their total travel time, resulting in significantly shorter paths and reduced energy expenditure. The effectiveness of this method has been demonstrated through simulations, where a swarm of 4 quadrotors navigated an internet graph comprising 20 nodes, achieving an average speed of 6.5 m/s and an energy efficiency 50% higher than traditional models.

Unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) is a statistical learning method that bridges the gap between a source, which has ample labeled data, and a target, which lacks such information. This gap arises from the fact that data from these two environments often exhibit disparate distributions, rendering the target dataset's unlabeled labels useless when utilizing the knowledge gained from the labeled source. Our research introduces CARLANE, a challenging UDA benchmark tailored for autonomous driving, featuring a simulated environment that mimics a real-world setting with photorealistic graphics. This environment is accompanied by a comprehensive range of tasks, encompassing lane detection, road segmentation, and others. The primary goal of CARLANE lies in facilitating the evaluation and comparison of diverse UDA techniques within autonomous driving, with the source code, detailed rules, and data set available at https://github.com/autonomylab/carlane

Our investigation focuses on how particles affect the wettability of hydrogel porous media. We found a correlation between particle inclusion and the contact angle measured using the Cassie-Baxter equation, where a linear relationship was established. A comparative study using a Young-Laplace model revealed that the main factor influencing this relationship is the particle size relative to the pore size. When particle sizes are comparable to or larger than the pore size, the contact angle diminishes due to decreased wetting. Conversely, when particle sizes are significantly smaller, the contact angle remains unaffected. This phenomenon is attributed to diminished pore sizes resulting from particle inclusion.

The study examined how student engagement and engagement metrics changed at a mid-sized US public university during the 2020 fall semester following a data collection period in 2019 that coincided with a student engagement award. Given that students were previously participating in an engagement tracking mobile app, the university conducted an online survey to assess students' current attitudes and behaviors. The survey collected data on students' engagement practices, attitudes towards technology, and perceived engagement environments. Following this, students' academic performance in the fall semester was evaluated. Results showed a correlation between students and their engagement behaviors during the survey period. It was also observed that students' engagement behaviors during the survey period were positively correlated with their subsequent academic performance. Following the survey, students were informed of their engagement quartiles. This notification led to higher engagement behaviors among students in the bottom and middle quartiles compared to those in the top quartile.

The wind speed in the upper atmosphere of the Sun varies greatly, and measuring this speed with accuracy above 300 km/s is quite challenging. To address this issue, a new technique using Doppler shift in the L-band range has been developed, and it was tested using data collected by Swift/SXRS during solar flares and coronal mass ejections. The technique involves analyzing the time series of the L-band signal and comparing it with data from high-resolution spectrometers operating in the X-ray and soft X-ray ranges. To account for data gaps, a statistical model was employed to fill in the missing measurements. The technique was validated through simulations of theoretical electron bremsstrahlung spectra and was then applied to real-world data collected during a series of solar events. The results showed that the new technique is effective in measuring wind speeds above 300 km/s with an accuracy of 20-30 km/s/s, and it is also capable of detecting changes in wind speed with an accuracy of 30-50 km/s/s. Furthermore, a statistical model was used to estimate the wind speed profiles of the events, and it was found that the technique is effective in measuring wind speeds up to 500 km/s. The new technique is also capable of detecting the time evolution of the wind speed and is useful for studying the dynamics of the solar corona during large-scale events.

We conducted a thorough investigation of the open cluster UBC 274, focusing on its internal dynamics, kinematics, and elemental composition. By utilizing the Gaia EDR3 astrometric data and comparing it to kinematic properties of the cluster's confirmed members, we identified potential substructures within the cluster. The resulting analysis revealed a prominent north-south elongation and eastward tilt in the cluster's proper motion distribution, which is indicative of its spatial configuration. By examining the radial velocity distribution, we found that the cluster exhibits a velocity gradient along the same elongation axis. The elongation direction is perpendicular to the cluster's tidal radius. The radial velocity dispersion within the cluster's half-mass radius is approximately 0.4 km/s. Furthermore, by examining the elemental composition of UBC 274's confirmed members, we found that the cluster exhibits an abundance of elements such as iron, silicon, and nitrogen, which is higher than that of other open clusters. The iron-to-iron-silicon ratio in UBC 274 is notably low. The observed elemental composition of UBC 274 suggests that the cluster is similar to the Hyades cluster. The similarities between UBC 274 and the Hyades cluster are intriguing, especially considering that the latter is an open cluster with a significant dynamical disruption. The observed characteristics of UBC 274 are indicative of a cluster that is being disrupted by tidal forces.

A significant issue in automatic text evaluation lies in the fact that it's difficult to measure the quality of machine-generated text objectively. To address this problem, we propose a new method to assess generated text based on its effectiveness in enhancing various machine translation tasks. This evaluation metric, called the Evaluation Metric for Enhanced Text (EMET), calculates the average improvement in bitext quality for a given text, and in turn, the quality of generated text. To demonstrate the potential of this approach, we developed a simple artificial translation method using the WMT 2020 metric, WMT-BLEU+, and applied it to the WMT 2020 Shared Task and various language pairs. The results show that our metric can accurately measure the quality of generated text, and in some cases, WMT-BLEU+ successfully produced bitexts that surpass even the original reference bitexts in quality.

We explore the concept of engineered dissipation self-adjusting entanglement in quantum spin chains via stochastic quantum master equation. Our research reveals that the type of interaction between local dissipation and spin chain can be controlled by adjusting the strength of interaction between dissipation and spin. In certain scenarios, dissipation can trigger a logarithmic entanglement shift, whereas in others, it may result in an area-law decay of entanglement. Notably, our findings also indicate that the entanglement can be shifted towards the quantum spin chain's original state under specific conditions.

The interaction between spin-orbit effects and lattice deformations in 2D materials has been under-investigated, despite its potential impact on electronic properties. We have developed a new theoretical framework to study this interaction in transition metal dichalcogenide materials, specifically focusing on their composition and structure. By applying this framework to different types of flat bands in these materials, we found that the spin-orbit interaction varies significantly, ranging from a few to hundreds of millielectronvolts. Interestingly, even the narrowest bands showed substantial interaction, while the widest bands showed interaction of up to 1.5 millielectronvolts. We also discovered that the spin-orbit splitting in certain bands can be controlled by adjusting their chemical potential, offering new possibilities for manipulating the electronic properties of these materials.

A novel quantum filtering approach, known as quantum reservoir processing, has been developed to enhance quantum communication systems. This method enables the creation of a virtual energy reservoir that filters incoming quantum information, effectively converting it into a more suitable quantum state for further operations within the system. This filtering effect is achieved without altering the original system dynamics. We have developed a new quantum reservoir processing method that utilizes a control system consisting of a network of quantum dots connected to reservoirs of phonons and electrons, which serve as a filter to purify quantum information, converting it into a more suitable quantum state for further operations within the system.

The development of a self-sustaining, compact, and portable laser system for cold atoms is feasible with a GaN-on-sapphire substrate, allowing for the miniaturization of a magneto-optical trap without the need for a separate vacuum chamber. However, a significant obstacle to creating a reliable magneto-optical trap on this substrate is the surface roughness, which causes excessive atomic loss. To overcome this, a chemical etching process was applied to a GaN-on-sapphire wafer, achieving a significant reduction in roughness, from 25 nm to 2 nm, after 10 min of etching. This improved surface quality enabled the successful creation of a single-beam optical trap with a 1.5 mm beam and a trapping potential of 2.5 Hz/cm, as well as a 5-beam optical trap with a 5 mm beam and a 2.5 Hz/cm potential. Furthermore, a 5-beam magnetic trap with a 5 mm potential was successfully established, demonstrating the potential of this substrate for a compact magnetic trap for cold atoms.

This research introduces a finite element method mixture for solving the Poisson equation,
utilizing the MFEM library. Two approaches are explored: Lagrange and Mixed finite elements.
Within these two methodologies, we examine multiple configurations of finite element spaces.
Our numerical outcomes are contrasted through error analysis in both H1 and L2-norms, highlighting
the distinct behaviors of solutions and gradients in comparison to the optimal optimal rate
of convergence.

We investigate the dynamic behavior of a specific model featuring sign-alterable interacting dark energy in a cosmological context, where a scalar field with a changing potential connects dark matter and dark energy. The energy interactions between dark matter and dark energy are represented by an altered coupling term, which varies according to a specific power law. The presence of a potential changes the dynamics of the scalar field, which in turn affects the evolution of the cosmic system. Our analysis focuses on the energy conditions and dynamic parameter analysis for different model parameters, which provides insights into the deceleration parameter, state finder, and jerk numbers. The findings indicate that the model's behavior aligns with observations from the Pantheon dataset for a specific model parameter range, which also satisfies energy conditions.

The collision of black holes with stars resulting in TDE events produces powerful electromagnetic signals, which researchers have been studying for decades. The radio bursts associated with TDEs have typically been attributed to synchrotron or maser radiation, but recent simulations suggest that the interaction between fast and slow streams at quasi-perpendicular shocks could also be responsible. The interaction generates a significant amount of Alfven waves, which can accelerate electrons to high energies, resulting in powerful shock fronts that can accelerate particles to high energies, producing radio bursts in the X-ray regime. The particle acceleration process is highly dependent on the shock's Alfvenicness, which can be predicted by estimating the Mach number and angle. The simulation results indicate that particle acceleration is most effective when the shock is highly quasi-perpendicular and has a specific Mach number and angle range. The predicted characteristics of the shock acceleration mechanism are consistent with those of observed TDE radio bursts, suggesting that particle acceleration at quasi-perpendicular shocks may be responsible for some of these events.

A mathematical model of acoustic wave behavior inside a liquid containing micro-bubbles is developed and solved using the boundary element method.  The model accounts for both transient radiation of sound by the bubbles and the response of the bubbles to the sound wave.  The model includes the effects of bubble volume changes due to acoustic cavitation.  The model's results are compared to experimental data collected by observing the movement of a highly sensitive detector in response to ultrasonic waves passing through a liquid containing micro-bubbles.

In various human-computer interaction applications, recognizing a user's tension state is a key focus. Our research introduces MUSER, a dataset consisting of multimodal social affective data collected from 40 users engaging in a banking task while wearing EMG and ECG sensors to monitor physiological signals. Along with a banking task, users were asked to express tension through verbal and non-verbal cues, which were categorized into acknowledged and unacknowledged interactions. Our dataset comprises 160 banking task sessions, with approximately 10 minutes of data per session, featuring a balance of acknowledged and unacknowledged tension behaviors. We employed a multi-modal transformer model to predict tension levels, employing both continuous and categorical models. Our experiments demonstrated that incorporating the acknowledged vs unacknowledged supplementational task improved the performance of both transformer-based models in tension recognition.

Large-scale graph data annotation is a critical task for machine learning and artificial intelligence researchers, particularly in natural language processing and knowledge graph management. Current methods are limited in their ability to efficiently scale and offer interactive training for models, such as transformer-based architectures. To address these challenges, we developed PanGEA, a versatile and scalable tool for generating and annotating graph data. PanGEA is designed to work seamlessly with pre-trained language models and supports the creation of entity embeddings. Our open-source framework is designed to be easily customized and expanded by the research community.

We have developed a new model to explain how star formation rates in galaxies change over time, taking into account variations in the birth rates of stars, the time it takes for stars to form, and the number of stars formed. This model also considers the possibility that stars in galaxies with different environments may have different lifetimes. We used this model to study the growth of elliptical galaxies and how they differ in their star birth rates and lifetimes. We found that galaxies in dense environments tend to have fewer long-lived stars, which can lead to a shorter average lifespan for their stars. This, combined with a higher rate of star formation in these galaxies, can explain why galaxies in dense environments tend to be smaller than their less dense counterparts. We also found that the number of supernovae in galaxies in dense environments is higher than in galaxies in less dense environments, which can be explained by a combination of a higher star birth rate and a shorter average lifespan for their stars. This suggests that the number of supernovae in galaxies in dense environments is influenced by a combination of a higher star birth rate and a shorter average lifespan for their stars.

This paper introduces a novel approach to image compressive sensing reconstruction, which incorporates a unique block-coordinate descent algorithm with the proximity operator to leverage the efficiency of dual-structured dictionaries. By combining the advantages of the matrix soft-thresholding operator and the dual update proximity operator, our approach enables the efficient computation of image reconstruction, achieving collective sparse representation with sparse image representation. Experimental results demonstrate the proposed method's ability to match state-of-the-art performance, even surpassing it in certain cases with reduced computational complexity.

A new approach called Reconstructive-Transformer network is proposed in this research. This method uses a step-by-step training process for individual skin problems, such as acne, blackheads, and age spots. RethNet employs a new transformer-based model that effectively identifies spatial correlations among various skin challenges, thereby improving the identification of individual issues. A novel method is introduced to split the skin region map into distinct areas for different skin issues, which is then used to retrain the network. Experimental results show that RethNet outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods by 1.4% and 3.5% in terms of mean average precision and mean average recall metrics respectively.

The efficiency and complexity of decoding sequential code sequences for communication have been extensively researched, particularly with the introduction of PAC codes, which offer a non-binary, non-uniform distribution approach. Sequential decoding methods, including maximum likelihood and sequential list-decoding, have been developed and analyzed for PAC code sequences. These algorithms have been proven to be efficient and capable of achieving optimal performance. Research has demonstrated that sequential decoding can handle more complex code sequences than traditional methods, including high-rate PAC codes. To verify the effectiveness of these methods, simulations were conducted to assess their performance and efficiency in decoding sequences.

Online learning platforms have gained popularity, but their effectiveness can be hindered by users who are new to online education. These users, referred to as "cold-start" users, often require personalized support to enhance their learning experience. To address this issue, we focus on "cold-start" users who want suggestions on what to learn next. Our research explores the potential benefits of sequential suggestions in online education, which take into account the user's long-term online footprint. To achieve this, we develop a new approach called Meta Transnational Education (Meta-TED), a virtual assistant that offers personalized suggestions by analyzing users' natural online behavior. Our findings indicate that sequential suggestions made by Meta-TED can effectively guide "cold-start" users in achieving their learning objectives, as evident from the significant improvement in their outcome validation ratings following interactions with the virtual assistant.

Galactic cosmic rays with extremely high energies (above 100 EeV) are a topic of interest due to their potential to help understand the origin of cosmic rays with lower energies (up to PeV range). A review of the current state of knowledge on the UHECRs, particularly their origin, composition, and deflection, is presented. The discussion is based on recent findings from the Pierre Auger Observatory and the Telescope Array.

The Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) mission, scheduled for 2022, involves propelling a gravitational manipulator called Dart against Dimorphos, the smaller moon orbiting Didymos, with the objective of altering Dimorphos's orbital period. The predicted period change is estimated to be between 0.6 and 1.7 years, but this discrepancy stems from uncertain parameters related to the projectile's shape and composition. We have developed a new method to estimate momentum exchange based on the projectile's shape and compare it with existing methods, showing that it provides a more accurate estimate. We have also created a dataset consisting of 1000 simulated impacts with various shapes and found that the minimum and maximum momentum exchange are directly related to the minimum and maximum moments of inertia of the projectile.

The primary goal of through-the-windshield driver recognition is to identify and monitor drivers operating a vehicle without a seatbelt. This critical task is crucial for enhancing road safety. In our research, we introduce the Mertens Unfolded Network (MU-Net), a neural network that integrates multiple enhanced interval networks to optimize the processing of interval images. MU-Net is designed to work with images captured through vehicle windshield glass, taking into account the unique distortion effects associated with this setup. We demonstrate the effectiveness of MU-Net through experiments on a large, custom-built dataset comprising 1.5 million images. Our results show that MU-Net surpasses other models in accuracy, yielding an error rate of 0.95%. Additionally, our experiments reveal that MU-Net's architecture is robust and adaptable to different image sources, achieving an error rate of 0.98% using a public dataset.

This study investigates the design requirements for online repositories of programming languages by examining user behavior, specifically how search queries influence content creation and curation strategies. A novel dataset, Extensive Blurb Archive Network (EBAN), consisting of 1.1 million entries, was compiled to explore key design considerations for future language repositories. Our research findings, such as the EBAN's semi-supervised classification efficiency, the frequency of coding-related content, and the importance of query-specific tagging, offer valuable guidance for designers of new programming language repositories.

A significant limitation of many machine learning and statistical techniques is that they assume complete data, necessitating the imputation of missing data or dropout rate specification. This is particularly problematic in biomedical research where data collection often spans multiple time points, and dropout rates are common. To address this issue, we developed a new family of multistage estimators capable of handling both missing covariates and dropout rates in outcomes. Our proposed approach is applied to a survival analysis problem where we aim to evaluate the effectiveness of a treatment for a type of lymphoma, and dropout is possible due to the end of follow-up. Our multistage estimators, which account for both missing covariates and dropout rates in outcomes, are compared to existing alternatives, demonstrating superior performance in terms of accuracy and model interpretability.

In 2016, the journal "Portugaleiro" published a study with the title "On the Inverse Hyperbolic Tangent Estimation of the Complete Elliptic Integral of the First Kind", proposing an inequality for the complete elliptic integral of the first kind. This investigation aims to validate a hypothesis presented in that paper.

Deep learning models are highly effective but require extensive training data.  However, creating a large amount of labeled data is often impractical.  Therefore, researchers have developed methods for semi-supervised learning that utilize unlabeled data to enhance model performance.  A novel approach called Decomposed Inductive Method Learning (DIML) addresses this issue by decoupling the model into two components: a base model and a method.  The base model is trained using unlabeled data, and the method is adjusted by retraining the base model with the new data.  This approach is repeated until the method is optimized, and the final model is the base model with the optimized method, which is referred to as the DIML model.  We applied this method to three different datasets and found that it outperformed traditional semi-supervised learning methods and a recently proposed method called ISM.  Our results show that the DIML model can be trained in a matter of seconds, and it achieved a higher accuracy than other models on the CIFAR-10 dataset by 3.1%, 2.1%, and 1.2% respectively.

The rapid dissemination of altered or fabricated information through social media significantly hampers governments, businesses, and society as a whole, making it crucial to develop efficient methods for detecting Altered and Fake News. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach that generates altered texts by manipulating individual words within a dataset while preserving the original meaning. This method is applied to Arabic news articles and evaluated using machine learning algorithms to identify the altered or fake nature of the generated texts. To the best of our knowledge, this research marks the first attempt to create a massive Arabic altered news dataset and employ machine learning techniques to identify its characteristics.

The connection between a local property of a quantum system and a nonlocal property of the same system is a recurring theme in quantum mechanics. In this work, we investigate the relationship between a nonlocal property, known as Bell's inequality, and the state of a set of qubits. We examine how noise on a single qubit affects the violation of this inequality in various states, utilizing a simulation method that employs matrix product operators. We discovered that, for certain states, the violation of the inequality is highly sensitive to local noise on a single qubit, while for other states, the violation remains robust. These results suggest that certain states are more susceptible to certain types of noise and that the sensitivity can be determined by analyzing the Wigner function of the state.

Machine learning heavily relies on data availability, which is often limited due to high annotation costs or restricted access. Web scraping offers a potential solution to bypass these obstacles, but its effectiveness is hindered by the presence of diverse and complex web page content. This paper introduces a new machine learning framework that leverages reinforcement learning and web scraping to efficiently collect data from specific webpage areas. The proposed approach uses a tree-structured policy learning mechanism, enabling the efficient exploration of webpage regions and their hierarchical structure. The resulting system demonstrates superior performance in collecting data from specific regions, outperforming conventional web scraping methods based on interest function learning and baseline rule-based algorithms.

The proposed research aims to address the issue of event description diversity in NLP. We define an event description as an assertion about an object's change in property, such as "the dog is tired." To create a comprehensive framework for these descriptions, we need a dataset that includes multiple perspectives on the same event. However, current NLP datasets primarily consist of singular event descriptions, which limits their use in modeling event variation. To address this gap, we have developed a new dataset called OFEI, which comprises 1,200 English event descriptions, 1,800 French event descriptions, and 1,200 English pairs showing variation in event descriptions, along with corresponding human translations. We also present two research questions that will facilitate the development of event description variation models, which involve either providing a description for a given event or suggesting possible variations in event properties.

We've developed a new method to restore incomplete images using partial data, which works with images of any size and doesn't need complex calculations. Our approach uses a limited-subspace version of the weighted matrix decomposition technique in conjunction with a sparsifying transform, which helps us filter unwanted data. We've tested our method with images from various transforms, including the discrete Fourier, Curvelet, and Daubechies wavelet transforms, on both synthetic and real-world data, showing that it produces high-quality images in less than 0.1 seconds.

A cost-effective, wide-aperture metalens with a flat substrate can achieve broadband circularly polarized fields with a wide field of view, thanks to an innovative design. By utilizing a symmetric array of microstructures, this metalens produces a large, 0.8D focal length and a 30-degree wide field of view. Experimental results show that the metalens maintains a system efficiency exceeding 30% across a broad spectrum of 2-18 GHz, producing linearly and circularly polarized fields with a uniform intensity.

A novel plasma device featuring a unique combination of atmospheric pressure plasma streams and radio-frequency influence has been proposed for various industrial applications. This paper delves into the physics governing such a system via computational modeling, focusing specifically on the plasma dynamics within a device utilizing plasma streams generated by interdigitated electrodes. Using a two-dimensional, time-dependent fluid model of ion mobility, this study examines the plasma's behavior in response to changes in plasma stream speed, ionization intensity, and RF power. The results show that RF power significantly affects the plasma's behavior, leading to variations in ion and neutral species concentrations, species drift velocities, and electron and ion temperature levels. The findings also reveal that increasing RF power initially boosts electron temperature, and that the plasma's behavior is highly sensitive to the plasma stream speed. The proposed model provides a foundation for future research and development of this innovative plasma device.

This study examines the eikonal approximation of string-corrected black holes in d-dimensional spacetimes, focusing on quasi-normal modes within the eikonal limit. The investigation then explores the implications of these modes on the silhouette observed from a distant distance by an observer positioned at r=circumflex r, where circumflex r represents the circumference of the last stable orbit. The findings indicate that the silhouette exhibits a characteristic behavior under the eikonal approximation, such as a finite size silhouette at the innermost stable orbit, an infinite silhouette at the innermost stable orbit, and silhouettes that exhibit oscillatory behavior. The research also reveals that the higher-order string corrections have a significant impact on the silhouette's shape and size, particularly in the case of higher-dimensional black holes.

The data from high-precision pulsar timing arrays is being used to investigate the properties of extremely long-scale gravitational waves through the application of n-body simulations. In this study, the effectiveness of two distinct methods, namely the common-band approach and cross-correlation analysis, is being compared in terms of their ability to detect the stochastic gravitational wave background. The common-band approach involves filtering out the gravitational wave signal from pulsar time series by utilizing a specific template, while the cross-correlation analysis involves correlating the timing residuals of different pulsars without explicitly accounting for the gravitational wave signal. By employing n-body simulations, the common-band approach is able to accurately determine the amplitude spectrum of the gravitational wave background. On the other hand, the cross-correlation analysis is capable of providing the cross-spectral power of the gravitational wave background. By comparing the results obtained from these two approaches, it has been found that the common-band approach is capable of providing more accurate estimates of the amplitude spectrum of the gravitational wave background.

Geometrically uniform low-weight (GHW) codes, specifically those with a uniform weight distribution, serve as a valuable resource for constructing efficient MDS (maximum distance) generator matrices, thus benefiting MDS codes and related systems like rank metric codes. To achieve this, specific subsets of GHW codes are selected based on particular criteria. This research proposes new criteria for MDS matrix construction, derived from the properties of GHW codes. These criteria are applied to various examples of MDS matrices, and further investigation is conducted on the properties of MDS matrices with specific dimensions. Notably, this study establishes a connection between an MDS matrix's dimensions and the number of non-zero entries in its parity-check matrix.

We examine a class of truncated Toeplitz operators based on matrix-valued kernels that are sufficiently small outside a specific interval. Our research expands on prior work involving functions bounded within the relevant interval. We investigate the properties of these operators, including their commutators, and derive conditions for their boundedness and compactness. Furthermore, we develop a representation that links sufficient decay in a function to the boundedness of corresponding matrix-valued truncated Toeplitz operators. This representation serves as a generalization of the classical Hardy postcondition, under the assumption that the associated kernel is an L^2 function on the interval.

In a Bayesian framework, we examine the impact of individual observations on a sequence of binary trials. To achieve this, we utilize a modified version of the beta distribution as a prior for the true success rate and update its parameters based on each new observation. A key aspect is that the posterior distribution of the success rate serves as a regularized version of the beta distribution. By calculating the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the posterior and prior, we can quantify the effect of each new observation on the success rate prediction. Furthermore, we have derived the expected value of this influence and found that it is directly related to the new observation's outcome. Additionally, we have developed a predictive regression model that incorporates the success rate estimate as a key predictor, which enables us to calculate the variance in predictions for a given new observation. By utilizing the posterior update, we can determine the contribution of this variance resulting from the new observation itself.

In scenarios where an audio system's normal operation is suspected to be at risk due to anomalies, identifying such instances is crucial. However, most current anomaly detection methods rely on data from normal operating conditions, which is insufficient when dealing with real-world domain shifts. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach that leverages unsupervised dimensionality reduction using UMAP and UCB Estimators to detect anomalies in audio data from a target domain. By mapping audio features onto a lower-dimensional manifold, we can effectively identify abnormal patterns and utilize UCB Estimators to quantify the uncertainty of each data point, which is then employed for anomaly detection. Experimental results demonstrate the proposed method's effectiveness in detecting anomalies in audio data from target domains.

In the context of SU(N) fermions at millikelvin temperatures, unusual behavior is observed when repulsive interactions are present. At zero population, there is no symmetry breaking, whereas an N-fold degenerate ground state is observed in the presence of a non-zero population, even at weak repulsive interactions. This phenomenon leads to a set of distinct ground states, each with distinct properties, characterized by a specific symmetry group. The transition between these symmetric groups is abrupt and temperature insensitive, resulting from a complex interplay between the Fermi sea and symmetry breaking.

Our study involved analyzing 79 gamma-ray pulsars using multiple search algorithms within the Green and 2FGL catalogs. We employed three different methods: Gaussian mixture models, a novel thresholding algorithm called EnPass, and the stacking algorithm Stact, in conjunction with the Fermi Large Area Telescope (LAT) data. We combined the results from Gaussian mixture and EnPass to identify 27 pulsars showing significant stacking signals, of which 22 were previously known gamma-ray pulsars. We further refined the analysis by selecting 20 pulsars based on their flux rates and performing a more rigorous stacking analysis, ultimately revealing a 5.9σ detection. We also explored the relationship between pulsar luminosity and magnetic field strength, and found that the most luminous pulsars have magnetic field strengths exceeding 3.4 × 10^12 G. We also discovered that the most luminous pulsar candidate, J1836-1955, exhibits a magnetic field strength of 3.7 × 10^12 G, comparable to the most luminous pulsars in binary systems.

In the study of strongly correlated quantum Hall fluids at zero temperature, we have discovered numerous "magnetorotons" and found that their densities are controlled by specific energy constraints. Our research reveals that the energy of these constrained states is regulated by the sum of two fundamental quantum forces: the interaction between particles and the effect of confinement within narrow channels around the edge of the material. This understanding has allowed us to develop a universal theory that explains how the densities of these constrained states change in response to varying magnetic fields and, in turn, influences the properties of the quantum Hall fluids.

The Intense Energy Occurrences experiment, utilizing the same light beam employed by the Critical Heat Flux experiment, has been characterizing the statistical energy output of a high-pressure GE 1/4-14 water reactor coolant tube using a single photomultiplier. The light beam's parameters were established through mathematical fitting of the total energy released from a subcooled liquid-to-vapor transition of a pure substance. The fitted model accurately reproduces the total heat released, but a discrepancy is observed in the light intensity measured by the photomultiplier. The experiment's results are presented and discussed in the context of a theoretical model proposed by Clavero and Whitworth, which describes how intense events occur in a distributed manner.

The Cauchy problem for the truncated Boltzmann equation is investigated under minimal initial data conditions. A local-in-time solution is proven to exist, provided the initial density function, $f(x,t;1)$, has a sufficiently low $L^1$ norm. For certain truncated models, an improved solution with global well-posedness is established, provided the initial density function meets specific density and weight requirements. Notably, these requirements are less stringent than those of the Boltzmann equation. A particular case of the truncated equation, corresponding to a mixture of gas molecules with finite and infinite mass particles, is also examined.

The presence of mislabeled data in real-world training sets is a common phenomenon, which can significantly affect the performance of machine learning models. To address this challenge, we developed and evaluated a set of robust machine learning classifiers capable of withstanding the adverse effects of corrupted label data. These classifiers, which include a baseline model and two alternative approaches, were applied to a modified MNIST dataset containing 20% intentionally corrupted entries. The resilience of each classifier was assessed through a comparative analysis involving three key metrics: the minimum sample size required to achieve a pre-defined accuracy threshold, the accuracy in the presence of corrupted data, and the ability to accurately identify and discard faulty data while achieving high accuracy on the remaining clean data. Our findings revealed that the best-performing classifier, which employs a simple majority voting strategy on neighboring neighbors, significantly outperformed the baseline model in all three resilience metrics, even when subjected to random label noise.

This research focuses on finding automorphism groups and symmetries in cyclic orbit codes, starting with the identification of automorphism groups through low-degree polynomial factorization. We then investigate the automorphism groups of twisted orbit codes and its connection to a specific field characteristic, before developing a method to determine the symmetries of orbit codes. The byproduct of this process yields the automorphism groups of twisted orbit codes. The study also explores connections between the groups of automorphisms, the semi-linear automorphism groups, and the Galois groups to derive the semi-linear automorphism groups of orbit codes over a specific transcendence degree. The results also enable us to determine the automorphism groups of certain special orbit codes.

The binary system K2-AT with its late A-type component (F9-10V) is a star located near the turnoff point in the 4 billion-year-old open cluster M67. By analyzing the star's rotation, rotation period, and rotation velocity, researchers have found that it exhibits characteristics of slow rotation for a star of its type. Furthermore, the star's radius, mass, and surface gravity have been determined using photometric data from K2 and Gaia EDR3, which indicate that the star is significantly more massive than expected for a cluster member. This, combined with the star's low space velocity, suggests that K2-AT is likely a long-period binary system.

We are examining the well-known Schrödinger operator $L_c = -I(d/dx)/dx + cx^\alpha$, where c is a complex number and α is a non-negative real number. The complex-valued eigenfunctions $\varphi_z(x)$ are defined by the integral kernel $K_c(x,y) = c\Gamma(\alpha+1)/(\4\pi \cdot y^\alpha)$. The kernel $K_c(x,y)$ has a non-negative imaginary part when α is greater than 1, and this leads to the sufficiency of $\varphi_z^2(x)$ as a probability measure for the given interval $[0,a]$. Specifically, for complex eigenvalues $z = r(\cos \theta + i \sin \theta)$, where $r$ is real and $\theta$ is real, we prove that the eigenfunction $\varphi_z(x) = \varphi_0(x) \cdot r^{1/2} \cdot \cos (\theta + \pi/4) \cdot \cosh (r \theta/2 x^\alpha)$. The function $\varphi_0(x) = \cosh (\pi/2 x^\alpha)$ is the eigenfunction corresponding to the real eigenvalue $z_0 = 1$ (i.e., $c = 1$).

A new, modified version of the SPH method, specifically designed for hydrodynamic applications, is proposed. The modification involves a conservative approach that utilizes density-dependent smoothing lengths. To achieve this, an innovative method is employed to determine the smoothing length, which enables the SPH equations to meet the continuity equation exactly. As a result, the SPH method requires minimal artificial volume correction and accurate volume estimation. Additionally, the modified method incorporates a novel technique for estimating node averages, which involves a combination of the average density and the average density-weighted smoothing length. This technique enables the method to be conservative and exact, both in one and two-dimensional cases. The modified SPH method is demonstrated to be accurate and efficient in a variety of applications, including shockwave propagation, Sod's shock-tube, Noh's problem, and anisotropic Riemann problem simulations.

The primary objective of Spectral Super-Enhancement is to generate a high-quality spectrum from a low-resolution image, which is a complex task. The existing methods primarily focus on analyzing the image's content and predicting the spectrum through a complex mapping. However, these methods are hindered by the inherent limitations of traditional convolutional networks that can only capture a limited range of spatial frequencies. This paper presents a new neural network architecture called the Pixel-sensitive Deep Function-blend Network (P-DFNet) for Spectral Super-Enhancement. The P-DFNet model consists of two key components: a Deep Function-blend Network (DFNet) and a Pixel-sensitive Refinement Network (PRNet). The DFNet is a convolutional neural network that utilizes a single network to predict the spectrum through a mapping function. This network is then combined with a pixel-sensitive refinement network, which refines the spectrum by analyzing the image's content and local spectral patterns. The proposed P-DFNet model is then further enhanced through the use of a spatial attention module and a wavelet-based spectral fusion module. The proposed P-DFNet model is evaluated using a new dataset and compared with the existing state-of-the-art methods. The results show that the proposed P-DFNet model achieves a significant improvement in spectral enhancement with a peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) of 35.11 dB and a structural similarity index (SSIM) of 0.97, outperforming the existing state

In the era of big data, effectively managing data in the field on a large scale poses significant challenges, particularly when utilizing manual data labeling, which is time-consuming and costly. Although automated data labeling using GPS and sensor technology provides an efficient solution, its accuracy is often compromised by GPS limitations. One potential solution to this problem is the use of object geotagging, which has been shown to be effective in small-scale scenarios. However, this approach is limited by the need for manual object detection, which hinders its application to complex field environments. To overcome this limitation, we propose a context-aware object geotagging system that leverages deep learning techniques to detect objects in complex settings.

The removal of dams in foreign dams is a pressing global issue, primarily due to their removals in developing countries, where they were constructed for agricultural purposes but are now considered obstacles to food security and local livelihoods. The problem lies in that many dams were built without detailed records of their construction, rendering it difficult to pinpoint which dams need to be removed. The dam removal community utilizes remote satellite imagery to monitor dam reservoirs and track water level fluctuations, an approach that has been employed in this research. A novel metric, customised to capture the dynamic characteristics of the reservoirs, has been proposed, and its effectiveness has been demonstrated through case studies. The study highlights the potential of this approach in enabling non-expert users to identify water level changes and thereby locate dams that are ready for removal, an essential step towards addressing a critical challenge in dam removal.

A Quantized Finite State (QFS) encoder and decoder were developed using zone-based quantization, where zones are defined by a state machine, to facilitate efficient quantization of continuous signals into digital formats. In this work, we investigate the characteristics of Frenet-Sinuoid (FS) zones, which are based on a specific type of curve in the 2-dimensional state space of the system. These curves are derived from the movements of a vehicle with a constant speed and a turning radius. These zones are found to be elliptical shapes in the parameter space of the state machine. A theoretical analysis of the FS-zone was conducted, and it was found that the elliptical shape of the zone changes with different states of the system.

The "point-of-attraction" (POA) refers to the store aisle where a customer has a higher likelihood to make a purchase after sampling a product. Accurately forecasting POAs for online orders of non-perishable items is crucial for optimizing store layouts, stock management, and delivery routes. We introduce an innovative approach that leverages customer data, including text and image analysis, to improve accuracy. Our data includes 1.7M customer orders, 1.3M product reviews, and 1.1M product images, all sourced from a large online retailer. We develop a deep learning model that combines text and image features to predict a customer's primary point-of-interest and then identify the most likely POA for the ordered product. We compare the performance of this multi-modal deep learning model to existing methods using the same dataset and find that it significantly outperforms them.

The purpose of quarterly earnings calls involving publicly traded companies is to provide investors with an in-depth understanding of their financial performance, facilitating the incorporation of crucial information into the market. Despite the significance of call transcripts in reflecting a company's progress, there is a knowledge gap with regard to how these transcripts influence share price fluctuations. This study aims to address this gap by examining the relationship between content and market reactions to quarterly earnings calls, with a focus on the impact of management's positive or negative comments regarding key financial aspects, such as revenue and profitability.

The placement of sensors in a network is a key issue in sensor planning, requiring consideration of the required sensor number, placement location, and other factors such as sensor coverage area, sensor diversity, and sensor connectivity. Existing research has focused on optimizing uniform coverage of large areas or diverse sensor activation rates but has not simultaneously addressed all these factors. This paper proposes a novel approach to sensor planning that considers all these factors under the assumption of uniform node density and a fixed communication radius. The proposed method uses Voronoi diagrams and a new distance metric to minimize sensor activation distances and offers two algorithms: one that optimizes sensor activation with uniform node density and another that optimizes diversity. Experimental results indicate that the proposed methods significantly outperform existing approaches in terms of diversity, connectivity, and a new metric that combines coverage, diversity, and connectivity.

A novel quantum algorithm has been developed to identify an eigenstate of a problem using a specific set of polynomials, which can be efficiently evaluated. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through simulations of a quantum system, specifically a quantum version of a linear system, to resolve a quantum equivalent of a linear problem. The results show that this method can achieve an exponential reduction in required samples, compared to a classical approach, while requiring a fixed preprocessing time independent of the circuit depth.

We examine compact $F$-gauged infant skyrmions within a nonlinear medium, and in our model, the medium's internal energy is represented by a single function that generalizes the well-known O(3) $\times$ O(2) model. The gauge field affects the medium's energy in a way that depends on the gauge's magnetic field. Our non-linear model generalizes the theory of compact $F$-gauged infant skyrmions, which are formed from the condensation of a low-energy component of a two-component scalar field. The gauge field in this model interacts with the non-linear medium in a way that depends on the gauge's magnetic field. Our analysis focuses on the static properties of these $F$-gauged infant skyrmions, which we find can exist in two forms, a monopole and a dyon. The monopole has a core that is magnetically charged and the dyon has a core that is a combination of a magnetic and electric charge. Our model also shows that the monopole and dyon have a finite size, which is a result of a non-linear effect. The non-linear effect also leads to the monopole and dyon having a finite size, which is a result of a non-linear effect.
