This thesis explores the phenomenon of novel interactions, which cannot be explained by the Standard Model and seeks to establish a limit on their existence. A new interaction framework, known as the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT), is employed to analyze data from past and upcoming particle colliders. SMEFT aims to describe the behavior of particles by accounting for small variations from the Standard Model's equations. A specific subset of SMEFT operators known as "H-4" is used in this analysis to investigate the interactions between the Higgs boson and a pair of Standard Model particles. These operators have the potential to explain the discrepancy in the measurement of the Higgs boson's mass and the data from its production. A global fit of this analysis, which combines data from several colliders, has established a 95% confidence level limit on the H-4 interactions at four-fermion and four-boson vertices. These results are found to be consistent with the current understanding of these interactions and provide a significant improvement over previous estimates.

A rotating super-polished diamond nanopillar with a diameter of 650 nm and a height of 3 microns was created through the use of chemical vapor deposition. We observed an initial gyroscope bias of less than 3 degrees per second per Gauss after coating the diamond with nitrogen-vacancy centers and superparamagnetic nanogranules, demonstrating its potential as a gyroscope based on its small size. By increasing the applied magnetic field to 1 Tesla, the diamond's gyroscope bias was reduced to less than 0.06 degrees per second per Gauss.

The development of complete-cell models has accelerated over the past decade, thanks to advancements in experimental techniques, computational power, and theoretical understanding. As a result, it is now feasible to create comprehensive models of biological cells and simulate them from start to finish, accounting for all processes and transport within the cell. In this review, we outline the core elements and progress in this rapidly evolving field, which involves simulating the entire cell to understand how it generates electrical activity. We will specifically focus on the challenges of simulating the plasma membrane, the cytoplasm, the intracellular fluid, the mitochondria, the endoplasmic reticulum, the lipid membranes, the transport mechanisms, the actin and myosin cytoskeleton, and the muscle fibers. We will also discuss the difficulties of modeling the cell's structure and behavior at varying scales, the integration of multiple models, the implementation of numerical methods, and the implementation of software tools. We will provide an overview of the current state of the field, the techniques and their limitations, and offer suggestions for future directions.

This paper explores the concept of mobile multi-view object visual search, which enables users to conduct a search for a target object by interacting with multiple views of surrounding objects using their smartphone camera. The research aims to develop a real-time visual tracking system that can accurately match objects and provide the correct view of the target within a limited time frame of 5 seconds. A novel tracking approach is proposed, employing a combination of a feature-based object matching algorithm and a 3D model-based inference technique. Experimental results using a custom dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

In the realm of Epileptic Seizure Detection using EEG data, hyperdimensional computing has shown potential as a robust learning method, offering benefits such as noise resilience and robustness to sensor malfunctions. This research aims to enhance the performance of hyperdimensional computing by exploring various strategies, including the selection of input features, optimization of hyperdimensional space representation, and the use of hyperdimensional computing for both feature extraction and regression tasks. By employing these techniques, we have achieved a 3.6% increase in classification accuracy compared to standard approaches, ultimately resulting in a classification accuracy of 98.6% on a test dataset.

Future observations of gravitational waves from binary black holes are anticipated to offer a precise measurement of the universe's expansion rate at late time, thereby enabling insight into the universe's evolution. This capability will stem from utilizing the stationary nature of gravitational waves as cosmological probes, often referred to as dark gravitational wave standard sirens. By combining the detection of gravitational waves with astronomical observations of the Hubble constant, it is possible to derive constraints on the universe's expansion rate. This can be achieved through the use of a network of space-based gravitational wave detectors, which will be able to pinpoint the locations of the sources involved. A recent study has utilized a deci-hertz gravitational wave detector to simulate the detection of 1000 binary black holes and determined the potential for constraining the Hubble constant. The analysis revealed that the uncertainty in measuring the Hubble constant is approximately 1% when the sources are detected with an accuracy of 0.1%. Furthermore, it is projected that the first-generation Deci-hertz Extreme Physics Observatory will be capable of constraining the Hubble constant to within 2% in the first year of operation.

We introduce a significantly expanded, multilingual version of the corpus QALD-9, specifically designed for question-answering using DBpedia and Wikidata. This enhanced version, QALD-9-plus, comprises responses from twelve languages, nine more than the original, and is characterized by a natural, conversational tone. Unlike QALD-9, the expanded version, qald-9-plus, is grounded in the interpretation of DBpedia and Wikidata by native speakers. A total of 1,500 inquiries and corresponding answers, divided into three categories: DBpedia-only, Wikidata-only, and cross-domain, are included in the corpus. Additionally, a standardized schema for the corpus's metadata is presented, and a detailed discussion of the challenges encountered in creating a multilingual, naturally interpreted corpus is provided.

The paper proposes an innovative data re-sampling and re-labeling technique, named Executive Function framework, to enhance the quality of understanding from initial re-sampling attempts. By analyzing the primary insights from each attempt using a specialized summarization method, the framework pinpoints the most valuable information to prioritize future re-sampling efforts. Utilizing a hypothetical medical case study, the authors demonstrate that their framework significantly improves the accuracy of diagnostic findings, surpassing existing re-sampling and re-labeling approaches.

A new, task-specific model has been proposed that detects biases within pre-trained self-supervised models when applied to medical imaging data, highlighting a concern that these models often learn from non-medical features present in images, like skin tones, patient equipment, and clothing. Unlike traditional computer vision bias detection that relies on external metrics, this model uses in-house signal processing techniques to identify bias caused by non-medical attributes in medical images, enabling the model to improve medical imaging data processing and reduce external bias influence.

This research focuses on the issue of noisy labels in the application of metric learning, particularly self-supervised learning, where learning is hindered by incorrect labels. To resolve this problem, we developed a novel loss function called proxy-anchor loss (PAL). PAL is based on the idea of leveraging a separate, noise-free proxy-anchor space, where positive and negative pairs can be accurately identified. To achieve this, we use a separate neural network to create a clean representation of samples, which we call the sleek network. We then pair the original samples with their clean counterparts using the proxy-anchor loss, enabling the learning of robust representations that are resistant to noisy labels. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of PAL in the presence of both synthetic and real-world noisy labels.

The 2-point density gradient-adjusted correlation function, an extension of the traditional 2-point correlation function, incorporates density gradients to address bias issues. By doing so, it can capture higher-order interactions like those exhibited by halo halos, which are strongly dependent on local density. By focusing on subhalos, this approach can provide insights into cosmology, unaffected by the limitations of 2-point functions. By applying this method to N-body simulations, researchers found that the LGTCF is an effective measure of cosmological parameters. A key advantage of this method is its reduced computational demands and dependence on resolution, which can make it a viable alternative to traditional 2-point functions.

A theoretical framework for understanding topological SO(5) superconductivity has been developed using an integrable model. By applying an SU(5) Hamiltonian to a system with a superconductor and a conventional 2D metal, researchers were able to study the behavior of the superconducting state. They found a unique way to stabilize a topological Fulde-Ferrell-Larkin-Ovchinnikov phase, where superconductivity coexists with specific types of chiral normal states. These states are characterized by quasiparticles with opposite spin and charge polarizations.

Researchers have developed and tested a new type of MAPD category avalanche avalanche detector. This innovative detector leverages a 25$\mu$m x 25$\mu$m x 100$\mu$m MAPD crystal, paired with a segmented photodetector consisting of 8 narrow PMTs, enabling the simultaneous measurement of signal charge and light yield. The detector's performance was assessed by analyzing the distribution of minimal ionizing photons across the photodetector's facets. As a result, the signal charge and light yield were found to be distinct for 5.75 MeV $\alpha$-particles across the 4 facets with the lowest resolution.

This research explores the properties of a graded algebra when its partial genera are examined, specifically for how they relate to the Gorenstein algebra concept introduced by Herzog and Trung in [H. T. Eide, V. H. Le, V. L. Lorenz, and S. O. Reiten, Nagoya Math. Journal 99 (2018), 177-210]. We demonstrate that for a Cohen-Macaulay algebra, its partial genera converge to a specific value at infinity. Furthermore, if the algebra is Gorenstein, then it is also F-Rat, providing a key implication of the Cohen-Macaulay condition in this context.

A specific type of magnetic material known as Aurivillius oxides holds significant potential for magnetic storage and data processing due to their unique properties. By applying pressure, the magnetic behavior of these oxides can be adjusted. A recent study focused on a particular Aurivillius oxide, Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$, and observed a change in its magnetic properties when subjected to high pressures. The goal of this research was to understand this transformation by examining the changes in the magnetic dynamics and spin-lattice interactions. To do this, the researchers used neutron scattering experiments on the Atomic Energy Corporation facility's instrument NECDI, which utilizes a time-of-flight technique to gather data. The results showed that the magnetic behavior of Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ changes significantly at pressures above 1.2 GPa, with a particular phase boundary at 1.4 GPa. The data also indicated that the spin-lattice interactions in the oxide are influenced by the applied pressure, which may be useful for controlling the magnetic behavior of this type of material.

A new statistical method has been developed to evaluate and compare the costs incurred by financial brokers as a result of their trading strategies. The approach is applied to compare the costs of two trading algorithms used by brokers, specifically Charles Schwab's LC Trade and Turbo Broker, to execute stock trades. The study found that Turbo Broker, offered by both Charles Schwab and E*TRADE, incurs significantly higher costs than LC Trade on a per-trade basis.

We've developed a novel add-drop optomechanical cavity with a novel design that allows for a wide range of completely adjustable operation within a specific operating range, overcoming a limitation of conventional add-drop designs which often require a fixed frequency range. This system can operate independently of resonance frequencies and can be controlled through precise tuning, leveraging the interaction between two coupled cavities and a mechanical mode to enable a wide range of applications.

The COVID-19 pandemic has brought to light the significance of community health and self-care, particularly in underserved areas. In response to this focus, various digital platforms have emerged to disseminate essential information on community health, offering a unique opportunity to analyze the impact of online content. This work aims to assess the effectiveness of these pandemic-related online resources in enhancing community health, leveraging the extensive web resources available. By developing a scalable automated system to extract public health information from the web, we aim to provide actionable insights to stakeholders, such as health organizations and the public.

The vast amount of image data being generated every day demands efficient storage solutions. To address this need, lossless image compression methods have gained significant interest, especially those that offer high compression ratios without sacrificing image quality. One notable method is the Progressive Image Coding (PILC) framework, which uses a neural network to achieve efficient compression. In this work, we present a novel PILC framework, where we optimize the network architecture to be GPU-friendly and refined the network's loss function. Our experimental results demonstrate that our approach can achieve a higher compression ratio and quality compared to existing PILC frameworks, outperforming it on the ImageNet dataset. Furthermore, our implementation on the TITAN X GPU allows us to achieve a high compression ratio of 1.77 bits per pixel with a processing speed of 165 FPS, making it a practical solution for large-scale image data storage.

The LHCb experiment has made the initial observation of the $B^{+}\to D_{s}^{+}K^{+}K^{-}$ decay and measured its branching fraction relative to the $B^{+}\to D_{s}^{+}\pi^{+}K^{-}$ decay flow. Utilizing a dataset with an integrated luminosity of 3.0 fb$^{-1}$ in the 7 and 8 TeV $pp$ collision energy from LHCb, the experiment found $B^{+}\to D_{s}^{+}K^{+}K^{-}$ decay rate to be $0.142 \pm 0.010 \pm 0.004 \times 10^{-6}$ with significance exceeding 7 standard deviations. Further, the same analysis revealed the $B^{+}\to D_{s}^{+}\phi$ decay's non-existence, with upper limit of branching fraction at 3.9 standard deviations beyond probability expectation.

The sensitivity of optimal solutions to perturbations in the cost function is a long-standing concern in the field of optimal transport, which is a fundamental concept in probability theory. This study aims to address this issue by exploring the robustness of such solutions to small changes in the underlying data through the lens of functional analysis and game theory. We establish that the set of optimal coupling solutions is an infinitely differentiable function of the cost function, and we investigate the sensitivity of the optimal coupling cost in the context of a random cost function, deriving an expression for its variance. We also examine the robustness of the optimal cost in the context of a game between two players, and we show that an optimal coupling can be constructed by combining optimal couplings of smaller problems. Furthermore, we provide a sufficient condition for robustness in the context of a general class of problems, and we apply our results to a specific example of a random cost function, deriving an explicit formula for the optimal cost.

In order to optimize performance in complex tasks, AI agents must be able to collaborate with each other, but current models of human decision-making are limited in their ability to predict and explain the behavior of cooperative AI teammates. A new model has been proposed that combines human decision-making theories with machine learning techniques to better predict how humans choose the most effective strategy in cooperative tasks. This model was tested using data from a simulated game and showed that it outperforms other models in most cases. Furthermore, the model was used to train AI teammates that use a new strategy called the Unique Action Model (UAM), which has been shown to be more effective than traditional strategies.

The unification of multiple forces, especially electromagnetism and the standard model strong force, is significantly enhanced when they are part of a larger gauge symmetry group. Introducing a basic supersymmetric model allows for a comprehensive analysis of both the model's beauty and its robustness. The addition of supersymmetry simplifies the explanation of the strong force, proposing a connection between quarks and gluons. As a result, the mass of the Higgs boson, the top quark's mass, and the observed value of the strong force coupling constant are all predicted within this model. Furthermore, the top quark's mass and the strong force coupling constant serve as indicators of the supersymmetry breaking scale, indicating that the breaking scale must be around 2 to 3 times the electroweak scale. The model's robustness is examined through its sensitivity to variations in the Higgs boson's mass, the top quark's mass, and the strong force coupling constant.

To enhance human-complimentary visualization capabilities, it's crucial to comprehend how humans contribute to the loop. Investigating how experts from various fields perform on visualization tasks can provide valuable insights. To address this knowledge gap, we conducted a study with 1,142 participants from diverse fields to compare their performance in three tasks: interactive visualization exploration, map navigation, and 3D object tracking. Our results indicate that experts outperform non-experts in all tasks, and that variations in professional expertise do not necessarily correlate with performance in visualization tasks. These findings highlight the significance of developing spatial and visual skills for experts to effectively interact with visualizations and perform tasks, and suggest that interactive visualization design should prioritize these skills.

We propose a novel loop construct, denoted as $\mathsf{Cloop}$, that facilitates reasoning about intricate quantified statements. This can be achieved by treating a loop as a defined function and subsequently expressing it as a propositional formula, allowing for efficient automated reasoning via satisfiability solvers. Notably, we establish that the base propositional fragment encompassing $\mathsf{Cloop}$ is decidable. Furthermore, we demonstrate the potential of $\mathsf{Cloop}$ in enhancing inductive theorem proving, particularly when applied within an E-matching framework that leverages $\mathsf{Cloop}$ to generate function definitions from loop invariants, thus facilitating complete automation of intricate inductive proofs involving multiple induction schemes.

We propose a novel framework for graph extraction, referred to as alignment-based graph extraction, which involves aligning two separate models against a common set of training data. By maximizing the likelihood of both models aligning with their training data simultaneously, our framework effectively extracts the underlying structural relationships between their latent representations. Our method outperforms traditional self-supervised contrastive contrastive contrastive learning approaches by introducing an additional alignment mechanism that leverages the entire training set, rather than isolating individual samples. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves superior results in graph representation learning and graph reconstruction tasks.

Deep learning models are commonly used in Natural Language Processing (NLP) 
to improve the efficiency of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) learning. This 
consists of techniques like momentum, NAG, LSTM, and Adam. These methods have 
been successful in NLP but have not been as widely applied in Physics-Informed 
Neural Networks (PINNs), which primarily use unsupervised methods like LSTM and 
the Euler method. Unlike NLP, PINN's focus on short-term problems may limit its 
applicability to complex, long-term transient dynamics. This paper introduces a 
new framework that incorporates NLP-based methods into PINN, allowing for the 
simulation of transient dynamics.

This research focuses on developing algorithms to fairly divide resources among multiple parties with varying demands, utilizing linear programming methods inspired by max-flow principles. We introduce a new approach for allocating shared resources like pipelines, and demonstrate its value in solving more complex problems like power distribution, which is particularly relevant in micro-grids and renewable energy systems. By providing a framework to address multiple demand scenarios with optimal resource utilization, our solution enhances the effectiveness of existing linear programming methods for distributing resources fairly.

The task of coreference resolution is particularly demanding when dealing with a substantial number of entities and connections within them. Datasets that focus on contentious topics and events, such as controversies surrounding vaccination or immigration, pose additional challenges due to the prevalence of ambiguous references and limited information available on specific entities. We introduce a new dataset, ContenTo, which encompasses 10,000 instances of coreference resolution, covering two contentious topics and utilizes a unique 'coreference occurrence' approach to identify and link relevant text segments. This approach allows for the creation of a comprehensive graph illustrating relationships between entities and connections over time. Experimental results demonstrate that our dataset and approach lead to more accurate and detailed representations of contentious topics, surpassing previous work in relevance and yielding improved performance in 90.1% of cases.

We suggest a comprehensive classification system for constraints in Complementarity Knapsack problems. Our proposal involves dividing the constraints into three categories: those that can be easily solved within polynomial time, those that mark the boundary between tractable and intractable cases, and those that result in intractable solutions. The classification is based on the use of surjective complementarity, a concept introduced in a recent study. Our system offers a clear distinction from previous attempts at classification, particularly for the tractable cases. The proposed framework is also applicable to a broader range of Complementarity problems.

This paper establishes the concept of generalized $(m, n)$-Jordan derivations and centralizers. We confirm that every $n\times n$ matrix, which is both a $(1, n)$ and $(2, n)$ Jordan derivation, is nilpotent. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a semiprime algebra with a finite Jordan derivation is also a Jordan derivation. If a semiprime algebra possesses a finite Jordan centralizer, it must be a derivation. These findings build on previous work by Lu and several other authors. We also examine the properties of generalized $(m, n)$-Jordan centralizers in $n\times n$ matrices, showing that a matrix with a finite Jordan centralizer property cannot be an algebra of this type.

We revisit Weinberg's approach to determining the most general low-energy Lagrangian
in a decoupling scenario, where a heavy particle couples to a light one.  It is established
that the Lagrangian's coefficients are restricted to two at most, with each corresponding
to a different helicity, based on the heavy particle.  Although this concept was initially
introduced in the 1980s, a clear and straightforward explanation for it in the context of
Weinberg's approach did not exist until now.  By analyzing the problem from a new angle,
we demonstrate that Weinberg's approach yields the two-parameter result, and show that
each parameter corresponds to a specific helicity, as initially proposed.  This method
involves expanding the heavy particle's propagator in terms of the light particle's momentum,
and then determining the most general form of the effective action.  It is noteworthy that
the most general form of the effective action also corresponds to the most general form
of the heavy particle's propagator.

The transversal group of a nonlinear transformation is a more comprehensive concept than its linear counterpart and encompasses the transversal of linear maps. This group plays a significant role in the study of Favard length. Specifically, we demonstrate that the transversal group of a Lebesgue-continuous mapping is zero if and only if the mapping has a Cantor past. Moreover, we prove that the transversal group decreases as the dimension increases, leading to the conclusion that the Favard length of a Lebesgue-continuous mapping is zero if it exceeds a specific dimension, which is theoretically infinite.

This study introduces a groundbreaking approach to directed policy search, which is a model-free method utilizing a highly efficient, data-driven algorithm to swiftly locate the best policy under specified performance constraints. The core innovation lies in a novel policy search method that combines a robust version of the tube-maximizing model predictive control (MPC) algorithm to ensure constraint satisfaction. The proposed method leverages the ability of the tube algorithm to convert the continuous policy search problem into a discrete one, thereby enabling the use of a discrete policy search algorithm to find the optimal policy within a short timeframe. The proposed method is capable of guaranteeing both the feasibility and constraint satisfaction of the search process. Furthermore, the proposed method is demonstrated to significantly outperform alternative approaches in terms of search efficiency.

The semiclassical theory of electronic transport, specifically the Berry phase effect, has been recognized as the primary cause of the anomalous Hall effect. In this study, we observed an unexpected third-order anomalous Hall resistance in a single InSb quantum wire under specific conditions of strong magnetic fields and certain energy levels. Utilizing the generalized semiclassical theory, we successfully predicted and explained this phenomenon. Notably, this third-order anomalous Hall effect is distinct from the conventional Hall effect and is influenced by the intrinsic properties of InSb, which sets it apart from other quantum anomalous Hall systems.

The task of comparing multiple call graphs at once is crucial for identifying similarities and anomalies in software, with real-world applications in security, testing, and maintenance. However, call graphs contain numerous elements that interact in complex ways, making direct comparison between multiple graphs highly impractical. Therefore, a new method has been developed to represent the overall structure of call graphs using a single numerical vector, in a way that captures the most essential patterns and relationships. By utilizing a novel algorithm to generate these vectors, it is possible to compare multiple call graphs using various machine learning techniques, with significant improvements in efficiency and scalability.

A widely used benchmark for evaluating language models, the 1 Billion Word dataset, has a fundamental flaw: it contains substantial errors in its label formatting, with words missing, mislabeled and in some cases, even from different languages. Our research reveals that correcting just 1% of these errors can lead to a significant, 10%, decrease in model performance, highlighting the need for a comprehensive review of data processing procedures before relying on large datasets to assess language model performance.

High-resolution observations of solar flares reveal the generation of radio waves at GHz frequencies from the flare current layer, which is crucial for understanding the physical processes involved. Using advanced particle-in-cell simulations, we demonstrate that the emission of radio waves is closely linked to the oscillations of magnetic field lines and plasma particles within the flare current layer. We find that the oscillations are influenced by the magnetic field strength and density of the ambient plasma, which can lead to the formation of quasi-periodic oscillations in the emitted radiation, allowing researchers to infer key parameters of the flare coronal magnetic field and the initial phase of high-energy accelerated particles.

The anomaly detection problem is a complex research area in machine learning, 
with various applications across different sectors. A new approach to tackle 
the anomaly detection challenge is presented in this research. A novel 
contrary multi-scale anomaly identification technique is proposed, which is 
inspired by the human brain's ability to detect anomalies. This technique 
can detect anomalies of different types and scales. It is capable of detecting 
both the anomalies that significantly deviate from the average pattern and those 
that slightly deviate from it. This technique is particularly useful in industrial 
quality evaluation where it can be used to detect defects in patterns. 

Furthermore, the proposed technique is able to identify defects that are 
difficult to detect using traditional methods, including small and subtle ones. 
Additionally, the proposed technique is efficient in terms of computational 
resources, making it suitable for real-time applications. Experimental results 
on multiple industrial quality datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the 
proposed technique in anomaly detection.

We investigate the $H^s$ well-posedness threshold for the KP-I equation with dispersion-generalized coefficients in the periodic domain. The model is characterized by the coefficients $\beta_j$ satisfying the condition $|\beta_j| \lesssim j^{-\sigma}$ with a fixed parameter $0 < \sigma \leq 1$. We demonstrate that the KP-I equation with these coefficients exhibits the same well-posedness behavior as the KP-I equation with constant coefficients, specifically that the model is globally well-posed in the subcritical range $s > 5/2$ and globally well-posed in the critical range $s=3$. Moreover, we show that the model is ill-posed when $s<3$.

Kramers' degeneracy is a fundamental concept in quantum systems that has been extensively researched, particularly in systems with broken time-reversal symmetry like ferromagnetic materials. However, this article presents a new perspective on KDG by demonstrating its breach and subsequent restoration in open many-body quantum systems. Our research reveals that when a system's internal symmetry is compromised, KDG is broken, but introducing a time-reversal-invariant bath can restore it. Conversely, a non-degenerate bath can also lead to its restoration. Our findings have significant implications for research in quantum systems, particularly in designing more effective quantum heat engines and resolving decoherence issues in quantum coherence.

In highly-mobile environments with many users, predicting future downlink channel state information (CSI) responses becomes increasingly important, enabling accurate filtering and enhancing system performance. A new approach called D-OFDM utilizes past CSI data in predicting current channel conditions. The method is further improved in this paper to account for user mobility through the introduction of a novel, time-frequency block-based channel model. The model allows for a more efficient and precise CSI prediction by considering a larger spatial-temporal area, thus reducing the need for a large number of base stations. The performance of this approach is demonstrated using a custom simulator that takes into account the specific characteristics of the channel and environment.

A novel statistical approach is introduced to estimate the region with minimal disparity in comparison to a common method grounded in the Gaussian Mixture Model. The proposed method leverages the Beta Kernel Density Estimation to evaluate the cost associated with different sub-regions within a dataset. To achieve optimal results, the proposed method selects the sub-region exhibiting the lowest estimated cost, thereby demonstrating superior adaptability compared to GMME. The proposed method exhibits enhanced robustness in handling datasets with anomalous data points. Furthermore, the proposed method facilitates the identification of clusters within a dataset. To validate the proposed method, the proposed method was put to test on both artificially generated and real-world datasets.

We investigate the scaling limits of the Szegö kernel on Grauert cylinders, which are sets defined as the zero set of holomorphic functions within a specific convex body in n-dimensional complex space, given that the convex body is strictly convex and the number of dimensions n is at least two.   We derive these scaling limits from a more general result about the asymptotic behavior of the Szegö kernel on Grauert cylinders, which describes the kernel's magnitude in relation to a specific distance measure. This general result is established through a combination of a variational principle and a comparison principle.

Renaming rows and columns of a data matrix to produce an inverse n-dimensional line chart is a key challenge addressed by the research. Two methods are proposed to accomplish this task: a modified approach, MARINLINGA, and an updated version of Roussopoulos's method. Both techniques are compared based on computational complexity, with MARINLINGA exhibiting a time efficiency advantage over Roussopoulos's method.

In the category of vector spaces, a certain module structure can be established from a semigroup of endomorphisms. The topology defined by this structure mirrors the Zariski topology if the vector space is considered to be of finite dimension. A mathematical conjecture has been proposed to extend this principle to arbitrary rings, and we present a proof that this conjecture holds for certain rings. The outcome of our proof demonstrates that this topological structure is equivalent to the Zariski topology for specific types of rings. The underlying idea of our proof relies on an existing theorem by Enochs and Mateus.

To maintain software quality, developers should adhere to the principle of keeping codebloat to a minimum, as excessive code can hinder performance and conceal bugs. This research project investigates how Java project JAR files grow in size over time, with a focus on specific components such as class files, resource files, and other libraries contained within. The study found that certain types of classes, like enums and classes with no parent class, tend to have their sizes artificially inflated over time due to the inclusion of referenced JAR files in the compilation process, often caused by unanticipated interactions with other libraries.

The biphoton source, a cutting-edge tool in quantum chemistry, has the potential to efficiently synthesize complex molecules through innovative methods. However, the intricate relationships between the multiple fields it produces hinder the process, resulting in reduced productivity. To address this challenge, we developed a novel approach that utilizes intertwined biphoton sources to create a controlled environment, effectively mitigating the detrimental effects of these interactions. Our research demonstrates that this method enhances the synthesis yield by leveraging the opposing effects of these fields. To further optimize the process, we introduced a new metric, the incompatibility of chains, to create a more efficient regulatory system. Our study examines the effects of this incompatibility on the system's performance, highlighting areas of improvement for future research.

We examine a challenging type of multistage optimization problem known as distributionally resilient optimization, which requires meeting interdependent long-term constraints at each stage on a limited resource, such as energy, while an adversary tries to disrupt the plan. This problem is particularly challenging because it involves complex probabilistic and multistep optimization, which makes it difficult to solve exactly. To address this challenge, we propose a novel approximation method that uses a limited set of scenario paths to optimize each stage on a given horizon, called a scenario horizon. This approach is efficient in terms of computational complexity and adapts well to changes in the scenario path discrepancy measure.

Research on predicting actions in videos has gained momentum in recent years,
driven by the need to anticipate future frames based on the current video frame.
Existing methods primarily utilize long short-term memory networks to model the
temporal dynamics within videos, but they often fail to capture the nuanced,
sequential nature of human actions, which tend to exhibit varying levels of difficulty.
To address this limitation, we introduce a new framework that leverages an
Recurrent Feature Map, which incorporates an improved feature mapping mechanism
that utilizes the radial basis function kernel to capture complex, sequential patterns.
This approach enables the framework to learn and analyze complex, long-term dependencies
within videos, ultimately resulting in enhanced action prediction capabilities.
Our experiments demonstrate the superiority of our proposed method over competing
approaches in terms of action prediction accuracy on the action recognition benchmark.

This research delves into the thermalization process of a system, which begins with a non-gaussian random state and is influenced by a time-dependent, system-specific Hamiltonian. This study focuses on a specific type of Hamiltonian, which has distinct periods of high and low activity. Analytical methods are employed to demonstrate that thermalization is expected to occur in a time frame that is approximately 3 to 4 times the average duration of a single cycle. Additionally, a general framework is developed to calculate the long-term expectation values of system observables. Notably, a distinct phenomenon is observed when the Hamiltonian is periodic, where the expectation values of certain observables exhibit a distinct "memory effect", effectively reverting to a prior value before achieving thermal equilibrium.

Pseudo-differential operators with a bounded symbol are considered on uniform trees. A necessary and sufficient condition for the boundedness on uniform trees is derived, which differs from that on $\mathbb{R}^d$ due to the absence of a Lebesgue measure on the frequency space. By defining a new norm on the space of functions on the dual of the uniform tree, pseudo-differential operators are shown to be bounded, indicating their closeness to nuclear operators. However, counterexamples demonstrate the operators may not be nuclear, offering a contrast to their $\mathbb{R}^d$ counterpart.

The rapid expansion of mobile broadband networks has led to widespread adoption of the 5th generation (5G) cellular network, which promises enhanced connectivity and performance. Nevertheless, various obstacles, for example, the lack of understanding of the performance of 5G cellular networks and the impact of mobile devices on traffic patterns, need to be resolved. This study examines the visibility of smartphones on 5G networks, uncovering that contemporary smartphones significantly surpass earlier models in their ability to connect to cellular towers, yielding significantly improved signal quality. This research reveals that newer smartphones, such as iPhone 13 Pro, can connect to cellular towers at higher rates, achieving a signal quality of up to 50 dB. In addition, the study demonstrates that iPhone 13 Pro exhibits greater resilience to tower-handover and reduced latency in comparison to older models, such as iPhone 6s. This study's findings are instrumental in informing the development of effective mitigation strategies for mobile networks.

Deep neural networks often overestimate their confidence when encountering out-of-distribution data, leading to unreliable predictions. To address this issue, we developed an in-distribution training approach called CODEs (Chamfer Out-of-Distribution Instances) that effectively reduces the overconfidence problem. By incorporating artificial OOD data points into the training set, we create a more challenging and diverse environment, enhancing model robustness. We utilize a Chamfer distance metric to evaluate the distribution of generated samples, ensuring accurate out-of-distribution detection. Furthermore, we demonstrate that CODEs can be combined with existing methods for generating OOD data to enhance their performance. Our research findings are supported by comprehensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets.

The study of the angular correlations between the two jets in high-energy proton-proton collisions at the LHC is presented, specifically for events with at least four jets in the final state. The analysis utilizes data with an integrated luminosity of 33.2 fb^-1 and focuses on azimuthal angles between pairs of jets within a range of 30-140 GeV, up to 2.5 radians in pseudorapidity, and with minimum separations of 0.3 radians. The data is categorized into subgroups based on the number of identified jets and is compared to predictions from multiple event generators, including PYTHIA 8, HERWIG 7, and PHEGAS 2, as well as to calculations from JHEP 2012 006 and JHEP 2014 109.

The exponential growth in digital images and videos has led to the development of content-based image retrieval systems, which utilize various features to facilitate keyword-based searches. However, the effectiveness of these systems heavily relies on the quality of the search features, which are typically extracted using deep neural networks. The traditional methods of feature extraction are often time-consuming and require a substantial amount of labeled data. To address this limitation, semi-supervised and unsupervised learning techniques have emerged as potential solutions, offering a compromise between traditional methods in terms of accuracy and the need for a large amount of data. This paper provides an in-depth analysis of existing semi-supervised and unsupervised learning methods for feature representation and content-based image retrieval, as well as their applications across multiple domains. The review also identifies the benefits and drawbacks of these approaches, followed by an examination of their practical applications. Finally, it highlights the potential of deep learning-based content-based image retrieval systems for real-world applications.

Identifying and flagging outliers in 3D point clouds, a critical component in many applications, is also a crucial step in depth estimation tasks. While recent deep learning-based methods have shown significant progress in this area, they still struggle with inconsistent and unreliable results. This paper proposes a novel approach to outlier detection, leveraging the reconstruction error of a point cloud as a distinguishing feature. By regressing the reconstruction error of each point, rather than directly predicting its likelihood, we achieve more accurate results. Our method demonstrates strong performance on KITTI and Virtual KITTI datasets across various tasks, including anomaly detection, camera pose estimation, and depth estimation.

This research explores the long-term behavior of intricate stochastic processes defined by non-linear equations with random disturbances, focusing on three distinct types of systems. Our primary goal is to establish the conditions under which these processes converge to a consistent outcome, and to identify the underlying factors driving this convergence. Each of the three systems presented exhibits unique characteristics, presenting both similarities and differences in terms of their mathematical foundations and mechanisms of convergence. By developing novel mathematical frameworks and techniques, we aim to establish the foundation for the study of long-term behavior in these stochastic processes, incorporating theoretical frameworks from probability, mathematics, and computational science.

Neutrino polarizability has significant implications for testing this aspect, as well as for baryogenesis and effective field theory constraints. The current limits of neutrino polarizability are relatively high, suggesting that they cannot be fully determined by terrestrial experiments. In this paper, we explore the potential of astrophysical observations to improve these limits by examining the effects of neutrino polarizability on supernovae explosions. We develop a new approach to calculate the neutrino distribution in the supernova's shock wave, taking into account the effects of polarization and their interaction with density. The effects of polarization on the neutrino distribution are significant and must be considered in addition to the effects of chemical potential. The current data from supernova observations already impose stricter limits on neutrino polarizability, specifically a bound of $|\mathcal{C}|<10^{-28}$ CL$90\%$, which is a full order of magnitude lower than the previous limit.

In the mean field approach, we've developed a framework to study and create rhythms within the neuron-glial network model. Our goal is to create and analyze different types of rhythms, including synchronized and out-of-sync rhythms, as well as a specific type of synchronized rhythm called the synchronized cluster state. To achieve this, we've derived equations that describe the dynamics of the neuron-glial network under various conditions and numerically simulated them using advanced mathematical techniques. Our results show that the network can exhibit various types of rhythms, and we've identified key conditions under which these rhythms emerge and break down.

This study examines a theoretical model consisting of a neutral spin-1/2 particle within a periodic landscape of magnetic fields, incorporating both time-varying and static components. We investigate the topological characteristics of this system, including the Berry curvature distribution and a non-Abelian generalization of the Berry phase. Additionally, a non-Abelian framework is proposed for describing the dynamics of this particle, with a focus on the underlying topological structure. This model is relevant to the fields of condensed matter and high-energy physics.

We introduce an innovative, time-efficient and energy-efficient method for eroding a fixed obstacle within a flowing fluid in a confined space. This erosion process is driven by the fluid's dynamic behavior around the obstacle, particularly at points where particles first collide with it. By using a simple, non-invasive marker-based approach, our method enables the erosion front to evolve in response to the fluid's circulation patterns. As a result, the obstacle's shape and size are gradually modified according to the fluid's behavior, offering a cost-effective and effective means of surface treatment. Notably, our approach can be adapted to various applications involving obstacle interactions, such as those involving multiple particles or fluid currents.

For each hyperbolic knot, there exists a corresponding formal semigroup known as $N(K)$, composed of elements in the form $p/q$ where $p$ is even, $q$ is odd, and $q$ divides $p$ modulo $2$. The set $N(K)$ differs from the set of ratios of lengths of link components in a given knot projection, but these ratios can be derived from the ratios in the corresponding hyperbolic knot structure $K^h$. Notably, the set $N(K)$ is a lattice in the set of all ratios in $K^h$. The article demonstrates that the number of distinct ratios in the set $N(K)$ is a characteristic property of a hyperbolic knot, and it is also equal to the number of distinct Alexander polynomials associated with the knot. Furthermore, it is shown that the set $N(K)$ is a characteristic property of a knot in the realm of hyperbolic knots, and it is also equal to the set of all ratios in the corresponding knot structure $K^h$. The article also investigates the properties of the set $N(K)$ for a particular class of knots known as hyperbolic L-space knots, and it is shown that the set $N(K)$ is a characteristic property of such knots. A kinetic theory of an ideal gas is developed, assuming particles follow a Poisson distribution around equilibrium positions, which leads to a hydrodynamic equation framework that accommodates non-uniform initial conditions, utilizing an entropic force to achieve local equilibrium.

The escalating threat of cyber threats to surgical procedures necessitates the development of robust artifact detection systems to counter them effectively. To this end, a novel approach to identifying artifacts within endoscopic video feeds is proposed, which leverages an ensemble of object detection models to optimize detection performance and improve the resilience of the system. By combining models with diverse hyperparameter settings into a robust collection, and then selecting and fine-tuning a subset of models using transfer learning, the approach significantly enhances the accuracy of artifact detection. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of this method, as it yields a substantial average gain of 16.2% in AP and improves the robustness of the system by enhancing its ability to generalize to unseen test cases.

In software development, identifying and organizing code is crucial, and the way source code files are named often reflects the organization process. This research delves into the relationships between how developers group files and the patterns reflected in those groupings. It examines specific types of syntactic connections between file names, discovers recurring patterns, and analyzes their meanings based on context. The results show that different syntactic combinations are used in varying contexts, and the relationships between them are not always consistent. Additionally, we found that different developers in the same project may employ different naming conventions, and that many existing names may not be easily classifiable under current guidelines.

We introduce a novel infinite-dimensional $\square_q$-structure derived from the $q$-shuffle algebra K_q, which is associated with the affine Lie algebra $\hat{\mathfrak{sl}}_2$. This new structure is characterized by its product * on the direct sum of indecomposable modules over K_q, and involves a generalization of the q-binomial theorem. Furthermore, we establish that the *-algebra satisfies the Rota-Baxter identity with a specific weight and demonstrate its equivalence to the $q$-Cauchy kernel, and also show its connection to the $q$-cyclotomic rational functions.

The current understanding of grain growth in multiphase systems is that it follows normal grain-growth behavior in single-phase systems only when grain boundaries are mobile. However, in multiphase systems, the outcome of grain-boundary mobility can be diverse, depending on the specific phases and their boundaries involved. To study this further, a theoretical framework has been developed to analyze grain growth in duplex and triplex systems, using a specific set of parameters to describe the interfacial energy between phases and the mobility of their boundaries. The framework uses a mathematical equation to simulate the growth of grains in different phases over time, and by applying it to various systems, researchers can gain insights into the kinetics of grain development and compare their findings with experimental observations. The study focuses on a specific example of a triplex system, where the grain boundaries of one phase are highly mobile, and the others are immobile, and explores how changes in interfacial energy and grain-boundary mobility affect the evolution of grain size and structure. The analysis also considers the role of grain-boundary pinning by phases and the formation of multiple phases on the microstructure of polycrystalline materials.

Estimating a person's three-dimensional posture from a single image is a crucial computer vision task. Current methods have made significant progress in this area, but they are often evaluated using datasets created through a specific technique that may not accurately represent natural posture scenarios. This paper introduces a novel dataset collected through a more realistic approach, consisting of 1,000 pairs of input images and 3D pose annotations captured using Kinect technology. To enhance dataset creation, we introduce a novel method for identifying and annotating prominent joints in a more precise and efficient manner. Our analysis reveals that existing techniques are still developing and can benefit from additional training data using our newly created dataset, particularly when images are taken from the front and side.

Our research indicates that the presence of intense electron-electron interaction alone can induce superconductivity in two-dimensional lattice systems, even in the absence of a critical electron density threshold. This phenomenon is found to occur in a sparse lattice arrangement where the sites are farther apart, and its emergence is more pronounced in such configurations. A numerical analysis was conducted to determine the superconducting properties of two specific models: the Hubbard model and the model incorporating Hubbard-U interaction. The results show that the superconducting order parameter is significantly enhanced in a sparse lattice structure, and this is further supported by a higher kinetic energy and lower interaction energy compared to their negative counterparts.

We investigate the possibility of scalar leptoquark interactions to explain neutrino mass and the alignment of quark and lepton families.  A specific global symmetry, known as GLQ, is assumed to be present and is broken at the same scale as the standard model, leading to the observed alignment.  A particular leptoquark model with the quantum numbers $(\mathbf{3}, \mathbf{1}/2)$ is used and the constraints imposed by the same-sign diboson and single-top production processes are examined.  It is found that the leptoquark couplings can be constrained to the range $g_LQ \lesssass 0.15$ at the 95% confidence level, corresponding to a mass scale of approximately 4 TeV.  Furthermore, the alignment mechanism can be tested by searching for lepton flavour-violating decays in the charged lepton sector.

The concept of categorization plays a pivotal role in machine learning, and this study delves into the fundamental challenges of categorization in machine intelligence, drawing inspiration from "The Philosophical Baby" by Gary P. Mar by examining the application of the concept cat($A)$ to define a category A. Through this lens, the study explores the interplay between categories, tasks, and objects, and how object categorization stands at the heart of machine learning, often involving hierarchical categorization. Additionally, the study presents a new categorization tree and corresponding tasks for images, and introduces the concept of categorization transfer to facilitate knowledge sharing across related tasks.

This research paper presents a novel method for tracking and regulation in second-order dynamic systems. The proposed approach leverages a combination of tracking errors in both position and velocity, and employs a specific form of sliding-mode control. The method optimizes the performance of the system by minimizing a weighted sum of these tracking errors, based on their relative importance. By doing so, it enables the design of control systems that can achieve optimal tracking and regulation outcomes. The paper provides a detailed analysis of the system's performance, including an estimation of the minimum settling time required to reach the final goal. Two distinct implementations of the optimal control approach are presented, one utilizing a gain matrix that remains constant over time, and another with a gain matrix that adapts to minimize settling time. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through the presentation of two numerical examples.

To enhance the charging and discharging capabilities of lithium-ion batteries, it's crucial to comprehend the internal workings of these batteries and identify strategies for optimising their performance. This study focuses on investigating how applying ultrasonic vibrations at the end of a 3.65V full discharge accelerates the charging rate. By employing a scanning laser wakefield technique, we observed the influence of these ultrasonic vibrations on the interfacial separation between the electrolyte and electrodes within lithium-ion batteries. Our results indicate that the ultrasonic vibrations can decrease the separation between the electrodes, achieving this in just a few minutes, a much faster rate than the normal charging and discharging times that take around 1.5 hours. Notably, this effect is highly repeatable and can be achieved with vibrations as low as 20MHz frequency and minimal energy input. Our findings demonstrate that the observed reduction in separation is correlated with the charge state of the battery, increasing as the charge level rises. This study sheds new light on the internal workings of lithium-ion batteries and offers a non-invasive technique that could be used to monitor the internal structure of these batteries and identify potential issues such as internal shorts and capacity degradation.

This research introduces a discrete-time controller for the vertical position of a flat-top crane, which serves as a model for a gantry hoist used in manufacturing. The proposed controller is based on an integral-level controller, which has been adapted to use discrete-time logic and control signals. To assess the performance of this controller, simulations were conducted using a flexible crane model that takes into account the effects of flexibility and dynamics. The simulations demonstrate that the flat-top crane can achieve high-level positioning accuracy and fast convergence, with the added benefit of significantly reducing discontinuous control actions compared to a traditional integral controller.

Recent advancements in vision-language models have significantly improved their descriptive capabilities. However, these models are heavily influenced by the quality of the data used to train them, particularly with regards to noisy data sources. This study investigates the impact of data noise on image description tasks and proposes an innovative training technique, the Collaborative Distillation method, to minimize its effects. The Distillation-COAB approach, a variant of traditional knowledge distillation, is presented as a suitable solution. The method involves training a student model simultaneously on clean and noisy data, allowing it to capture both its own capabilities and the performance of a strong, pre-trained teacher model. The Distillation-COAB method has been successfully tested on the COCO dataset and achieved better results compared to existing models.

A collection of infinite sequences, each with real entries in the interval [0,1], is considered strongly linked if any finite segment of the sequences can be followed by a sequence from the collection. It is demonstrated that any collection of strongly-linked sequences must contain an element that can be removed, resulting in a collection of weakly-linked sequences. Furthermore, a collection of infinite sequences, each with real entries in the interval [0,1], is considered weakly linked if any sequence of finite length from the collection can be extended by a sequence from the collection. It is shown that any collection of weakly linked sequences can be partitioned into infinitely many non-overlapping subsets, each of which is strongly linked.

This paper provides an overview of category theory and Ehresmann semigroups, focusing on their applications and arrangements. By defining an Ehresmann semigroup arrangement and partial order, we can explore the interconnection between these mathematical constructs and classify them through structural analysis.

The self-focus phenomenon is characterized by a sharp, narrow minimum in a system's minimum value, which is reached at a specific point in time. In this context, the delay between the onset and peak of self-focus is referred to as the "depth." Research has shown that the length of this delay is directly proportional to the "width" of the underlying physical mechanism. This study examines the relationship between depth and width in various scenarios, using a linear system as an example. It highlights how different initial conditions can affect the depth-to-width interaction, which in turn influences the system's behavior. The research also explores the implications of this interaction for the performance of machine learning models, particularly in the context of deep neural networks.

The production of BiFeO$_{3}$ nanoparticles via a sol-gel method at 450~\text{°C} yielded a significant improvement in magnetization and a notable presence of antiferromagnetic interactions. The utilization of a lower temperature for nanoparticle formation, specifically 300~\text{°C}, resulted in particles possessing ferromagnetic behavior and a higher surface area. The particles produced at 450~\text{°C}$ and 300~\text{°C}$ possessed average particle sizes of 30~nm and 25~nm, respectively. The enhanced magnetization in the 300~nm particles was attributed to their increased surface area. The ferromagnetic properties of the particles were further confirmed by hysteresis loops and neutron diffraction. The presence of antiferromagnetic interactions in the particles was determined through alternating gradient field magnetometry. The particles produced at 450~\text{°C}$ and 300~\text{°C}$ were found to possess perovskite and orthoferrite structures, as confirmed by X-ray diffraction. The particles produced at 450~\text{°C}$ and 300~\text{°C}$ were found to exhibit a higher photodegradation efficiency for methylene blue, resulting in 80~\% and 90~\% degradation, respectively. The particles produced at 300~\text{°C}$ were found to exhibit a

In the context of the ${\rm SU}(6)$ model, we examine the transverse momentum distributions of heavy flavor particles produced in proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 7 TeV. Utilizing a generalised version of the fragmentation function, accounting for the effects of heavy quark masses and binding, we have calculated the inclusive distributions for bottom quarks and leptons. Additionally, we have computed the inclusive distributions for charmed particles and leptons, incorporating both charm and bottom quark mass corrections.

We introduce a novel task of estimating 3D pointclouds of objects held at rest
by a human hand. The proposed method leverages the hand as a static reference
point to create detailed geometric models of objects, which can be used to
overcome challenges in reconstructing an object's complete shape from a single
hand-held camera view. Our approach uses a single deep neural network that
produces pointclouds in response to an input image, which can be trained using
synthetic data generated through a physically-based rendering system. The
generated data accounts for the complex physical interactions between a hand and
an object, such as contact, occlusion, and deformation, which are difficult
to replicate in real-world settings. The method exhibits superior performance
on a newly created dataset of 20 common objects, which can be found at
https://www.robots.ox.ac.uk/~vgg/research/3dhand/.

The Ca-K index, used to measure solar activity levels through sunspot area and number, has been calculated from photographs taken at the Kodaikanal Solar Observatory, a century-long dataset. We analyzed 170,000 images from 1929 to 2013, converting them into digital images and applying an enhancement technique to extract features related to the Ca-K line. We developed a novel method to quantify the fluctuations in the Ca-K index, a characteristic linked to solar magnetic activity. The proposed approach involves edge detection, thresholding, and perimeter analysis of active regions, providing a direct measurement of their size and total area. The resulting fluctuation data were compared with traditional sunspot and area-based indices, showing a strong correlation. Furthermore, a correlation analysis was conducted between the Ca-K index and other solar activity indicators, revealing a robust correlation with the Wolf sunspot number and magnetic flux, and moderate correlation with the Greenwich sunspot number.

The $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ decay has been detected at the LHCb experiment, utilizing the 2016 p-p collision data with an integrated luminosity of 2 fb$^{-1}$ and a centre-of-mass energy of 13 TeV. This is the first observation of the rare decay process, and it was identified through the reconstruction of $\Sigma^+$/ $\overline{\Sigma}^+$ hyperons in their neutral modes by combining their decay products: $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ and $\overline{\Sigma}^+ \to \overline{p} \mu^+ \mu^-$ followed by $\mu^+ \overline{\mu}^-$ pair reconstruction. The analysis focused on the $\mu^+ \mu^-$ mass spectrum in the range of 200-1600 MeV with a signal-to-background ratio of approximately 0.1%. The results revealed a statistically significant signal of 5.2 standard deviations, indicating the occurrence of the $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ decay. Furthermore, the $\mu^+ \mu^-$ mass distribution was found to be consistent with the decay of a $\overline{K}^0 K^0$ system produced via the $\Sigma^+ \overline{K}^0$ to $\overline{p} K^

A novel, distributed approach has been created for performing symbolic analysis of intricate software systems, which cannot be efficiently handled by existing methods due to their complexity. This new method relies on test-depth segmentation, a technique that breaks down software components into smaller units based on test cases, enabling the analysis of each segment concurrently. By integrating test-depth segmentation, the method allows for the distribution of computational workload across multiple machines, significantly accelerating symbolic analysis in large-scale projects. As a result, the proposed solution can efficiently handle complex projects, such as the Apache httpd system, where a single machine falls short, by leveraging the resources of multiple machines.

The long-standing issue of magnetic nanoparticle arrangement and its impact on device performance has been explored. We have developed a novel method to create a precise and stable magnetic structure within a polymer film, enabling the control of magnetic interactions and disorder effects. By adjusting the thickness of the polymer layer, we observed a transition from an ordered, relaxed structure to a more disordered arrangement, as confirmed by both magnetic and optical measurements. The findings demonstrate the potential to create tailored magnetic structure and disorder in polymer films, offering new possibilities for advanced spintronics and optoelectronics applications.

In a collaborative learning setting, a central server facilitates knowledge exchange and aggregation across users in a decentralized network, with the goal of minimizing communication overhead and efficient use of resources. To achieve this, a new framework, CS-Collaborative Learning, is introduced, which eliminates the need for a central server. The framework is based on a decentralized network structure and utilizes a distributed aggregation method to combine local models, with the aim of reducing communication overhead while maintaining performance. The CS-Collaborative Learning framework is scalable, efficient, and adaptable to various network configurations, with the potential to outperform traditional collaborative learning approaches that rely on a central server.

This research focuses on a specific type of problem known as Sequential Brief-Text Categorization (SBTC), where inputs consist of sequences of brief texts and classification is needed. Examples of such problems include spam email detection, social media post categorization, and more. In this context, a new deep neural network architecture is proposed that integrates recurrent and convolutional models to tackle SBTC. By combining these models, a comprehensive representation of each input sequence is generated and subsequently processed. Results from testing on two real-world datasets demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed architecture in SBTC compared to other cutting-edge deep neural network models.

The derivation of analytical expressions for telecentric etalons is outlined in this work. Building on previous research, the etalons are characterized by a complex reflection and transmission behavior, necessitating the development of a comprehensive analytical expression to accurately reproduce the phase properties of etalons. This expression enables the calculation of etalon performance and is adaptable for use in various optical system designs.

The concept of pairing-based cryptosystems has been a cornerstone in many modern cryptographic systems, particularly in identity-based encryption and many others. Notably, a significant number of these pairings are congruent, enabling the use of a useful characteristic - the Jacobi ideal - which can facilitate the development of various applications. Building on this insight, researchers have introduced a method for determining the Ramanujan pairing, which is a specific example of a congruent pairing, by leveraging the Jacobi ideal, and demonstrated its potential in identity-based encryption. Furthermore, they have applied this technique to another type of congruent pairing, resulting in a more efficient and expressive framework for multicollinearities.

Chiplets are compact, modular components used in the design of complex integrated circuits. They enable a modular approach to chip design, similar to how sub-circuit blocks are integrated in System-on-Chip (SoC) design. By breaking down large chips into smaller chiplets, manufacturers can more efficiently and cost-effectively produce a wider range of products. This design approach also facilitates the combination of multiple technologies, such as combining CMOS with non-traditional materials and processes. A new framework called Codette is introduced, which streamlines the design of codetta-based systems by standardizing interfaces, data management, and package design. Codette's architecture is designed to optimize data management, including the use of standardized interfaces, data modeling, and package design, to facilitate efficient design and integration of chiplets.

A novel approach to evaluate the reliability of a nonparametric cure model is proposed. This method involves a two-stage process where a pre-smoothing technique is employed to enhance the accuracy of the parametric component, which is subsequently integrated with the nonparametric component via maximum likelihood estimation to yield a refined model. This model, which is free from any distributional constraints, is capable of capturing a broader range of models, including those that have been previously developed, which often rely on specific assumptions about the error terms and latent variables. Comprehensive simulation studies and real-data analyses have demonstrated the effectiveness of this proposed approach.

The nonlocal measure dimension of a graph, denoted as $w_G$, is a quantity representing the minimum dimension in a nonlocal cover of $G$. This dimension is defined as the dimension of the smallest nonlocal ball expansion covering $G$, with the nonlocal ball expansion of a set $S$ defined as the set of all vertices with hyperbolic distance to $S$ less than a certain threshold $r$, where the threshold is determined by $|S|^{-1/r}$. The nonlocal measure dimension of $G$ can be compared to other graph dimensions including the standard dimension of $G$, the strong measure dimension of $G$, and the visibility dimension of $G$, with the relationships being proven as $w_G \leq h_G \leq s_G \leq w_G$. We also show that the nonlocal measure dimension of $G$ does not exceed the standard dimension of $G$ by a factor of $2$, if the graph is either doubling or has integral dimensions.

In-memory computing enables rapid data processing by storing and analyzing data within the compute unit itself. This approach is particularly suitable for computationally intensive applications such as machine learning and big data analytics. However, in-memory computing systems are vulnerable to security breaches through side-channel attacks. This research investigates and evaluates the risks posed by side-channel attacks against in-memory computing frameworks. Our findings indicate that existing side-channel attack techniques developed for other architectures are not directly applicable to in-memory frameworks. To address this, we have introduced and tested two novel in-memory side-channel attacks - one based on timing and another utilizing power consumption.

We have developed a method to simplify extensive calculations in FeynGold, which is part of the Flexible Electromagnetic Coupling (FEC) suite. This approach optimizes the extraction of polarization functions in FeynGold, enhancing efficiency and precision. The enhanced capability enables the calculation of the full set of two-loop vertex corrections for all quark and lepton vertices in the Standard Model, including massless and finite cases.

Recent years have seen significant interest in developing self-supervised methods for noise reduction in seismic data, as they eliminate the need for paired labeled data like deep learning methods. However, most existing self-supervised techniques heavily rely on signal characteristics and struggle when faced with complex seismic signals featuring limited distinctive elements. To address this limitation, researchers have turned to blind-spot convolutional neural networks (CNNs), which utilize a distinct set of filters to isolate seismic characteristics. Yet, blind-spot CNNs require extensive training on uncomplicated seismic data and struggle with robust generalization. To overcome these challenges, we introduce a novel approach, where we merge the strengths of traditional blind-spot CNNs and self-supervised methods by incorporating transfer learning. Specifically, we first train a self-supervised model using uncomplicated seismic data and then leverage its learned filters to construct a simplified blind-spot CNN, which can be further trained on the original seismic data in a blind-spot framework. This transfer learning technique enables the improvement of the blind-spot CNN's generalization capability. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our proposed method in reducing seismic noise.

The elastic scattering of charged leptons and anti-leptons off protons has been studied using a first principles approach, taking into account the emission of charged pions and other mesons. The approach involves using a modified Dirac equation that incorporates a new interaction term, and using a first principles method to solve the resulting equations. The results show that the scattering cross sections are sensitive to certain types of interactions, and that the inclusion of meson mass effects leads to a good agreement with existing experimental data.

A recent study of Sr$_2$IrO$_4$ using scanning tunneling spectroscopy found evidence of a Mott gap opening due to spin-orbit interactions. The acquired spectra were analyzed using numerical methods to compare the findings with theoretical models. The analysis revealed that specific parameters for the models can be determined and the calculated density of states aligns with results from angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy. The study's conclusions suggest that a specific model accurately describes the data, but an alternative model with a different parameter range also fits when the lowest energy state is heavily suppressed. The study's results indicate that a specific correlation among the system's particles is essential for understanding the data, and the models' conclusions align with previous theoretical and experimental findings.

A widely used concept in causality, called mediation examination, aims to quantify the influence of an intervening variable on the relationship between a treatment and outcome. Researchers have developed various methods to assess direct and indirect effects, assuming that the mediator affects the outcome only when it is triggered by the treatment, and that the mediator does not independently influence the outcome. However, this assumption is not always valid in real-world applications. To address this limitation, we propose a new framework called multiply resilient causal mediation, which considers situations where the mediator affects the outcome regardless of the presence of the treatment. Our framework includes two novel methods to estimate the direct and indirect effects in such scenarios. The first method is a generalized version of existing approaches, and the second method is a semiparametric estimator that controls for confounding factors. Our approach enables researchers to examine the mediating effects of variables that have a direct influence on the outcome, regardless of the presence of treatments.

This is a selection of excerpts from the two-volume "Special Issue on Starshades" published by the journal Optics Express in 2019.  Starshades, which are devices that work in conjunction with telescopes to amplify or reduce the light entering the primary aperture, have garnered significant interest over the past few years.  A selection of findings from the most recent research on this subject is provided in this editorial.  Following the excerpts, a brief conversation on starshades is presented in which we address and clarify several points of confusion.  The conversation specifically addresses the frequently asked question of whether starshades can be considered true apertures, as well as other misconceptions surrounding their use.  The answer to this question is complex and depends on how one defines an aperture, ultimately leading to the conclusion that, in certain instances, they can be considered true apertures, while in other cases, they are merely auxiliary devices used in conjunction with the primary aperture.  The primary goal of this conversation is to clarify these points of confusion and provide clarity where necessary.

The prevalence of mental health issues, including suicidal ideation, has been exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic, making it essential to develop effective detection and prevention strategies. To address this challenge, researchers utilize data-driven approaches grounded in natural language processing, which rely on extensive, high-quality datasets. Currently, no large-scale suicidal text collection exists, limiting the development of data-driven solutions for mental health.
