To address this gap, a comprehensive suicidal text dataset, Robin, is introduced, featuring 124K annotated texts, 103K of which are manually labeled by experts as suicidal or nonsuificial. The remaining texts are automatically classified using a sophisticated framework. The collection includes a set of 10 domain-specific features and is evaluated using multiple domain-specific evaluation metrics. The need for specialized NLP tools and resources is emphasized, along with the development of a novel tool that can identify suicidal content in real-time. The dataset, along with its associated code and classification resources, is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/robin-suicide-dataset.

A foundational concept in gravity research is the Schwarzschild metric, which has inspired numerous studies, particularly those focusing on the effects of gravitational fields on the motion of light. These investigations, which date back to the early 20 19s, have become a significant area of study within the field of gravity. Building upon this work, a new chapter has emerged, which seeks to extend these findings to other forms of matter and particles. As part of this research, a new category of gravity has been identified, which is referred to as "Blackian gravity." This concept is also used to describe a specific phenomenon in quantum mechanics, which is referred to as "Blackian quantum mechanics." Furthermore, a more advanced form of this gravity has been developed, which incorporates additional features of black holes, known as "super Blackian gravity." An interesting application of this concept has also been identified, which is referred to as "Blackian mechanics." This concept is particularly relevant to the study of quantum systems, which exhibit both Blackian and non-Blackian behaviors.

This paper investigates the bounded solutions of the difference equation $x_{n+1}=ax^\alpha_{n}+bx^\alpha_{n-1}$ within a specific parameter region in the $\mathbb R^3$ space, with $\alpha$ between 0 and 2, excluding 1. It identifies unbounded solutions and finds that boundedness is ensured when $\alpha$ is less than 1 or falls within a particular region of $(a, b, x)$. This research has practical implications in medicine, particularly in evaluating the efficacy of a proposed treatment for patients with atrial septal aneurysms.

We have developed a group of Born-Infeld-type electrodynamic theories, which are characterized by a variable Born-Infeld parameter. This parameter is directly related to the electric field strength, ensuring it remains below the unit value. The action of this electrodynamic model is also influenced by a parameter, g, which is associated with the magnetic charge of black holes. This allows us to derive a charged black hole solution within the anti-de Sitter spacetime, and we find that the outer event horizon remains stable across all possible configurations of the electrodynamic model. Notably, we are able to obtain a broad range of the black hole's temperature and entropy, which are found to be consistent with the Bekenstein-Hawking theory under specific conditions. Furthermore, we have investigated the behavior of the black holes' magnetic mass and magnetic surface area within the context of the anti-de Sitter spacetime, and we have found that they exhibit properties consistent with the Bekenstein-Hawking laws.

A specific type of arrangement in n-dimensional space is called a Sidon arrangement if every line it contains is a unique set of points where one point is directly above another on the same line. The study of Sidon arrangements was initially explored by Carpi and others in 2007. The present research delves into Sidon arrangements formed by linear structures such as projective lines, affine lines, and elliptic lines in projective spaces of higher dimensions. The study discovers that Sidon arrangements of this type are equivalent to specific types of group actions on those spaces. The study also shows that in higher dimensions, the only possible arrangements of this type are those resulting from group actions on rational curves in elliptic and projective spaces. The study further extends this concept to linear subgroups within projective spaces of higher dimensions and demonstrates that the resulting Sidon arrangements are equivalent to specific types of arrangements derived from finite groups. The study also identifies the characteristics of the resulting Sidon arrangements.

The behavior of magnetic susceptibility at finite temperatures has been analyzed within a two-dimensional XY spin system. A specific ratio of magnetic susceptibility at a particular temperature to its value at absolute zero was calculated relative to a reference temperature, which resulted in a scaling effect towards a critical temperature. Our findings show that the geometric phase in the magnetic system changes as a function of temperature, indicating a critical temperature that scales according to finite-temperature scaling.

Our research involves simulating the Ising model on a cubic lattice where a finite cluster of spins is embedded within an extremely large isotropic ferromagnetic system at absolute zero temperature. To initiate the cluster, all spins are randomly assigned in the + or - direction. Simulations demonstrate that the initial cluster configuration significantly impacts the conversion process. A cluster configured in the + direction has a greater likelihood of converting compared to one with spins in the - direction. A surprising observation reveals that the system with the +-oriented cluster exhibits a higher temperature at which the transition occurs compared to the one with the -oriented cluster. To further investigate this phenomenon, we performed additional simulations. Our results indicate that the system with the +-oriented cluster displays a lower kinetic energy and a higher correlation length compared to the system with the -oriented cluster. These findings demonstrate that the +oriented cluster moves more slowly and forms a more stable state compared to the -oriented cluster. These results are consistent with the earlier study by Janßen and Binder (2018). Our research also shows that the system with the +oriented cluster displays a higher temperature at which the transition occurs in the vicinity of the critical point. This phenomenon can be attributed to the stronger interaction between the finite cluster and the surrounding large ferromagnetic system.

We examine the behavior of a coupled pair of particles within a one-dimensional Almeida–Thouless quasicrystal, characterized by a unique potential that varies over multiple length scales. By analyzing the system under a range of temperatures and coupling strengths, we derive an analytical expression for the thermal conductivity of the system. Our findings indicate that, at temperatures exceeding a particular threshold, the system exhibits diffusive behavior with a distinct dependence on quasiperiodic potential strength. Conversely, below this threshold, the system displays localized behavior with minimal dependence on the strength of the quasiperiodic potential, ultimately resulting in insulating properties. Our study also reveals that the localization length of the system is power-law dependent on the strength of the quasiperiodic potential, while the conductivity of the system is found to decrease exponentially as temperature is reduced.

Conversational systems are being increasingly used in interactions between humans and machines, where users expect specialized tools to manage expectations and provide tailored support. A key challenge is developing a system that can efficiently process and respond to user queries within a specific domain. A crucial step in this process is using natural language processing techniques to break down user input into meaningful components that machine translation systems can understand. However, current approaches often focus on processing user queries at individual interaction points rather than considering the broader conversation context. To address this limitation, we propose a task-centered framework for multilingual conversational systems, which involves designing a vocabulary and semantic spaces that can accommodate multiple languages. Our approach involves building a shared semantic space for multiple languages using techniques like cross-lingual word embeddings and semantic translation. We also discuss how to develop a vocabulary and pre-trained language models tailored to a specific application scenario.

The intricate process of alternative splicing allows a single gene to encode multiple proteins, significantly expanding the repertoire of protein diversity by offering distinct proteins with varied functions. To investigate the dynamic nature of splicing, we analyzed short-term data from mice and humans to uncover the mechanisms behind splicing regulation. By examining the expression of nearly 20,000 mRNAs in mice and over 30,000 mRNAs in humans, we discovered that splicing patterns in both species exhibit a high degree of variability. Focusing on a subset of 1,500 genes, we found that the proportion of alternatively spliced genes is significantly higher than expected, indicating that many genes are regulated by alternative splicing. Furthermore, we observed that the expression of these genes is often influenced by both stochastic and regulated processes. By analyzing the expression of individual isoforms, we found that the splicing of these genes is frequently regulated by both alternative transcriptional and post-transcriptional mechanisms. The findings suggest that the regulation of alternative splicing is complex and may involve various modes of regulation, including both stochastic and regulated mechanisms.

The issue of data protection has been a persistent concern within the healthcare sector, where professionals must make strategic decisions to ensure sensitive patient data is handled in a secure manner. To address this challenge, this qualitative study examined the methods used by healthcare professionals to achieve data privacy, focusing on the reasoning behind their actions. Through interviews with 19 experienced healthcare professionals, we explored their decision-making processes and strategic approaches to data protection. The findings suggest that professionals consider multiple factors when ensuring data privacy, including external factors, individual data requirements, and organizational influences. To achieve this, they employ a range of technical strategies and regularly review patient data to identify areas for improvement. However, they acknowledge the need for more automated tools to support data protection and express frustration with outdated EHR systems that hinder their efforts. These professionals envision a future where data protection is integrated into clinical workflows, reducing the need for manual reviews and enhancing their ability to deliver high-quality patient care.

The study of particle production in collisions between a proton and a nucleus offers valuable insights into the characteristics of quark-nucleon interactions. An in-depth examination of particle correlations in proton-nucleus collisions has been conducted, leveraging data from the ALICE detector at the LHC. Specifically, the focus is on the two-dimensional correlation between the azimuthal angles of charged particles, including those near and away from the collision's midplane. These correlations are analyzed in terms of the sum of azimuthal angles, known as Δφ, and its distance from the collision's center, known as Δη. An observed pattern in particle distributions near the collision's edge reveals a dependence on particle pair angular differences, Δψ, and the number of particles produced (Npart). These findings demonstrate that the pattern in particle correlations is consistent with a picture in which the nucleus's matter is influenced by a combination of two effects: the effects of energy loss and the effects of collective motion.

The production of light nuclei such as deuterons, tritons, and helium-3 and four nuclei in collisions between gold atoms at high energy can be explained by applying a model called the statistical hadronization model. According to this model, the light nuclei originate from the coalescence of particles in the thermal medium through a statistical process. Calculations done using the SHM model agree with the results of experimental measurements.

The study of exoplanets has significantly advanced in recent years, revealing numerous planets in diverse settings.  A key focus area is the study of rocky planets in temperate environments, as these are most likely to support life.  By examining the characteristics of nearby rocky planets, researchers can gain insights into the types of environments that support life and inform the search for biosignatures.  This chapter examines the diverse planetary environments that exist, including those of rocky planets and giants, and discusses the unique properties of each.  It also touches upon the possibility of discovering similar planetary architectures around white dwarf stars.  A significant aspect of this chapter is the discussion of planetary systems with multiple massive planets, as these can significantly impact the environment of rocky planets.  By analyzing the distribution of planetary semi-major axes and eccentricities, researchers can infer the types of massive planets that formed in these systems and the resulting effects on the surrounding rocky planets.  This chapter also explores the role of massive planets in shaping the environment of rocky planets, including the effects of gravitational perturbations, tidal interactions, and the delivery of material from massive planets to rocky planets.  A key example is presented of a planetary system with a close-in giant planet that has undergone significant changes, as evidenced by the presence of a debris disk around the rocky planet.  By examining the diverse planetary environments that exist, researchers can gain a deeper understanding of the complex relationships between planets and their environment, and how these relationships can be leveraged to reveal

A set of complex numbers is called circulant if its elements can be obtained from a single set element by cyclic permutations of its entries. A circulant graph has a similar property, with vertices corresponding to specific subsets of complex roots of unity. A set of complex roots of unity is said to fully solve a circulant graph if its elements can cover every vertex of the graph. This text explores new approaches to finding such sets, specifically focusing on those produced by products of roots of unity. It also proves the existence of certain specific subsets that can cover particular types of circulant graphs.

This study introduces a broadened adaptation of iterative methods like Order $N^0$ and Order $N^1$ techniques to accelerate the inversion of matrices both on conventional CPUs and more effectively on GPUs, where matrix inversion operations are commonly required in various applications. These adaptations, specifically Order $N^1$ and Order $N^2$ methods, have been thoroughly examined and demonstrated to be highly efficient in reducing matrix inversion computation time on both CPUs and GPUs. Consequently, the proposed techniques have been found to be highly suitable for implementing on conventional systems and efficiently utilizing GPU acceleration to significantly shorten the matrix inversion duration.

We examine the power spectrum of initial disturbances in a slow-roll inflationary scenario with a significant ultra-slow-roll period, taking into account the impact of quantum back reaction. By employing a perturbative approach, we extend the slow-roll equations to their quantum equivalent and calculate the power spectrum using a slow-roll approximation, demonstrating that the power spectrum can be expressed as a simple function of the number of e-folds. The power spectrum is found to be reduced from its standard slow-roll values when the ultra-slow-roll approximation is involved.

This paper presents an optimization challenge known as Enhanced Selection (ES), which is a critical component of evolutionary algorithms and is typically applied at the initial step of the process. We formulate this problem mathematically to identify the most suitable individual from a given population, yielding two variants of the ES problem. We prove that these variants are computationally intractable, establish their approximation complexity, and categorize their computational complexity in relation to different oracles. Furthermore, we provide a summary of existing approximate algorithms and review the ES algorithms developed within various evolutionary computation frameworks.

The standard method of presenting survival data, using time-to-event curves, is limited in its ability to compare different subgroups of patients. A proposed new method, called 'casebase', provides an alternative way to examine and compare event rates between groups. The 'casebase' plot consists of two parts: a vertical bar chart showing the number of patients at risk, and below it a series of lines indicating the total number of events expected to occur. Under a null hypothesis, observed event counts should fall within a range of possible event totals. If the observed event counts are outside this range, the null hypothesis can be rejected. The 'casebase' plot can also be used to investigate interactions between groups by splitting the chart into separate sections for each subgroup. A case study demonstrates the use of 'casebase' for comparing two clinical trials with event data.

High-energy physics requires precise calculations of $2\to 2$ scattering amplitudes to a few percent accuracy.  To achieve this accuracy, precision calculations of Feynman integrals with scale-dependent coefficients are necessary.  The existing methods for calculating Feynaynman diagrams fall short in this regard, as they are unable to handle loop integrals with multiple scales simultaneously.  We have developed a new method for calculating Feynaynfan integrals that can handle loop moments with arbitrary topologies and complex kinematic dependencies.  Our method has been applied to several benchmark cases and has demonstrated the ability to achieve an accuracy of a few percent in the calculation of loop integrals with up to four loops and arbitrary kinematic dependencies.

High-performance applications are increasingly generating vast amounts of simulation or measurement data that can be classified as objects, necessitating efficient data management solutions. Although object storage systems are still in their infancy, the market offers various options, and each has its own set of advantages and disadvantages. The storage service approach, introduced by the Open Cloud Systems Initiative, allows users to access data regardless of the underlying storage technology, providing a uniform interface to object storage systems. Our study focuses on a specific use case, evaluating the performance of DAOS and Lustre in a single-server configuration. The results indicate that both systems are suitable for handling data retention, and the storage service approach enables seamless integration of various object storage systems, enhancing interoperability.

To address the rapid expansion of electric vehicles, a public parking infrastructure upgrade is necessary. To manage the limited parking capacity and prevent unbalanced distribution across facilities, a novel Virtual Enrollment Regulation (VER) system is introduced to mitigate congestion and utilize available parking resources more efficiently. By leveraging a deep learning-based approach, VER enables cross-parking lot vehicle exchange at no additional cost. It comprises two modules: the enrollment module, which assigns a parking spot virtually to a vehicle without occupying the physical space initially, and the exchange module, which facilitates the switch from virtual to physical spot at different parking facilities. To optimize enrollment, VER employs a distributed online learning method that utilizes real-time parking availability data, generating an optimal virtual parking location and resource utilization. To facilitate vehicle exchange, VER uses a graph theory-based algorithm to minimize the physical inter-parking lot vehicle exchange time. Evaluations using real-world data from 13 parking facilities in a downtown area demonstrated that VER can reduce congestion by 10.7% and save resources by 16.5%.

This research paper explores two key concepts, namely, the existence of certain types of error-free codes and the creation of more error-free codes from existing ones. Focusing on a specific type of error-free code known as the linear comma codes, this study examines their existence and presence in both prime and power of a prime finite fields, and also delves into creating new error-free codes from existing ones. Furthermore, this paper provides a detailed example to illustrate these concepts and demonstrates their applicability through a specific case study.

We examine the gravitational sector of 4-dimensional Chern-Simons-like gauge theories with a specific Lagrangian derived from loop integrals of three-particle amplitudes. By applying a deformation technique, we isolate the gravitational interaction Lagrangian. At low energy, our theory corresponds to a modified version of Newtonian gravity with an adjustable parameter that influences the effects of high-energy loops on the gravitational constants.

The expansion of renewable energy across the Western United States faces challenges due to competition with agriculture, urbanization, and conservation priorities. To identify efficient solutions, we developed an optimization model that considers power generation, land use, and other factors, allowing for the assessment of various trade-offs between land conservation, urban growth, and energy production. Our results indicate that decarbonizing the power sector in the American West can involve allocating approximately 1% of the state's land for infrastructure development, which is comparable to 1.2% of current agricultural use and 0.6% of current urban and agricultural use. By prioritizing certain locations, the land required for this process can be contained within a region where intense conservation efforts are already in place, thereby minimizing the need for new conservation initiatives and preserving valuable natural and arable areas.

A cluster-randomized trial involves entire groups rather than individual participants, leading to a unique set of estimands that differ from those found in traditional randomized trials. In order to accurately evaluate the treatment's causal effect on an individual, one must consider the varying sample designs that can be employed in cluster-imbedded data sets. This consideration necessitates careful planning and the incorporation of appropriate statistical techniques. This article aims to provide an overview of current trends in estimation and inference for cluster-randomized trials, with a focus on applying estimands derived from individual trials to population-level assessments. Furthermore, it explores the potential benefits and drawbacks of recent approaches that allow for more adaptable and responsive cluster designs.

A specific fractal network called the M\"{o}bius Octagonal Network (MOF) has been introduced, which is a variation of the Octagonal Network. This new network is formed by projecting a certain fractal structure onto a two-dimensional plane using M\"{o}bius transformation. The Standardized Laplacian Spectrum of MOF at different stages is calculated and analyzed. The connections between this network and well-known fractal networks at certain stages, such as Sierpinski Octagonal and Koch Octagonal Network, are also explored. The characteristics of MOF at its initial stages are discussed, and potential applications of standardized Laplacian spectrum examination for MOF and related fractal networks are identified.

We address the distributed linear bandit problem in a multi-agent setting, where agents collaborate under a common objective despite being in separate environments with identical reward functions but potentially different reward parameters. Our task involves designing a distributed algorithm that minimizes regret and communication. In this context, a setting refers to the parameters of the linear bandit, including the mean reward and noise variance. We develop a shared, distributed, and efficient bandit algorithm that achieves a $\tilde O (d + \sqrt{T})$ regret, where d represents the number of setting parameters and T denotes the number of iterations. Our solution leverages a shared model where agents exchange parameters, use a shared solvers, and rely on a shared model, enabling them to collaborate efficiently. We also introduce an innovative distributed bandit algorithm that minimizes regret and requires minimal communication, specifically a single parameter vector sharing. This algorithm achieves a $\tilde O (1.5\sqrt{T})$ regret, and its efficiency is independent of the setting and parameters.

Cystic fibrosis patients' medical data, when combined, can provide valuable insights for medical research and improvement. However, the lack of such data, particularly in low-income and middle-income countries, severely hampers global health advancements. To bridge this gap, researchers developed a synthetic patient population model for cystic fibrosis patients in Ghana, using data from actual patients at a local hospital. Their model incorporates individual patient records of medication usage, hospital visits, and travel history. It also accounts for the relationships between patients' medication intake, hospital visits, and travel history. Furthermore, the model reflects the impact of medication non-adherence on patients' clinical outcomes. Utilising the developed model, the researchers conducted a series of 1000 simulations to assess the effectiveness of the National Cystic Fibrosis Treatment Protocol in Ghana, as well as the potential benefits of introducing travel restrictions and vaccination requirements to prevent the spread of cystic fibrosis and its associated infections.

The decays $D^0 \to K^\mp\pi^\pm\pi^\pm\pi^\mp$ are analyzed using 3 fb$^{-1}$ of collision data from the LHCb detector. The phase space is divided into 25 distinct bins and the $D^0$ decay amplitudes are determined in each bin. The $D^0 \to K^0_sK^0_s\pi^+\pi^-$ and $D^0 \to [D^0_{s} \to K^0_s K^0_s]\pi^+\pi^-$ decays are also studied. The findings are used to determine the $D^0 \to K^0_sK^0_s$ and $D^0 \to K^0_s\pi^+\pi^-$ decay amplitudes and the CP asymmetries in the $D^0 \to K^\mp\pi^\pm\pi^\pm\pi^\mp$ decay.

Originality and disruptiveness are essential for a successful invention, yet they are often overlooked in evaluation. New metrics have been proposed to address this gap, but they are currently limited by being implemented only in specific programming languages. To address this limitation, we developed Novelpy, a Python library that calculates the Novelpy indices to assess originality and disruptiveness. Novelpy leverages the SciPy library, making it a reliable tool for assessing innovation, and comes with pre-computed datasets for easy access.

We've developed a straightforward approach to dynamically control the output power of
laser pulses. The method relies on the nonlinear interaction between the target laser
and a secondary 'control' pulse. By modulating the control pulse, the power of the main
pulse is adjusted due to a process called cross-phase modulation. We demonstrate this
technique using two-photon absorption microscopy, and our experiments reveal a direct
proportionality between the control and main pulse's powers. Furthermore, we can
manipulate the dynamic range of this control by regulating the duration of both
pulses. The technique holds promise for a range of applications, such as generating
pulses with variable wavelengths or performing fast, high-resolution imaging.

This research outlines the results of a preliminary study aimed at exploring the potential of deep reinforcement learning in developing the ability to accurately hit targets with a longbow, specifically during Olympic-level competitions. An instance of this skill can be seen in archery, where athletes use a combination of physical and mental abilities to consistently hit targets within a 10-inch radius. This paper details the reasons why this task poses a challenge to current deep reinforcement learning methods and documents the findings of a previous attempt to apply these methods to the problem using TensorFlow and the Tensorforce framework.

Online e-commerce platforms rely on recommender systems to drive growth and profitability by showcasing their products to users with the highest value potential. However, these systems face a challenge when users from diverse demographic backgrounds shop at different times, using various devices, and exhibiting unique browsing habits. To bridge this gap, we present an innovative dual-metric training method that optimizes recommendation accuracy for both low-income and high-income users. By leveraging two customized distance metrics, our approach effectively targets diverse user segments. Additionally, we develop an efficient sampling technique to minimize computational costs in the training process. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our dual-metric training method, yielding significant improvements in recommendation accuracy for low-income users, while maintaining excellent performance for high-income users compared to traditional standard training methods.

Recent research on decentralized automata has demonstrated that many problems previously thought impossible to solve, such as the expressiveness problem, become feasible when considering asynchronous behaviors. Decentralized automata can represent asynchronous behaviors of systems through the use of labeled transitions, where local transition functions are applied to the shared variables' values. The authors' previous work introduced decentralized automata with a specific type of logic called $\mu$-calculus, which is used to describe asynchronous behaviors. The current paper extends this work by introducing a more robust version of $\mu$-calculus, called $\mu$-segment calculus, that retains the same level of expressiveness as the original. The authors also developed a characterization of the automata that can model the behaviors described by $\mu$-segment calculus, which is a significant step towards understanding the complexity of decentralized automata.

This research explores heat transfer in complex, two-dimensional plasma systems, utilizing a method of transforming complex systems into simpler ones through integration. The approach, which is applicable to both regular and irregular plasma systems, can be employed in a wide range of scenarios including those involving thermal instabilities.

The problem of reconstructing a hidden vector x from linear mixtures, such as y = Ax, is investigated. This problem arises in numerous fields, including data compression and recovery of lost data, and is particularly relevant when dealing with incomplete and noisy data. A general framework for addressing this issue is developed, focusing on the scenario where data is missing and contaminated, and utilizing the concept of entropy as a key metric. A novel approach to reconstructing the original vector x is proposed, and its effectiveness is validated through the application of information-theoretic principles. Experimental validation is conducted using both simulated and real-world datasets, and the findings are used to parameterize an algorithmic implementation of the proposed method.

Cardiac angiography via standard X-ray radiation poses a significant risk of cardiac damage and cancer, particularly with the increasing trend of performing procedures on younger patients. This study explores the potential of deep learning to minimize the need for X-ray radiation in cardiac angiography by automatically generating and utilizing intermediate frames between captured images. A deep neural network is trained to create these frames, and its effectiveness is evaluated using a specific measurement called the Structural Similarity Index. Our results show that our approach can significantly reduce radiation exposure while meeting the required standards of image quality.

Heavy-flavor physics at future $e^+e^-$ colliders has significant potential but is
currently hindered by the limited luminosity and short running period of the
existing B-factories. The proposed all-polarized electron-positron
collider, the Flavor Flavor Physics Compact Experiment (FFCC) at the Future
Circular Collider (FCC-ee), is expected to overcome these limitations, offering
an ideal environment for studying heavy-flavor physics by providing high
luminosity, precise time resolution, and extensive center-of-mass energy
coverage. The potential of the FFCC to measure heavy-flavor production will be
examined in detail, focusing on semileptonic $B$ decays, heavy-quark pair
production, single-wounded $Z$ production, heavy-quark fragmentation, and
charmonium production. Theoretical and experimental synergies will be highlighted,
and the feasibility of measuring the CKM matrix element $V_{tb}$ via the
$Z\to b\bar{b}$ process will be discussed. Theoretical issues that need to be
resolved to achieve the proposed measurements will be addressed, and the
challenges and prospects of the FFCC in measuring rare and CP-violating decays
will be discussed.

We investigated the impact of a new $U(1)$ gauge symmetry, specifically $U(1)_{L_{\mu}-L_{\tau}}$, on the type II seesaw mechanism in the standard model extended by the right-handed neutrinos. Our analysis revealed that incorporating the new gauge symmetry significantly alters the neutrino mass mechanism. By introducing a lepton number non-conserving $U(1)$ gauge interaction, it becomes feasible for right-handed neutrinos to interact with leptons and facilitate the neutrino mass generation. Consequently, this interaction can be viewed as a mechanism that enables right-handed neutrinos to cross a barrier and ultimately lead to neutrino masses.

The existence of high-speed stars traveling through the galaxy at speeds over 1000 km/s is a result of the galactic core's influence. It is hypothesized that the galactic core's intermediate-mass partner, which orbits at a distance of tens to hundreds of parsecs, can cause a long-term disturbance in the galactic core's structure. This effect, which is secular in nature, can lead to the ejection of high-speed stars from the galactic core. Our analysis shows that the ejection of these high-speed stars can occur in the real galaxy, with approximately 0.1% of the galactic core's stars being ejected per billion years. This rate is comparable to the rate at which the galactic core's stars are ejected due to the influence of the galactic bar.

This study investigates the existence of feeble solutions for singular multiplicative stochastic differential equations. A novel approach is introduced, employing the process of regularization by disturbance in the monotone framework. This method yields a solution that is feeble and unique, with no need for the strong monotonicity condition or gradient requirements, unlike other techniques. This solution is shown to be sensitive to initial conditions and, under specific conditions on the nonlinearity, it is also Lipschitz continuous. Additionally, this method provides a new existence result for feeble weak entropy solutions in the context of multiplicative stochastic SDEs with singular coefficients.

The definability of the nonstationary ideal for $\omega_1$ is established within the framework of a certain class of generalized outer models, which are characterized by their adherence to a specific set of axioms derived from ZFC. In particular, it is demonstrated that the Prikry Forcing axiom, Brown's tree property criterion, and the Sacks Forcing axiom each guarantee the existence of a forcing that introduces the ideal's complement along a Cohen real. Furthermore, it is established within the context of a certain class of generalized J\'onsson models, which are characterized by their adherence to a specific set of axioms derived from ZFC, that the real of a forcing that generates a well-ordered sequence of ideals equivalent to the nonstationary ideal for $\omega_1$ is projective.

Achieving top performance on downstream tasks relies heavily on the similarity of source and target tasks, which poses significant challenges for handling tasks with distinct structures. To address this issue, we introduce the concept of Adapter - a framework that enables language models to tackle various tasks by leveraging a lightweight structure that aligns each task with a specific objective. The Adapter framework is comprised of two primary components: a flexible structure that allows for the creation of task-specific networks and a versatile adaptation method that facilitates the adaptation of models to different tasks. Extensive experiments on multiple datasets demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, showcasing its ability to achieve comparable performance to pre-training based models while reducing computational requirements by a factor of 30 to 50. The corresponding implementation can be found on our GitHub repository at https://github.com/ghsed/Adapter.

The development of autonomous vehicles relies heavily on accurate traffic sign recognition. In order to improve the accuracy of such systems, a large dataset of 5000 images of traffic signs from around the world has been collected. This dataset, known as the Mapillary Traffic Sign Dataset (MTSD), is designed to evaluate state-of-the-art methods for traffic sign recognition. It consists of images of various types of traffic signs from MTTS (Mapillary Traffic Sign) dataset, which was captured using Mapillary Streetlamps equipment in multiple countries. The MTSD is composed of 18 different categories of traffic signs and is suitable for use in global settings, as it includes a diverse range of images. The MTSD is also accompanied by a simulator that allows users to train and test their algorithms with it. The MTSD is available for use at the following link: https://osf.io/9khs/.

Traditional collaborative filtering methods are hindered by data sparsity issues, particularly when dealing with large, sparse datasets. To address this challenge, researchers have introduced self-supervised learning techniques that can enhance CF models using self-attention and reconstruction methods. However, most existing self-supervised CF methods fail to leverage user and item interactions, instead focusing solely on self-supervised learning. To address this limitation, we propose a novel framework called SelfCF, which incorporates a novel cooperative loss function. This loss function enables CF models to learn from both user-item and item-user interactions, leading to improved performance. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of SelfCF, showcasing significant improvements over existing self-supervised CF methods on various real-world datasets.

We have broadened the scope of Tevelev's levels to encompass arbitrary closed subsets within the projective line over an algebraically closed field. This expansion is underpinned by a natural map from a certain semigroup to the monoid of ideals from Tevelev's semigroup, which we call the generalised Tevelev semigroup. This map is an extension of the inclusion of the monoid of ideals from a semigroup to a group. This map is an extension of the inclusion of the monoid of ideals from a semigroup to a group. Our research reveals that this map is a surjection, and it yields a natural isomorphism between the generalised Tevelev semigroup and the monoid of ideals from a semigroup. Furthermore, we have identified the generalised Tevelev semigroup as a polynomial semigroup. This discovery enables us to characterise the generalised Tevelev semigroup as a semigroup of polynomials.

We examine a specific 2-dimensional Dirac semimetal model and its unique spectral behavior. The model's energy spectrum consists of two types of dispersion patterns - linear and parabolic - which intersect at the Fermi level, resulting in four significant degeneracies. We demonstrate that these degeneracies are protected by the symmetries of the system, generating distinct bands in the energy spectrum. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of a specific symmetry breaking on the model, resulting in the gapped Dirac cones being split into parabolic dispersion patterns. The model's energy spectrum is also analyzed as N-dimensional Dirac semimetal under various symmetry conditions, which are then validated through the experimental verification of the model in 2D settings.

We investigate the dynamics of curves featuring a softness, specifically those meeting specific flatness criteria, and focusing on semi-stable curves. We examine the entrance and exit points of these curves within the halo, and establish that these points coincide with the curves of flatness closest and furthest from the center of the balance, growing in length as the parameter approaches zero. We also demonstrate that the speed at which these points increase is equivalent to the speed at which the center of flatness converges towards the center of balance.

The detection of gravitational waves has been made possible by the development of highly sensitive instruments such as ground-based detectors and space-based observatories. Ground-based detectors have been successful in identifying linear gravitational waves, while space-based observatories have been detecting the combined effects of linear and quadratic gravitational waves. As a result of the gravitational memory effect, it is predicted that non-linear gravitational waves will be detectable in the future. In this study, we propose a new type of gravitational wave known as gravitational elevated order modes, which is a higher-order harmonic mode of gravitational waves. This type of wave is characterized by its higher frequency content than the fundamental mode and is expected to be amplified in the future, making it potentially detectable. Our study includes a detailed analysis of the propagation of gravitational elevated order modes and the detection of these waves using the third-generation ground-based detector, including estimates of the expected signal-to-noise ratio. Our findings suggest that gravitational elevated order modes may be detectable in the future, providing new insights into the universe.

Astronomers have long been intrigued by the enigmatic "dwarf companions" found near bright stars, sparking a debate over their true nature. By combining Gaia's astrometric data with optical spectroscopy, it is possible to identify and measure the orbits of these objects, even when only a partial orbit is available. In this study, we demonstrate a method for determining the masses of these objects, using the Gaia shadow as a reference point. By applying this method to known binary systems, we were able to derive accurate mass estimates that closely matched previously published values. By applying this method to a large sample of stars from the DANCe survey, we were able to identify and weigh 19 additional systems, including 13 newly resolved binaries. The resulting mass measurements are remarkably consistent, with a mean error of approximately 0.2 dex. The sample of weighed binaries from the DANCe survey is the largest to date and spans a wide range of spectral types, from B to M. The resulting mass function is consistent with field star mass functions, suggesting that the companions are predominantly main-sequence stars. The study also reveals a significant number of companions with masses between 0.5 and 0.6 solar masses, which is consistent with the theory that these companions are formed through the fragmentation of molecular cloud cores.

This paper explores crossover and mutation operators within genetic algorithms to optimize the 0/1 Knapsack Problem, and investigates the impact of selection strategies on the optimal solution. A comprehensive genetic algorithm is developed to solve the 0/1 KP, and its performance is evaluated across three scenarios – single-optimization, multi-objective, and multi-objective with constraints – using benchmark problems from the Galileo library. Notably, the results demonstrate that the selection method influences the convergence of the genetic algorithm, and a modified algorithm is proposed with simulated annealing and adaptive selection to address the maximization version of the 0/1 KP, achieving an optimal solution within a reasonable time frame.

This research paper extends the work of Miao and Peng's paper, in which they investigated L^2 bounds for trilinear oscillatory integrals with a phase function from a homogeneous function. The phase function used in the present study differs by being homogeneous but non-invariant under dilations, resulting in the derivation of improved L^2 bounds.

English hate speech is a pressing issue due to its ease of dissemination and the harm it can inflict on individuals and society as a whole. In this study, a range of pre-processing and evaluation techniques are presented to identify and classify hate speech. The proposed method employs a cutting-edge transformer model and incorporates a unique attention mechanism for hate detection. The model is trained on an extensive dataset comprising over 58,000 annotated tweets and 6.8 million unlabelled ones. The approach is evaluated through a novel metric that considers the interconnectedness of hate and counter-texts within the same social network. The performance of this model is compared to existing state-of-the-art techniques, achieving superior results on a range of metrics, including accuracy, precision, and recall.

Achieving high-accuracy calculations for complex quantum systems is a significant challenge in physics, particularly when it comes to heavy ions. To overcome this, researchers have proposed using the Variational Monte Carlo (VMC) method, which can efficiently evaluate interaction energies. However, a major hurdle is minimizing computational costs while maintaining optimal performance. To address this issue, a new approach, called Hierarchical VMC (Hier-VMC), has been proposed, which can handle a wide range of systems by iteratively refining calculations. To determine the optimal scaling properties, a theoretical framework has been developed, and simulations were conducted using a simplified model system. The results show that the Hier-VMC method can efficiently scale for systems involving up to 1,000 electrons.

The 2020 US presidential election saw an unprecedented number of false claims about the integrity of the vote, primarily disseminated on social media. The widespread dissemination of these false claims has led to an erosion of public trust in the electoral process. To better understand this phenomenon, we have compiled a comprehensive dataset of election-related falsehoods shared on Twitter. The dataset, dubbed VoterFraud2020, encompasses 55,551 election-related assertions of fraud, sourced from 29 different types of alleged irregularities. Utilizing this dataset, we have developed a novel approach to validate and quantify the extent of each claimed fraudulent activity. Our analysis reveals that the majority of claims were based on unproven or disproven allegations, suggesting a significant disparity between perceived and actual levels of fraud. The VoterFraud2020 dataset serves as a valuable resource for researchers examining the spread of election-related misinformation and could potentially inform policy decisions aimed at mitigating the negative impacts of such misinformation.

We establish the existence of nontrivial topological entropy in homotopy classes of diffeomorphisms on compact, flat Riemannian manifolds of dimension at least 3, with the added constraint that at least one Lyapunov exponent is nonzero. This result is achieved through the development of a novel construction, referred to as "fattened systems," which serve as an extension of a previously known construction for systems of dimension 2. A crucial component of this new construction is a significant improvement to a prior analysis by Pollicott, that has been enhanced to accommodate higher-dimensional manifolds.

Recent research has shown that Bayesian Neural Networks can effectively capture uncertainty in regression tasks. However, these networks often struggle with complex problems, particularly in situations requiring multiple predictions. In such cases, using a network to encode the posterior distribution of model parameters can be a viable solution, allowing for the estimation of uncertainty from a limited number of observations. This approach was demonstrated through an experiment in which a simple feed-forward network was trained to predict the posterior distribution of a Gaussian Bayes point estimate model. The results indicate that this technique can produce accurate results even with a small number of observations, surpassing the performance of standard Bayes Point Estimation and Monte Carlo dropout methods.

Instantons in a quantum field theory represent tunneling processes in a statistical ensemble of systems, allowing for a more detailed analysis of non-adiabatic decay processes than the traditional Golden Rule can provide. A specific instanton calculation technique has been developed to obtain instanton trajectories in a modified quantum field theory that incorporates a complex potential describing electronic transitions between molecules. The resulting instanton bubbles correspond to the Marcus theory of electron transfer at the microscopic level, and their bubble size determines the rate of non-adiabatic transitions. The technique can be applied to a broad range of problems, such as studying the rate of non-adiabatic charge transfer between molecules in a solvent environment.

This research introduces a novel approach for managing pathways at a signalized intersection where the green phases are modulated in real-time to optimize traffic flow. The approach combines a dynamic optimization model and a simulation model to minimize average wait times while preventing bottlenecks. The approach was tested using a case study in Mexico City and resulted in a more efficient traffic flow compared to a traditional fixed-time approach, with the ability to easily adjust the study and achieve significant benefits.

A theoretical theory has been developed to explain significant thermoelectric effects in certain materials, specifically those with a specific type of magnetic ordering. The theory involves the movement of magnetic particles within the material, causing a flow of current. These particles can move even when the temperature is not uniform, resulting in a flow of current without electrical resistance. The theory predicts that this phenomenon will be more pronounced in certain materials, specifically those with a specific type of magnetic ordering. The theory also suggests that it may be possible to observe this phenomenon in experiments using a type of alloy made from a rare earth metal and a transition metal.

This article introduces a probabilistic approach for solving the sum problem, a method that involves simulating the evolution of a stochastic process over a finite time frame. We examine this probabilistic method's efficacy in approximating the ideal sum solution as the simulation time approaches infinity.

In the past, monomials have been the primary focus of research in the field of finite fields, with a notable exception. This study shifts its focus to polynomials of a higher order, specifically those defined by binomials of a particular field Fq, with a focus on their irreducible components. The study first establishes a connection between the degree of a finite field extension Fq(y) and the degree of its irreducible polynomial f(x) over Fq. The study then examines the properties of finite fields Fq, with a particular emphasis on those that can be expressed as Fq(t) or Fq(t1, t2,..., t_k). The study also provides a detailed classification of finite fields that can be expressed as a composition of three or four quadratic extensions of prime fields, along with a detailed analysis of the properties of finite extension fields Fq(t) over finite extension fields Fq(t1, t2,..., t_k).

This research introduces a novel method for defining source code abstractions
utilizing the UPPAAL verification tool, enabling exploration and validation of code
structures. A systematic approach is presented to construct an abstract model from a
given source code, allowing for analysis of essential characteristics. Furthermore,
the method facilitates the creation of test cases to evaluate source code
compliance.

A breakthrough in nanotechnology has led to the development of metasurfaces, 
which are thin, flexible surfaces capable of adjusting electromagnetic waves 
in various ways through small, integrated components. Although metasurfaces hold promise for applications in imaging systems, their performance can be compromised by imperfections in manufacturing and uneven performance across the frequency spectrum. To address these challenges, we have developed a comprehensive system that enhances metasurfaces for use in imaging, starting with a new method of frequency scanning using metasurfaces with specific, hexagonal patterns. We then created a simulation model to optimize the performance of these metasurfaces for specific imaging tasks, followed by a method for refining their performance based on their actual behavior. To further improve the efficiency of our system, we have developed a new compression method that reduces the amount of data needed to manufacture these enhanced metasurfaces, allowing for their production at a lower cost.

The occurrence of ac-Stark-shifted frequency components in an intense, circularly polarized laser field has been confirmed. A time-dependent Hamiltonian is used to calculate the first-order correction to the cyclotron frequency, resulting in cyclotron and Landau gauge frequencies all experiencing the same shift. A linearly polarized field, however, distinguishes between the cyclotron and Landau gauge frequencies, leading to their different shifts. Consequently, intense, circularly polarized fields act as universal reference points for frequency measurements.

The primary goal of semantic image blending is to create a seamless image by combining two distinct images without any visible boundaries. While current techniques excel at visually blending images, they often fail to account for the potential changes in the meaning of the combined images. To address this limitation, we have developed a novel approach that enables the creation of new images with altered semantic meanings. Our method involves producing two modified images, each with a different meaning, by manipulating the pixels of each original image based on a probabilistic rule. We then combine these modified images using state-of-the-art blending techniques, resulting in new images with distinct semantic meanings. Our experiments demonstrate that this approach effectively alters the meaning of the combined images, and we also provide a wide range of blending examples that can be used across various applications.

The study of gene expression as a cellular computing mechanism is complex and requires a combination of mathematical modeling and computational techniques to analyze the inherent noise in the system. To address this challenge, we developed a novel method for analyzing time-series data from experimental studies on gene expression. Our approach utilizes a data reduction algorithm that identifies the most representative paths in the Markov model, which can be computed efficiently using Markov Decision Process tools. The proposed method enables an in-depth examination of the dynamics of gene expression, which we demonstrated by applying it to a single-input single-output model of the lac operon. Our results illustrate how the model can be used to gain insights into the system's dynamics and compare them with experimental observations.

A significant obstacle to developing AI tools for education lies in the lack of accessible, structured data from educational settings, limiting the potential for meaningful and context-specific interventions. To address this issue, we've created a semi-supervised platform that allows educational institutions to efficiently collect the necessary data while maintaining student, teacher, and educational environmental data under full institutional control. This tool enables educators to prioritize data collection activities, such as monitoring or interactive lessons, according to their needs. Furthermore, our system facilitates the creation of customized educational scenarios, including virtual classrooms and learning tasks, and provides real-time data capture capabilities. This includes automatic data collection and the option for manual input. Our semi-supervised approach enables educators to decide how much human oversight is required. Additionally, our system integrates data from various sources, including self-reported information from students and teachers, and makes it possible to analyze and annotate data in a user-friendly manner. This includes the ability to search, filter, and annotate data with minimal effort. We have successfully implemented our system in two large-scale schools in the UK and the Netherlands.

A widely used method for training Noisy-Intermediate-Scale Quantum Circuits called Layerwise Quantum Approximate Optimization has been found to face significant challenges when scaling up. This challenge stems from the large number of circuits required for training, where the complexity grows exponentially with the number of layers. This complexity leads to a substantial increase in training time, a resource that is scarce on NISQ devices. Our research reveals that the training process can be overly demanding, causing it to slow down significantly as the number of layers increases. This slowdown is particularly concerning, as adding more layers can increase training time by a factor of ten for certain problem sizes. To address this issue, we have developed a new approach that reduces the strain on the training process. Our method involves dividing the training process into manageable segments and using these segments to improve the model's performance. Our experiments show that this approach can improve training efficiency by up to 10 times. Additionally, we have developed a new method for evaluating the efficiency of training, which takes into account both the time and cost required to improve accuracy. Our results show that this new metric can effectively identify the optimal balance between accuracy and training resources.

The significant concern of re-identification in data sharing stems from the fact that removing identifiable elements does not guarantee privacy preservation. We investigated the re-identification vulnerability of data owners by evaluating their ability to retrieve data with the highest likelihood. Our proposed IR-index provides a comprehensive solution to measure this re-identification risk, which can be applied to both categorical and numerical data, offering various attributes at different granularities. We also developed a suite of algorithms to accelerate the IR-index construction and re-identification process, which can be integrated with existing databases to ensure data users' privacy. Our experimental results demonstrate that IR-index achieves a balance between accuracy and efficiency, surpassing existing state-of-the-art methods in both speed and precision.

The increasing availability of grid data has enabled researchers to study power grids more effectively, but often this data is incomplete, necessitating the development of advanced recovery methods. To address this need, this paper introduces a novel approach to recovering full-scale time series data from limited samples. By leveraging the inherent structure of power grids, where data from different locations can be expressed through shifts of a single signal, the proposed method employs a linear transformation model and uses data carvings to learn these relationships. Experimental results, utilizing real data from the 2020 IEEE PES PMAPS, demonstrate the method's effectiveness and efficiency in various scenarios.

We examine a scenario in which a given operator, $A$, is not constant, but meets the requirement that for any given direction, $d$, the operator maps an open neighborhood around $A$'s action on $d$ to an open neighborhood around $A$'s action on $d$. This enables us to demonstrate the convergence of a specific algorithm to the sole solution of a variational inequality problem under the assumption that initial conditions fall within a specified open set. Furthermore, we extend the proof by considering iterative processes that involve disturbances, which remain bounded in relation to the distance between the current state and the solution to the problem.

This study investigates the patterns formed by specific points on a hyperbolic plane section, which are shaped by repeated transformations of a geometric figure. We demonstrate that these patterns can be created using a type of Fuchsian ensemble and that a corresponding model exists where repeated transformations correspond to changes in a parameter, resulting in a uniform distribution of resulting patterns. We utilize this model to study large ensembles and derive various results, including the convergence of certain probability distributions and the characteristics of the longest paths in these patterns. We also show that an extreme scenario in which points lie on a hyperbolic plane section, known as the geodesic crosspoint, can be achieved in both the large ensemble and large deviation limit, which is surprising given that these two limits typically do not converge.

The process $\Upsilon (3S)\rightarrow e^{\pm}\mu^{\mp}$ is analyzed to study a potential signal of lepton flavor violation. Utilizing the decay $\Upsilon (3S)\rightarrow \gamma 3S$, which has a established branching ratio, the estimated upper limit of the branching ratio for $3S\rightarrow e^{\pm}\mu^{\pm}$ is less than $10^{-7}$ at the 90% confidence level. This prediction is consistent with other theoretical studies.

The application of hydrostatic pressure to the flat-band superconductor Pd$_3$P$_2$S$_8$ leads to a significant increase in the critical temperature from 3.8 K at standard pressure to 9.2 K at 1.2 GPa, making it the highest pressure-enhanced superconductivity observed so far. Our investigation into the single crystals reveals that the increase in the superconducting transition temperature can be attributed to a shift in the Fermi energy towards a nearby peak in the density of states, which is located at approximately 0.2 eV. In contrast, the Fermi surface remains largely unchanged under high pressure, while the effective mass exhibits a notable increase, leading to a significant enhancement of the superconducting properties. Our findings demonstrate that the application of pressure can be used to control the Fermi level, leading to a precise tuning of the superconducting characteristics.

We have developed a method to extract black hole data from gravitational theories that do not propagate degrees of stress tensor beyond the leading order. Our approach involves identifying the canonical momenta associated with the boundary terms of the action and demonstrating that the resulting Hamiltonian and momentum equations yield black hole data, including the mass, angular momentum, and charge of the Schwarzschild-(A)dS black hole, as well as its event horizon area and temperature, in the JT gravity framework.

Neural ODEs have become a popular choice for modeling complex system dynamics due to their ability to handle high-dimensional data, yet they often struggle with noisy and erratic information. To address this issue, we introduce a new method for learning neural ODEs from noisy and erratic data. By incorporating a hidden Markov property, we model each observation as a latent system state, allowing the learning process to rely on either sequential or batch training approaches. A novel loss function is also developed to account for the variability in transition dynamics between different states. Experimental results on both simulated and real-world data demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in improving neural ODE accuracy and robustness.

The objective of object-target navigation is to guide an agent to a target object in a scene. Current methods primarily utilize object appearance features to determine the target location. However, these methods are hindered by the agent's limited perception of the target, resulting in suboptimal performance. In this study, we introduce the Object Recall Transformer, a novel navigation method that leverages an object-language model to efficiently recall the target's appearance from memory, ultimately facilitating an efficient and effective navigation solution.

Current pre-trained language models are typically trained using a fixed set of tasks, yet this approach can be improved upon. A new method called OPT-IML utilizes the CLIP visual backbone to create a shared space for tasks, enabling more effective learning and transfer between visual and text domains. Unlike previous approaches, our method trains language models without relying on manually designed tasks or human annotations. Instead, it leverages automatic cross-validation to automatically generate tasks on raw text data. As a result, OPT-IML achieves notable improvements in performance on widely used benchmark datasets like SuperGLUE and HellaSWAG. Notably, it outperforms GPT-3 and zero-shot models in zero-shot settings, while also demonstrating strong generalization capabilities across various domains.

The Scratch online platform allows children to create and share computational media and has enabled researchers to study how children engage with and produce digital content. By analyzing the data from Scratch, this study examines the characteristics of children's digital footprints and the paths they create on the platform. The results show a wide variety of unique digital signatures, and that children are increasingly using Scratch to interact with the system. This study also identifies areas for future research and suggests paths for children to follow when navigating the platform.

Theoretical modeling of chemical and spectroscopic properties of numerous substances relies heavily on the homogeneous electron gas. Our research focuses on the effects of perturbations on the homogeneous electron gas, specifically using a transcorrelated Hamiltonian. We develop a method to calculate these effects, starting with the uncorrelated Hamiltonian and then adjusting it to account for the transcorrelation using a specific operator. We then apply this adjusted Hamiltonian within the adiabatic switching framework to derive a perturbation theory series. We validate the accuracy of our method by comparing our results to full configuration interaction calculations and reference values obtained using the uncorrelated Hamiltonian.

This research develops a physically limited covariance growth model for random sets representing particle flow, driven by uncertainty in position and velocity. It is shown that covariance growth is restricted by physical constraints when considering velocity uncertainty separately from position uncertainty. By applying optimal transport theory, we establish a unique relationship between the covariance of a random set and the joint probability density of its components, given its marginal velocities. This relationship is applied to simulate particle flow in turbulent flows, with the covariance of an random set representing particles initially at rest constrained by the flow.

The rapid growth of tensor data in fields like computer vision, physics, and mechanics necessitates efficient tensor decomposition techniques. This paper presents a novel randomized three-dimensional tensor decomposition algorithm that prioritizes data privacy by keeping intermediate results secret. We've developed a corresponding computation model and analyzed its efficiency, and our algorithm's time complexity is optimal. Experimentally, our method outperforms traditional tensor decomposition approaches in terms of speed.

The primary goal of learning-based methods in autonomous driving and robotics is to develop a reliable system that can be safely integrated into real-world applications. However, existing approaches often overlook the potential risks associated with learning from simulation and directly transferring policies to real-world settings, which is a significant drawback. To address this critical issue, we introduce a novel method, SafeAPT, that leverages a simulation-based approach to develop a safety net that ensures the learned policy's reliability before deployment. This method involves creating a diverse set of policies with varying levels of risk and using them to generate a dataset of low-risk trajectories. By utilizing this dataset, we can safely train a robust policy while also enhancing its reliability. Our approach has been successfully tested on the Carla Challenge and the Safe Learning Environment, and it has demonstrated the capability to significantly reduce risks in real-world applications while also achieving high reliability.

This review examines the occurrence of jet activity in various cosmic objects,
including active galactic nuclei (AGN) and radio galaxies, along with their
associated radio jet features. We also explore the connection between jets and the
underlying black hole, its surrounding environment, and the galaxy hosting it. We
investigate how the composition of jet material influences the observed radio
emission and identify key areas requiring further research.

This research focuses on the estimation of time-nonstationary parameters within complex time series regression models. A new approach called Concurrent Sieve Estimation (CSE) is proposed for two distinct models: the autoregressive time-nonstationary model and the bilinear time-nonstationary model. In these models, CSE is demonstrated to be consistent under weak dependence conditions and reaches the same asymptotic distribution as the Sieve Extreme Learning Approach proposed by Cheridito and Guggiehramti (2021) under stationary parameters. In contrast, CSE diverges from the traditional sieve estimation under stationary and/or nonstationary parameters. A Monte-Carlo simulation is used to compare the performance of CSE and traditional sieve estimation methods.

This research explores the challenges of Automated Aggressive Language Classification (AALC) at a broader scale, particularly in low and medium resource environments. AALC tasks are complicated by the subjective nature of aggression and the distinct cultural contexts in which it manifests. Current datasets primarily originated from countries with high resources, leaving the task less understood in low and middle-income nations. We propose a collection of datasets for AALC in low and middle-income nations, created by combining publicly available data with new samples from low and middle-income countries. The resulting dataset comprises 21,000 examples across 15 languages, including 9 from low and middle-income regions and 12 from diverse countries with varying resource levels. We also introduce a neural framework for AALC, which incorporates a multi-layered bidirectional long short-term memory model with a multi-layer perceptron for classification. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed model outperforms existing models in the field, achieving a macro F1 score of 0.64.

The brain's connectivity plays a vital role in determining how different brain regions interact with one another.  However, the current methods used to study brain connectivity are often limited by the fact that they rely on analyzing a small number of resting-state scans, but these scans do not provide a complete picture of how brain connectivity varies across both individuals and resting states.  To overcome this limitation, we have developed a new approach that uses a type of artificial neural network to create a detailed map of how brain connectivity changes across different states.  Our method involves training the network to predict the strength of the connection between two brain regions based on the patterns of the time series data from those regions, and we have found that it produces highly accurate maps of brain connectivity that are comparable to those produced by more traditional methods of analyzing resting-state data.  Our results also show that this new approach can be used to identify the specific connections that contribute to different patterns of brain activity, and it may be useful for studying the effects of various neurological conditions on brain connectivity.

A time-varying linear system with a time-varying coefficient influenced by a time-varying noise is considered, with the coefficient following an exponential growth pattern and the noise adhering to a certain dissipative condition. It is shown that noise-driven perturbations can induce instability in the system under specific conditions. Building on this concept, a related problem in optimization is formulated, with the objective of minimizing the worst-case value of an integrable function over an infinite horizon. A novel control strategy combining a linear feedback and noise manipulation is proposed, enabling the elimination of perturbations and the achievement of a desirable asymptotic performance.

This research develops a novel, implicit-explicit Runge-Kutta method tailored for hyperbolic systems with nonlinear source terms, designed for use on regular and irregular grids. It leverages the implicit-explicit strategy to enhance computational efficiency by optimizing the solution of linear system components. A key aspect of this approach is the use of an explicit stage to reduce the complexity of solving nonlinear source terms at high stages, where computational costs become significant. Additionally, this method requires the solution of a linear system at each stage, whose coefficient matrix features non-trivial boundary conditions. We address this challenge through a novel approach, where we transform the implicit-explicit scheme into an equivalent semi-implicit form, thereby reducing the complexity of the system's solution and enabling the use of standard solvers. We provide a comprehensive analysis of the method's stability and convergence, along with numerical results demonstrating its effectiveness on a variety of test cases.

The absorption of solar cells can be significantly improved by reducing thickness 
and increasing the absorption of ultrathin films by utilizing short wavelengths, 
especially in the visible spectrum. To enhance absorption, a novel approach 
involves integrating a textured back reflector with a thin silicon film, 
demonstrating that absorption can reach 85% across a wide wavelength range for 50 nm and 
500 nm thick silicon films, with the textured reflector boosting absorption by 20-40% 
compared to a smooth reflector at different wavelengths.

In cases where data is uncertain or unreliable, it's often represented using a credibility scale, rather than a precise measurement. A common framework for handling uncertainty in data analysis is called credal sets or lower and upper probabilities. However, when dealing with complex data structures, like networks, it's difficult to account for the uncertainty in each connection. We propose a new method, called credal assessment networks, which allows us to assess the uncertainty in large networks, even with uncertain measurements at each node. By applying these networks to a real-world problem, such as inferring a graph of genetic relationships based on uncertain DNA data, we demonstrate their value and discover some surprising insights.

The task of recommending top-K items based on a query, also referred to as top-K suggestion, is a fundamental problem in various natural language processing and information retrieval applications. To address this challenge, researchers have developed distance learning models that utilize the similarity between an query and an item to predict its relevance. Nevertheless, existing models have several limitations, including the inability to handle multiple relevant items and the need for a fixed margin. To address these issues, we propose a novel model called Probabilistic Distance Learning, denoted as PDL, which is capable of identifying multiple relevant items and adapting to different margins. The model utilizes a probabilistic approach to predict item relevance, leveraging a mixture of similarities between a query and an item. The model is trained using a novel loss function that integrates both classification and regression losses, enabling it to handle ranking tasks with multiple relevant items. The proposed model also adapts to different margins, including a learned margin and a fixed margin. The experimental results demonstrate that PDL outperforms state-of-the-art models in various recommendation tasks, including query-level and item-level tasks.

We investigate the concept of non-Markovianity in quantum systems that don't lose their initial properties by losing their purity. It's found that such behavior is a common occurrence in systems that don't lose their energy, specifically in systems that can't remove energy from their system. Furthermore, we provide multiple examples of systems that exhibit this behavior. Additionally, we introduce a new set of operations for a type of quantum communication process called a quantum channel, which involves removing energy from a system. It's found that this type of operation leads to a kind of non-Markovianity in the system that doesn't lose its purity.

The primary goal of classification is to forecast an unknown target variable.  However, the underlying data generating process can be intricate, making it difficult to forecast the target variable reliably.  To address this complexity, this study suggests a novel method called Counterfactual Inference and Engaged Learning (CIEL) that leverages the strengths of counterfactual thinking and inference to enhance the accuracy of classification.  By utilizing a causal graph to pinpoint the most influential features, the CIEL approach can accurately predict the target variable.  To ensure that the underlying causal graph is accurately represented, the CIEL method incorporates a learning mechanism that adjusts the model's parameters through a learning process.  Furthermore, the study proposes a new loss function that complements the CIEL approach, resulting in superior performance compared to existing methods.  Experimental results demonstrate the CIEL method's effectiveness in classifying intricate problems, especially when faced with limited data.

The field of robotics has seen significant advancements in mapping and navigation
capabilities, but still lacks a standardized approach to evaluating the effectiveness
of semantic mapping algorithms. To bridge this gap, we introduce a novel tool,
