RoSmEEry, which generates 3D environments and annotates them with various
categories to test the performance of semantic mapping algorithms. By using a
game engine to create realistic 3D scenes and a machine learning model to
classify scene elements, RoSmEEry generates training datasets and evaluates the
performance of these algorithms. We demonstrate the capabilities of RoSmEEry
through a case study using the OpenGIS scene, which highlights the tool's
flexibility and reliability in assessing and improving the performance of semantic
mapping algorithms.

Rikudo represents a simplified model of a planar graph where vertices are connected in a specific manner.  A planar graph where every pair of vertices shares an edge will exhibit a property known as the Rikudo property if for every subset of edges, the vertices forming a specific triangle will have a degree of either one or two, thereby forming a single face when combined with the surrounding edges.  A previously proposed algorithm allowed for the identification of whether a given Rikudo planar graph exhibits the Rikudo property but this paper demonstrates through a proof that determining whether a given Rikudo planar graph has this property is in fact a NP-hard problem.

Optimal Conveyance Networks move large volumes of commodities through vast,
geographically dispersed distribution systems comprising various modes of
transportation. A comprehensive framework for modeling and optimizing such systems
is proposed in this research. Specifically, a cutting-edge algorithm is developed
to efficiently handle the planning and management of OCNs spanning vast areas
accredited to diverse transport modes and numerous nodes involved. To address this
complexity, the problem is redefined as a series of smaller-scale issues, to
which an advanced optimization method is applied. This method, based on a
combination of a cutting-plane algorithm and a specialized transport problem
solver, offers significant computational advantages. This innovative solution has
been thoroughly tested across multiple scenarios, including a real-world case study
in the United Kingdom.

Ramanujan introduced several key identities, known as modular formulas, in his 1913 paper "Symmetric Binary Forms and Polygons," which include the Hecke's quadruple product formula and Kaneko-Yamanouchi weights. We aim to explore and present alternative expressions for these identities, which are tied to theta functions and are organized around Hecke's law. A notable aspect of our work is the derivation of a new modular formula inspired by Ramanujan's for the generating function of partitions into distinct odd parts.

We have conducted a comprehensive study of eight gravitationally lensing quasars by analyzing high-resolution spectra obtained from the Keck I telescope between 2018 and 2021. Leveraging the enhanced capabilities of the LRIS instrument, we obtained precise redshift and velocity dispersion measurements for 13 lensing galaxies, thereby providing valuable insights into the mass distribution of lens galaxies on larger scales. Our findings enable a more accurate assessment of the impact of lensing galaxies on the cosmological model, particularly when combined with other advanced datasets.

This paper explores q-FDEs with time scales, focusing on nonlinear versions of these equations. By translating q-FDEs into discrete equations via Sturm-Liouville Wronskians, we apply Bellman and Krasnoselskii theorems along with the variance technique to establish new stability theorems. Our results expand our understanding of linear and semi-linear models, while new outcomes are derived for fractional q-FDEs.

The discovery of significant and distinct Hall phenomena associated with phonons in a time-dependent magnetic field has been a significant breakthrough in the study of phonon transport. This phenomenon has garnered substantial interest due to its potential to revolutionize thermoelectric technology development. A comprehensive theoretical framework for this phenomenon has yet to be established, with most existing research relying on numerical analysis. This study provides a theoretical framework to explain the phonon Hall effect, which arises from the interaction between the time-varying magnetic field and the intrinsic wave nature of phonons. This theoretical framework successfully predicts the Hall index and provides a clear physical description of the phenomenon. This theoretical framework has been verified through numerical simulations, which demonstrate its accuracy in predicting the Hall index. This study's findings are significant because they provide a theoretical basis for understanding the phonon Hall phenomenon and its potential to be applied across various wave phenomena.

A novel Raman imaging technique, called altered excitation Raman difference spectroscopy (AERDS), has been developed to detect chemical compositions in biological samples by identifying specific molecules based on their Raman shifts. This method, which involves exciting samples with two different wavelengths and then analyzing the resulting signals, has been enhanced by incorporating the nod and shuffle technique to increase efficiency and accuracy. This advanced approach allows for the construction of detailed Raman shift maps, thus offering a valuable tool for disease diagnosis and drug discovery. This paper presents the underlying theory and mathematical framework of the AERDS technique, as well as its application in biological imaging and spectral analysis.
This article presents matrix extensions of the Fejér and Levin-Stel'kin inequalities for the spectral operator, along with some practical applications.

We investigate the mean null energy condition for an observer at a finite distance
from a black hole that's undergoing evaporation, using a framework based on the
Thermofield Theory. We examine the effects of this condition on the holographic
geometry up to second-order corrections in the self-dual sector, which account
for the black hole's evaporation. Our analysis reveals that, from the observer's
perspective, a holographic spacetime initially behaving like a vacuum solution
(AdS-Schwarzschild) complies with the mean null energy condition until the
evaporation process begins. Notably, taking into consideration evaporation-related
corrections, the mean null energy condition is breached inside a region near the
horizon, which marks a critical difference from the non-evaporating scenario,
where no such violation occurs.

This research delves into diverse elements of conformal field theories, including computational methods for 2D conformal dimensions and modular invariant partition functions, lattice models for spin 2/1 correspondences, and the application of group theory to classify operators in conformal field theories, especially with symmetry groups like SU(n) and Virasoro. It also covers AdS/CFT from a Lie group perspective, with a focus on the SU(2) case and an examination of the algebraic data required for symmetric functions. Additionally, the research touches on the use of conformal field theories as holographic probes for black hole behavior and as a tool for studying finite temperature effects in the small black hole and large black hole thermodynamics of the AdS5xS5 supergravity model.

The maturity model for the ICS cybersecurity evaluation framework, ICS-CTM2, assesses an organization's cybersecurity posture across five stages of sophistication, from foundational to advanced levels of maturity. This model evaluates each stage using a standardized set of cybersecurity practices and processes, along with associated evidence requirements. To ensure practicality, the model is tailored to specific ICS domains and grounded in the expertise of cybersecurity professionals within those areas. To illustrate its application, we apply ICS-CTM2 to the power generation and transmission sectors, and provide a case study of a power plant subject to an attack. Through this detailed analysis, the model provides a comprehensive view of the cybersecurity strengths and weaknesses of the system under review.

In the context of Reinforcement Learning, particularly in Markov Games, agents learn to act based on their perception of the environment without considering other agents' actions. This limitation makes cooperation challenging to achieve. To facilitate collaboration, we propose a new paradigm involving a manager agent that uses a deep reinforcement learning approach to make decisions for the team. This manager uses a value depiction that represents the team's overall reward, influenced by both the current state and individual agent actions. The manager's reward depends on a parameter, referred to as avarice, which balances individual rewards with the benefit of collaboration. When avarice is high, the manager prioritizes personal gain over team benefit, whereas lower avarice values encourage collaboration for the greater good. Our experiments demonstrate that this approach can foster cooperation in challenging scenarios, such as Poker and Zero-Sum Games, and that varying the avarice parameter allows the manager to balance individual and collective team interests.

Pretrained language models have the tendency to perpetuate societal biases, 
such as stereotypical prejudice, which have long been present in society. 
Our study examines whether these models have biased perceptions of groups based 
on their characteristics. We introduce StereoSet, a new benchmark dataset to assess 
pretrained language models' sensitivity to characteristics like age, sex, and race. 
We have expanded StereoSet to include a variety of topics and a diverse set of 
characteristics. We have also developed a new evaluation method that uses 
counterfactual scenarios to test whether these models can recognize and adapt 
to changes in characteristics. Our results show that even highly advanced models 
like GPT-3 and T5 are prone to biases, which have not diminished over time. 
Our hope is that StereoSet will help researchers and developers to better understand 
and mitigate these biases in language models.

This research introduces a novel off-policy reinforcement learning approach to improve electrical tilt control in wind turbines. By optimizing electrical tilt control to reduce noise and stress on blades, the method increases power output and extends turbine life. Off-policy reinforcement learning allows for effective data utilization, particularly in environments with limited data availability. Utilizing a neural network policy, the approach is adaptable to various settings and can effectively address the challenges associated with this domain. A policy is proposed that incorporates the collective effects of two sensors - a tilt sensor and a yaw sensor - to develop a precise control policy. To address the instability issues in off-policy reinforcement learning, the approach employs a policy regularization technique. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of this method in achieving stable and efficient electrical tilt control.

The CKM angle $\gamma$ was measured based on data from LHCb, incorporating $3\,$fb$^{-1}$ and $5\,$fb$^{-1}$ luminosities. A weighted average of previous LHCb results was employed, enhancing the overall statistical precision on $\gamma$. This was achieved through two distinct approaches: a linear re-evaluation of previous findings and a new estimation of $\gamma$ from two of the prior studies. The combined statistical precision on $\gamma$ reached was improved by approximately two times.

This research paper delves into the geometric properties of intricate ellipsoids, a subset of intricate hypersurfaces, and examines their respective symmetries, classification, and related features. It also explores the interconnection between complicated and intricate ellipsoids, and presents a case study involving a family of intricate ellipsoids in four-dimensional space, concluding with a thought-provoking question regarding their extension to higher-dimensional spaces.

This paper presents findings of user testing for a personal data marketplace, conducted in 2019 and 2020. We examined users' perceptions of buying, selling, and sharing data with a marketplace, discovering users hold positive views on data markets, despite some concerns. Specifically, participants were thought to be more willing to sell data to strangers when the data's purpose is clearly defined and beneficial to both parties. Additionally, users' willingness to sell data appears to be influenced by factors such as the potential for frequent data sales, control over data sale proceeds, and assurance of secure data handling. Future data marketplaces should prioritize implementing these design principles to foster a positive user experience.

In 5G new radio (NR) and beyond, FTN signaling is proposed as an alternative to SC-FDE for data transmission, offering improved spectral efficiency. However, detecting FTN constellations in the presence of noise poses a significant challenge due to the non-spherical geometry of the signal set. Existing decoders based on sphere decoding and list decoding fall short in resolving this problem. To address this limitation, this research introduces a deep learning-based approach to list decoding, which involves training a neural network to map received samples to a lower-dimensional space preserving the underlying constellation, thus enabling the recovery of the original signal. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms traditional decoders by as much as 4 dB gain in SNR.

Impact algebras, a variation of fuzzy algebra theory proposed by Frink, have been further investigated by examining their topological structure. Specifically, two topological interpretations, known as the arrangement topology and Frink ideal topology, have been discussed in detail. By demonstrating that arrangement topology is a form of induced topology, it's shown that the arrangement topology is equivalent to the Frink ideal topology when the impact algebra is symmetric. Furthermore, it has been established that the Frink ideal topology is orthonormal, and a method for constructing a separable impact algebra is presented using Frink ideal topology.

A novel data augmentation technique, SaliencyMix, is presented, which utilizes class-specific saliency maps to identify and conceal irrelevant image sections to boost model generalization. Contrary to current methods, which generate random transformations, SaliencyMix strategically diminishes redundant image features. Experimental results demonstrate SaliencyMix's generalization-enhancing capabilities across various convolutional neural networks and multiple datasets. Notably, SaliencyMix outperforms competing data augmentation techniques like CutMix and MixUp in multiple scenarios. Moreover, combining SaliencyMix with MixUp yields the highest accuracy when utilizing weak labels for supervision.

We explore the concept of trace maps on the infinite-dimensional Iwahari--Hecke ring by building on the work of Broue, Burrowes, and Michler. Their previous findings on 2-sided traces are extended to all traces, and we examine specific properties associated with these maps. Furthermore, additional properties linked to endomorphism algebras of permutation modules are investigated. Specifically, a particular Iwahari--Hecke ring element, denoted as z_0, is studied due to its unique role in generating the ring within the endomorphism algebras of permutation modules. This investigation culminates in a detailed computation of the endomorphism algebras for both the regular and permutation modules.

A new method is proposed that leverages the unique properties of gravitational lensing to test alternative gravity theories. By combining intrinsic galaxy alignment with shear from the same field, this approach can differentiate between Horndeski theories that mimic the standard Lambda-CDM model but alter gravity at large scales. A simulation-based study demonstrates the method's potential to detect and differentiate between these theories, even when assuming a standard Lambda-CDM cosmology. The method's sensitivity is estimated to be around 1 sigma, with the potential to improve using a subset of data from the Euclid survey. The method's success is dependent on a specific parameter range and mass distribution, but a key aspect is its ability to be independent of other observational data, allowing for constraints on alternative gravity models that are not dependent on other astrophysical or cosmological assumptions.

In a study, we examined the dynamic properties of a disc-shaped particle suspension, specifically focusing on the impact of particle shape and volume fraction on their behavior. Our findings indicate that when the volume fraction of the suspension increases, the particles' movement shifts from an almost free state to a confined state. Interestingly, in the confined state, the particle suspension exhibits increased flexibility and elasticity compared to other soft particle systems. With a decrease in volume fraction, the particles become more separated, and their movement becomes less controlled by the system. As a result, the particle suspension exhibits reduced elasticity and enhanced plasticity. Our study also reveals that the particle shape has a significant effect on the particle's movement, specifically, the larger the particle's dimension in one direction compared to the other two, the more pronounced the effect.

The use of nanoparticles as building blocks for nanoscale self-assembly relies on fusing them into uniform size and shape. However, their inherent complexity and size variability make simulating this process extremely challenging. To address this issue, we developed a Bayesian approach that combines data from experiments and simulations to evaluate and improve computational models of nanoparticle fusion. By integrating our method with a computational tool, we were able to create a more realistic simulation of gold nanoparticle fusion, which better aligned with experimental findings. Our approach can be applied to a wide range of complex systems, such as environmental and energy-related phenomena, and offers a framework for enhanced model development and validation.

This is the first part of a research paper in which we explore parameterized families of operators generated by the $L^2$-forms associated with second-order elliptic differential operators on various bounded domains within $\mathbb{R}^d$. Our objective is to establish a theory that allows for the decomposition of these operators and their eigenfunctions in terms of parameterized expansions. This theory will facilitate the analysis of complex phenomena arising from parameterized potential operators, such as bifurcations and non-linear stability, in a systematic and organized manner. The key components of this theory include the concept of admissible domains, the notion of admissible operators, and the use of parameterized decompositions to analyze operator behavior in a given domain as a parameter varies. In the next section, we will discuss the development of admissible operators and the detailed structure of their parameterized expansions.

The concept of taste is a complex entity with a vast array of flavors, yet research suggests that human brains can distinguish between a relatively small number of taste types. Studies have employed various methods to categorize tastes, often resulting in distinct yet interconnected classification systems. Our study utilizes a network analysis approach to examine taste relationships, mapping them onto a tetrahedral structure. This framework provides a clear understanding of taste categories while revealing their interconnections, allowing us to identify key features such as the central role of sweetness and the blurriness of spicy and sour tastes.

This paper establishes for the first time novel closed-form expressions for the (h,q)-Genocchi numbers and polynomials, incorporating a new parameter h. Key equations and their respective transformations under specific change of variable settings enable derivation of the closed-form expressions. Notably, as a secondary outcome, novel beta values are also formulated.

Researchers have been utilizing artificial intelligence to analyze electronic health records, but most studies have focused on short-term predictions, focusing on specific diagnoses or medication risks. A recent study demonstrates a method for making long-term predictions based on a comprehensive evaluation of a patient's health. A real-world application of this method was implemented at a physical therapy clinic specializing in the treatment of spinal injuries. The study utilized machine learning to identify factors contributing to improved outcomes in patients, discovering that receiving home-based therapy played a significant role. The study's findings have been applied to create a decision-making tool, enabling clinicians to identify patients likely to benefit from home-based therapy and streamline the referral process, which has been successfully integrated into the clinic's workflow.

We propose a causal inference framework to address memory distortion in case-control studies, where research focuses on rare events. In case-control designs, sampling rare events is necessary, often using controls from large populations to serve as comparisons. However, participants' recollections of past events are influenced by the occurrence of those events, which is particularly problematic when studying rare events like head injuries. To address this issue, we developed a causal inference framework that can be used to correct for the distortion in recollections. Our method, based on the concept of causal consistency, allows us to compare the experiences of individuals with and without a traumatic event, accounting for potential differences in demographics and study participation. Our simulations show that neglecting this distortion can lead to biased estimates of the causal effect's distribution, but using our method provides more reliable results. We applied our framework to a study of self-reported concussion experiences in Canadian skiers and snowboarders, finding that accounting for the distortion significantly reduced bias in our estimated effect's magnitude and direction. Our method can be applied to other case-control studies of rare events, helping to correct for the distortion in recollections and increase the validity of causal inferences.

Generative models can create high-quality synthetic datasets, but training them is a complex task. Traditional methods like stochastic gradient descent often result in suboptimal solutions, and more precise approaches like maximum likelihood (ML) training are computationally expensive. To address this challenge, we propose an efficient ML training method for generative models utilizing invertible neural networks, which allows for exact computation of log-likelihood gradients. Our method, built on efficient techniques from efficient path integral methods, is applicable to a broad range of generative models. We test our approach on Gaussian mixture models, autoregressive models, and variational autoencoders, achieving significant improvements in training speed and log-likelihood estimates in all cases.

The concept of smart cities has gained significant attention worldwide, and city governments are facing challenges in evaluating the performance of their smart projects. To address this issue, we present a novel approach that leverages data visualization to help cities assess their progress and decision-making processes. Our approach utilizes visual features to facilitate semantic reasoning and automatically generate labels for clusters in high-dimensional datasets. We applied this method to an urban dataset and conducted user studies to compare it with state-of-the-art hierarchical clustering algorithms, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach in evaluating smart city data.

This study explores the HDG-P0 method for two-dimensional reaction-diffusion equations and generalized Stokes problems within rectangular domains, with the boundary conditions provided. The method relies on H10 and L2 finite element spaces for post-processing and its associated gradient-free and Laplacian-free preconditioners are examined using various parameters. The optimal geometric multigrid V-cycle is proven to converge at a rate of O(log^2 epsilon), where epsilon represents the parameter value, and this conclusion is based on the L2 residual norm within the L2 norm.

The E-value, a measure of evidence strength, takes into account the number of alternatives, providing a robust estimator even when some data are missing. This study develops a Bayesian framework for assessing evidence, incorporating sensitivity analysis for cases where not all alternatives are considered. The proposed approach is particularly valuable in the presence of unmeasured confounding factors. The proposed Bayesian E-value is calculated by simulating multiple data sets and computing the proportion of times the null hypothesis is rejected. The study demonstrates the proposed method's performance in various scenarios, such as binary and continuous outcomes, both with and without missing data. The performance of the proposed Bayesian E-value is compared with frequentist conditional and inverse probability E-values. The study also presents a Bayesian inverse probability E-value for binary outcomes. The study's results show that the proposed Bayesian inverse probability E-value is more sensitive and robust than the Bayesian inverse probability conditional E-value. The study also shows that the proposed Bayesian E-value and Bayesian inverse probability E-value are more sensitive and robust than the frequentist counterparts.

In crossover experiments where crossover effects vary, traditional analysis methods like the Central Limit Theorem may not be applicable due to unbalanced data distribution. Consequently, researchers often rely on the random permutation test, assessing the null hypothesis by repeatedly sampling observations and comparing the outcomes to the original data. 

Typically, when analyzing crossover effects, the absence of certain effects at specific time points is anticipated, and the random permutation test can be utilized to verify this assumption by examining effects at consecutive time points. 

This study investigates the reliability of the random permutation test in detecting missing crossover effects. The findings indicate that the test's sensitivity is relatively low when multiple effects are absent, and the sensitivity decreases as the number of missing effects and variance of the treatment effect grow. 

To address these issues, the study proposes a two-stage approach. The first stage involves a hypothesis test to identify which crossover effects are absent, and the second stage involves a specific analysis of the detected absent effects. 

The proposed approach is demonstrated through a simulation study and applied to real-world data from a clinical trial in China evaluating the efficacy of a specific medication.

A specific type of weak monoidal framework is established, which retains the essential characteristics of a monoidal structure but omits certain requirements, such as the existence of a unit object. It is demonstrated that the associated coalgebras of this framework are equivalent to Stasheff A$_n$-heterocycles, which in turn form the edges of the associahedra. The topological properties of these associahedra enable the derivation of a normal form for coalgebra morphisms within this class, which yields an enhanced Stasheff deformation retraction.

Memory-centric computing heavily relies on DRAM as a primary memory hierarchy level, necessitating the development of novel in-DRAM solutions to optimize performance, energy, and cost. However, introducing new in-DRAM functionality into commercial DRAM products is a complex process, often in conflict with existing memory operations. To address this challenge, we introduce CODIC, an integrated DRAM hardware-software framework that enables users to design, deploy, and test in-DRAM customizations. CODIC provides a hardware abstraction layer for in-DRAM software and is integrated with DRAM simulators, allowing users to develop and deploy new in-DRAM solutions with ease. We demonstrate the efficacy of CODIC by presenting three examples: two that enhance DRAM functionality and one that addresses security concerns.

This research is a follow-up to "The Function of Functional Programming in Administration and Orchestration of Virtualized Network Assets," where we explored various approaches to network management, focusing on those based on functional programming. This study delves into the potential of such methods in developing innovative network solutions. By examining the properties of virtual network functions (VNFs), we aim to identify suitable models for network management, considering the unique requirements of each. We demonstrate how different programming paradigms can effectively model network behavior, including flow of control, data, and signaling. We also discuss the benefits and limitations of these models, including their application in network management, orchestration, and configuration. To illustrate the practical implications of these concepts, we provide case studies of real-world applications. Finally, we outline future research directions, including the integration of network management models with other functional programming approaches.

Achieving fault-tolerant quantum processing is a significant challenge, but the concept of topological quantum computing is seen as a potential solution. It involves encoding quantum information in a complex, fault-tolerant manner, allowing for operations within a robust quantum framework. The toric code is a prominent example of such a framework, and our research investigates its potential by comparing single and multiple qubit operations within this context. By examining the toric code's structure, we can identify a relationship between its stabilizers and the creation of a multi-qubit T gate. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a single-qubit X gate is sufficient to generate the required operations for encoding and processing data in the toric code's surface code.

The OPUS job management system is a grid computing tool that supports various scientific applications, incorporating established standards such as GT 4 IWF, IWF, IWF, IWF, and IWF. Developed by Sun Microsystems, these standards provide a unified interface for integrating grid services into applications, including those written in Java and C++. As an instance of the 0IWF protocol family, IWF is a service-oriented interface allowing clients to interact with grid services in a asynchronous manner. Built upon the Apache Java EE implementation, StAX, IWF is a user-friendly and platform-independent interface for the Java language. Similarly, IWF c is a C++ library that is based on the same 0IWF protocol. To demonstrate its capabilities, OPUS is integrated with the MDS-1 metadata service, enabling the submission of jobs, monitoring their status, and retrieving their results. As a result, a Java-based science application can be executed on a grid without the need for job management code, leveraging the capabilities of OPUS to interact with the grid infrastructure.

Data and voice transmission rely heavily on wireless communication systems. However, these systems are susceptible to interference and require a thorough understanding to optimize their performance. Currently, traditional teaching methods lack the ability to provide students with hands-on experience for complex wireless network systems. This paper proposes a novel interactivity-based model, called Game-Based Learning of Wireless Networks (GBLWN), to address this issue. By transforming complex wireless network concepts into digital games, GBLWN enables students to develop their understanding through hands-on learning, allowing instructors to easily create customized games that facilitate student engagement and active learning.

The relationship between molecular oxygen and atmospheric properties is crucial for understanding past and future habitability. A reliable method for determining an atmosphere's oxygen level is the measurement of ozone, which is produced by chemical reactions involving oxygen. However, this correlation may not always hold true, particularly in atmospheres with low oxygen levels. A study has found that a certain pattern of atmospheric composition results in an overestimation of oxygen levels by as much as 30% when ozone is used as a proxy, which suggests that atmospheric models should be cautious when using this method to infer oxygen levels.

We've developed a method to create stable non-equilibrium currents in three-dimensional systems by exposing them to periodic pulses. By applying this technique to a 10-site Hofstadter model, we've created robust out-of-equilibrium surface currents that resist thermal fluctuations and external interference. Furthermore, our approach enables the control of the direction and amount of current transport, as well as its resistance to modification via nearby sites. In addition, we've found that these sustained currents can be transferred to adjacent sites and altered by changing the driving frequency, thus allowing us to control the direction and quantity of current in a 3D system through a single parameter.

Recent advancements in multilingual neural machine translation (NMT) have made it a more suitable option than traditional phrase-based machine translation for certain languages, such as English-Spanish. Nonetheless, these models can falter in translating rare or novel phrases, ultimately affecting the accuracy of professional interpretation. In medical NMT, this challenge is exacerbated by the need for precise translation of specialized terms, which is further complicated by domain-specific vocabulary and limited training resources. In an effort to address these limitations, we propose a novel approach that leverages domain adaptation to enhance the performance of ESNMT in medical contexts. By fine-tuning ESNMT on a target domain corpus and employing a domain adaptation layer to refine the encoding of source and target sentences, we demonstrate the potential of this approach in both low-resource and high-resource language pairs.

Investigations into the properties of solitary and shock waves in ion-acoustic systems have been conducted utilizing a fluid model incorporating both the pre-formed electron population and the temperature function of the ion fluid. These studies, which considered the effects of ion and electron temperatures, as well as the density of both, have led to the identification of distinct characteristics of the resulting solitary and shock waves. Specifically, the findings indicate that the primary cause of the solitary and shock waves' formation is an electron-related nonlinearity, which is influenced by the electron population's density and characteristics. Notably, the present research has also revealed that the temperature function of the ion fluid significantly affects the properties of the generated solitary and shock waves, particularly in terms of their speed, amplitude, and structure. Importantly, the present study has also demonstrated that the solitary and shock waves can effectively accelerate the pre-existing electron population, which in turn can lead to the formation of high-speed electrons.

Dense retrieval models have achieved top results in various natural language processing tasks, both in English and in multiple languages. However, the adaptability of these models to new languages has been limited, mainly due to the lack of available data for training and fine-tuning. This research explores the potential of unsupervised methods for pre-training multilingual dense retrieval models, using both monolingual and cross-lingual data, and proposes a novel approach called context-sensitive sentence representation. This method utilizes a transformer-based language model to capture sentence-level representations. By leveraging the attention weights from these representations, the approach can generate dense vectors that are more meaningful and context-sensitive. Experimental results on 12 languages demonstrate the effectiveness of this method, particularly when combined with other unsupervised pre-training techniques, and show that it can significantly outperform the baseline model trained only on in-language data.

Neural networks often struggle to merge information from multiple inputs effectively, and conventional methods rely heavily on feature alignment and inter-modal interactions. However, these approaches can only align features if a common semantic meaning exists between modalities, and their interactions can only capture general patterns, not individual samples' unique characteristics. To address these limitations, we propose a novel method, Prototypical Modal Adjustment (PMR), which adjusts modalities to fit pre-learned, modality-agnostic prototypes. This method enables the creation of a common semantic space where different modalities align naturally, and individual samples can be viewed through modality-specific lenses. Moreover, PMR allows for the identification of samples that deviate from expected behavior, serving as a learning signal for further specialization. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of our approach, and a thorough analysis of its intermediate representations is provided.

We expand on classical conveyance theory to a stochastic process framework and apply it to a hidden Markov model with a hidden state influenced by both a Brownian motion and a Poisson point process. The emerging process is then subjected to interference from a Poisson point process, leading to a new state that is observed by agents engaged in optimal filtering and transmission of this information. The engagement of these agents is modeled as a two-state Markov process, where each state represents either an engaged or a non-engaged state. We derive the stochastic equations governing the motion of this system, determine the optimal policies for the filters and transmitters, and develop a corresponding dynamic programming equation.

Verbal command recognition has become increasingly prominent in the field of human-computer interaction due to advancements in speech recognition technology. A novel approach utilizing deep learning networks, specifically tensor-train networks, has been proposed to tackle this challenge. In this study, the TT network's hybrid structure is explored as a means to enhance verbal command recognition. The TT network's ability to efficiently process high-dimensional data, coupled with its reduced computational requirements, makes it an attractive foundation for this investigation. A series of TT network variants, incorporating varying numbers of convolutional and recurrent components, is employed to identify verbal commands. The TT network's hybrid structure is put to the test using a custom dataset, comprising 10 classes of verbal commands, and compared against conventional neural network architectures. The experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed approach, yielding improved recognition rates and accelerated training times.

A novel approach to derive the Lindblad operator in the master equation of open quantum systems is presented through a new, unique factorization of the system's Hamiltonian. This factorization enables the discovery of non-standard and non-Markovian dynamics when the factors interact with their respective environments. The factorization is applicable to a broad range of Hamiltonians, including those with time-dependent terms, and can capture a wide range of dissipative behaviors. The utility of this factorization is demonstrated by applying it to a harmonic oscillator with a non-standard coupling to its environment, resulting in a variety of quantum dynamics.

A novel approach to enhance silicon thin-film solar cells' absorption capability is presented by integrating a thin Si layer on top of an ordered periodic nanostructure composed of alternating aluminum and air sections. By adjusting the thickness of the Si layer and using aluminum nanostructures with S-polarized light, it is possible to achieve a considerable boost in absorption. Numerical simulations demonstrate the effectiveness of this technique in significantly increasing the solar cell's absorption, with particular emphasis on the influence of different aluminum materials, including conventional, large-bandgap, and high-refractive-index varieties.

The increasing use of deep learning in video applications has led to significant energy consumption by training and deploying models on hardware platforms. To mitigate this issue, we present an efficient co-design method combining algorithmic and hardware optimization for energy-efficient Long Short-Term Memory networks in video identification. By decomposing model weights using the Hierarchical Tucker method, we reduce memory requirements, while customizing the Cholesky filter of LSTM cells and implementing them on Field-Programmable Gate Arrays allows for a wide range of kernel sizes without additional hardware costs. Our proposed approach has been integrated into an FPGA-based accelerator and demonstrates an energy efficiency improvement of over 30x compared to a conventional CPU implementation, without compromising accuracy.

The MAVLink protocol, used by the ArduPilot and PX4 projects, is widely used for communication between unmanned aerial vehicles and ground control and may be vulnerable to attacks. A comprehensive security analysis of the MAVLink protocol has not been previously conducted. This paper presents a security evaluation of MAVlink, identifying potential security risks and developing a security framework to safeguard it. The proposed framework includes a modified MAVLink protocol and a system for secure message authentication. The authors also suggest mitigating measures for system administrators and pilots to reduce the risks associated with using MAVLink.

The simulation of complex systems with diverse structures is a critical task in numerous fields. To address this challenge, we present a framework that efficiently runs parallel and adaptive simulations across fragmented and ever-changing graphs. To achieve this goal, we developed a novel distributed system, called Kollaps, that is capable of simulating dynamic graphs with millions of vertices and edges within a few seconds. Kollaps is a distributed system that is executed on a cluster of shared-memory nodes, with each node processing a portion of the graph's structure. To ensure accurate and efficient simulation, Kollaps employs a hybrid approach that combines a physics-based method with a machine learning-based method. The physics-based method utilizes a discrete element model to simulate the system's behavior, while the machine learning-based method enables the prediction of potential vertex collisions. These predictions are then used to trigger additional simulation steps, with the frequency of these steps determined by the system's complexity and adaptively adjusted to maintain accuracy. To demonstrate the effectiveness of Kollaps, we conducted a series of experiments using synthetic and real-world datasets, with the results showing that Kollaps is capable of handling large, dynamic graphs with millions of vertices and edges, with an average simulation time of under a second.

A detailed analysis of the twistor properties of the Kerr and anti-de Sitter spacetimes reveals their underlying structure, and further extends to cover Maxwell fields and solutions to the Einstein-Maxwell system in a comprehensive manner. This investigation yields a unified, explicit description of the Kerr and anti-de Sitter spacetimes in terms of domain of integrability, thereby providing an alternative foundation for their standard representation through Penrose conformal compactification. This alternative foundation is rooted in a natural, intrinsic space of null directions, and is achieved through a novel application of the Bergman method, where solutions to the associated twistor equations are constructed from integral formulas in complex domains of twistor punctures. This process results in a comprehensive, explicit representation of solutions to the Einstein-Maxwell system, encompassing a wide range of solutions, including those of the Kerr and anti-de Sitter types.

The Muon Tomography project aims to create underground imaging using muons as probes. Muons are high-energy cosmic rays produced in the Earth's atmosphere, which can travel through solid matter before disintegrating. Researchers have utilized muons as probes in the past to map the Earth's atmosphere, rock formations, and even celestial bodies. This study focuses on developing a detector that utilizes muons to create detailed 3D maps of underground tunnels. Specifically, this detector can produce cross-sectional images of tunnel structures, allowing for the detection of concealed objects. We outline the design principles of muon detectors, review relevant experiments, and describe our own detector design. We also present the results from a simulation using the Geant4 toolkit, demonstrating its potential for underground mapping.

A recent research paper by the Facebook AI team on Graph Linear Logic has sparked an investigation into its potential applications in programming languages across multiple domains. Our analysis focuses on a simplified version of Graph Linear Logic, referred to as Expression GLL, and demonstrates its close relationship to Linear Lambda Calculus. By translating the process of reducing graphs into linear typing as a type system for Expression GLL and proving its soundness, we establish a fundamental connection between the two. Furthermore, we explore three distinct scenarios for reducing graphs and examine their implications in terms of soundness and the preservation of types.

This research explores how thermal effects alter the vacuum Cherenkov radiation process in a $Q$-ball dominated state, where a charged particle's radiation occurs due to its massive vector field presence. A theoretical model was developed to investigate how temperature influences radiation emission rates and particle interactions within the $Q$-ball. Our findings indicate that temperature significantly impacts both the radiation and $Q$-ball properties of the particle in question.

To better understand how the brain creates predictions for spoken language, researchers have developed a novel method using deep neural language models. This approach overcomes the limitations of traditional methods based on finite state machines, which are prone to underestimating contextual dependencies in predicted words. By employing a more powerful infinite-state model, researchers can create a more accurate framework for testing neural language prediction in the brain. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this new approach, researchers have created a new neural language model, which was then used to monitor brain activity in individuals as they listened to a story and made verbal predictions of the narrator's upcoming words.

A crucial aspect of robotics research is the ability to determine an object's three-dimensional pose in a given environment. Traditional methods often rely on specific sensors, such as structured light systems, which can be cumbersome and not always available. This research presents an innovative approach to estimate a object's three-dimensional pose based on a single two-dimensional image, leveraging the observed motion of a rotating object. By analyzing a series of images of a rotating object, a proposed network can accurately estimate its three-dimensional pose. To address potential ambiguities in pose estimation, the method incorporates a module that resolves the object's center position, allowing for more precise rotation angle estimation. Experimental results demonstrate the method's effectiveness, achieving an average absolute error of 0.25 rad in rotation angles and 0.04 m in center position calculations.

In a hybrid semiconductor-superconductor nanowire with proximity-induced spin-orbit coupling and a break junction, we demonstrate the control of Andreev bound states through the gate voltage, allowing for the regulation of crossed Andreev reflection and co-tunneling behavior. The separation of these processes is achieved by adjusting the binding energy of these bound states. Furthermore, by modulating the barrier strength, we can control the transparency of Andreev processes. Our findings, obtained at low temperatures, are consistent with theoretical predictions and open up new avenues for the manipulation of Andreev processes in hybrid structures.

The acceleration of energetic particles in magnetic reconnection is still not fully understood.  One of the key factors that influences this process is the scattering of particles in all directions.  In this research, we have developed a new method to model this scattering and have applied it to various types of magnetic reconnection.  Our findings show that the strength of the scattering depends on the magnetic field's orientation in relation to the particle's trajectory.  As a result, the most significant scattering occurs when a strong guide field is present, leading to a slower increase in the particle energy distribution.  Our research suggests that the scattering may be sufficient to explain the formation of power-law distributions observed in certain types of magnetic reconnection.  The results of this research have important implications for understanding the acceleration of particles in various astrophysical environments.

The Large Hadron Collider's discovery of the Higgs boson has reignited interest in theories that go beyond the Standard Model. The Standard Model's simplicity and its unique scalar sector are particularly appealing as they can be easily expanded. However, this expansion could potentially resolve the strong CP problem and provide a natural explanation for the observed Higgs boson's mass. The possibility of a second Higgs boson with significant mass has significant implications for both e+e- collider experiments and future LHC studies. In this work, we investigate the effects of a second Higgs boson with significant mass on the accuracy of e+e- collider investigations of the Higgs boson. The investigation of the Higgs boson decay into photons is particularly relevant for a second Higgs boson with significant mass. Based on this, we derive constraints on the Standard Model of new physics, focusing on the relationship between the coupling of the Higgs boson with standard and non-standard particles. The derived constraints can be applied to a wide range of theories that go beyond the Standard Model, such as the two-Higgs-doublet model and the real triplet model.

This paper computes the subdifferentials of the combined numerical radius for normal operators on a specific space, yielding specific particular outcomes. It also derives dual formulas for the subdifferentials of this radius in relation to the geometric mean of two operators and the numerical radius of their sum.

A decentralized financial network, where multiple nodes manage the system, 
presents a challenge in maintaining user confidentiality due to the potential 
exposure of account activity and funds. To address this issue, a new approach 
is introduced, which employs a stealthy token and a stealthy account mechanism 
alongside a differential privacy method. This method is based on Laplace 
noise and meets the required privacy parameter.

This research focuses on stochastic mappings and random allocation fields, 
introducing a novel approach to studying stochastic processes with complex 
properties. By defining a stochastic mapping as a measurable function mapping 
a probability space into a random allocation field, a new framework for 
analysis is created. Notably, the concept of a stochastic mapping is more 
general than that of a stochastic process, offering a more detailed understanding 
of complex systems. The study demonstrates that any stochastic process can be 
seen as a specific type of stochastic mapping, and develops a formula to 
calculate the degree of correlation between two stochastic mappings. The 
analysis also provides a method for comparing the correlation between a stochastic 
mapping and a function. The framework of stochastic mappings is then used to 
develop a new approach to measuring the correlation between a stochastic process 
and an external function. The analysis is shown to be consistent with existing 
methods when applied to stationary stochastic processes. The study also provides 
a method for calculating the correlation between two stochastic mappings. The 
analysis is shown to be more efficient than traditional methods when applied to 
stationary stochastic processes. The findings are also applied to a specific 
case study involving a stochastic process with time-varying parameters.

Research has shown that high-energy, low-pressure laser-induced shocks in gases can be capable of triggering similar systems at much higher pressures, a concept known as multi-scale energy transfer. To investigate this phenomenon at elevated pressures, we used a compact, point-laser setup to create a shockwave in a He-H2-O2 mixture and triggered a larger, pressurized cylinder nearby, containing the same gas mixture, using an unfocused laser beam. The study found that the shockwave generated from the compact cylinder could successfully trigger the larger cylinder under specific conditions, with the success rate reaching nearly 100% when adjusting the gas composition and pressure levels. The study further analyzed the shockwave characteristics generated from the compact cylinder and found that the conditions that led to successful triggering also produced a stable shockwave that traveled at a speed of 2.2 km/s at a pressure of 16 bar, a value that matches predictions based on the conditions at the boundary of the pressurized cylinder.

A critical component of computer vision systems, object segmentation, has seen significant advancements in recent years, driven by the emergence of deep learning techniques. However, the focus of these innovations has been largely on improving the accuracy of object boundary detection. In this research, we introduce a new boundary-aware segmentation network that balances object detection and boundary identification simultaneously. By using a dual-branch framework, our network enhances object boundary detection, ultimately leading to more accurate segmentation results in real-world applications. To validate the effectiveness of our method, we conducted experiments on multiple public datasets and an in-house collection of mobile phone images, and the accompanying code is available for access.

This research proposes an innovative system to facilitate collaboration among driver assistance systems by enabling the exchange of information between systems of the same and different types, which was demonstrated through a lane change assistance system. The system's effectiveness was evaluated using simulator-based experiments, with qualitative analysis conducted using a driving simulator to identify any potential issues. The results show that the proposed system can support the coexistence of diverse systems and enhance driver-car communication.

Mathematical studies of passive particles moving in two-dimensional space have been extensively conducted, but a thorough analysis of similar dynamics in one, two, or more dimensions with limitations on particle interactions remains incomplete. In this research, we examine the influence of spatial constraints on one-dimensional, one-dimensional with reflection, and two-dimensional systems of particles interacting via hard-core interactions, with a focus on how these systems behave as interaction limits are approached. Our findings indicate that introducing spatial constraints does not alter the system's behavior as the interaction limits are approached, with one notable exception - in a circle containing many particles, a unique phase transition emerges at a specific interaction limit, preventing the particles from filling the entire circle.

In a one-dimensional single-channel model of atomic level decay, we consider an excited atom that can return to a stable state with a probability that depends on energy. This is modeled after a specific mathematical problem and we calculate the probability of this transition occurring, taking into account the atom's ability to return at any time. Our results show that even though the atom can return to its stable state at any energy level, it is primarily affected by a specific range of transition energies, leading us to define a new type of transition probability which we call the 'typical atom model'. This probability has a distinct distribution that is influenced by the width of the transition and we calculate its properties. This model is relevant to current scientific research on this topic.

Using the Fast Imaging Plasmatic Channel on the Interface Wideband Imaging Coud\'e \`Echelle Spectrograph (SWIFTS), we observed rapid changes in solar flare spectra and conducted an in-depth analysis to pinpoint the source of the fluctuations. Our analysis revealed that the Si~IV intensity, which is indicative of non-thermal processes, experiences significant variations in the low corona during solar flares. We discovered that the Si~IV line intensity exhibits a rapid increase and decrease on a sub-second timescale, which is consistent with the primary phase of solar flares. Our investigation suggests that the Si~IV line intensity is influenced by the non-thermal velocity of coronal plasma rather than other factors, which is driven by the magnetic reconnection process. Our findings have implications for the study of flare heating mechanisms and the dynamics of coronal plasma.

We investigate the interplay between the CP dilemma and the observational constraints on the axion mass, particularly in the presence of an explicit breaking term. Our findings suggest that these two issues are intricately connected. Specifically, we discover that the axion mass remains unaffected by the explicit breaking parameter, yet its interactions with this parameter have a profound impact on the axion's potential. As a result, we establish that the axion's vacuum value is influenced by the explicit breaking parameter. Notably, we derive a relationship that correlates the axion's vacuum value with its mass, thus linking these two quantities to the explicit breaking parameter. Furthermore, we explore the implications of this connection on the CP dilemma and the experimental limits imposed on the axion's mass. Specifically, we demonstrate that the axion's mass is constrained to be within a certain range, and we further show that the axion's interactions with electric and magnetic fields are directly related to the explicit breaking parameter. Consequently, we derive a bound on the axion's electric dipole moment, and we also examine the implications of this bound on the axion's destiny.

Theoretical models of light-induced migration in irradiated polymers suggest a fundamental relationship between material structure and molecular movement, with the angle at which shadowing occurs being a key factor. Research indicates that irradiation can alter the relationship between molecular orientation and the physical properties of polymers, expanding the range of angles associated with selective polymerization-induced diffusion. An in-depth examination of the effects of irradiation on polymer structure reveals that the internal forces within the material play a more significant role in shadowing than the effects of radiation, with some limitations related to the specific characteristics of energetic particles.

The concept of anti-cheating technology has been around for a while, but most existing approaches have limitations, including being language-specific and failing to address cheating through source code modifications. In response, we have developed a novel anti-cheating system called source code anti-cheating, or SCA, which can detect cheating attempts regardless of the programming language used. SCA works by translating source code into a intermediate format, called a source code graph, before executing it, thus preventing cheating attempts. In this paper, we demonstrate the effectiveness of SCA through an experiment using a C# code and a well-known anti-cheating algorithm called the routing method. In the experiment, a malicious version of the C# code was created to introduce a cheating attempt. However, when the routing method was applied to the malicious code, it successfully detected the cheating attempt, thus preventing it from executing malicious code. In conclusion, the results of this experiment demonstrate the potential of SCA to effectively detect and prevent cheating attempts in a variety of programming languages.

This article explores the complete convergence of a specific type of Dirichlet series, which are based on quadratic forms originating from here and there. The investigation relies on the use of the long hybrid Dirichlet series; a key outcome is that the complete convergence of this series implies the complete convergence of the original forms. Additionally, we examine the asymptotic behavior of a related estimate involving the maximal values of form sums.

This research investigates the interaction between metric near-subgroups and the related distance, introducing new findings such as a characterization of metric near-subgroups through the distance graph connection, demonstrating a characteristic of uniform metric near-subgroups, and developing an efficient method to construct metric near-subgroups.

We propose a new computational framework for determining parameters in density models that follow a log-concave distribution, based on a combination of MCMC sampling and traditional maximum likelihood estimation methods. This approach improves upon maximum likelihood estimation by leveraging low-discrepancy sequences and MCMC simulations to sample the posterior distribution, thus circumventing the issue of high model complexity. Our method is capable of handling large datasets of up to 10,000 observations while maintaining a moderate number of latent variables. Our results demonstrate that this approach yields improved estimation results, particularly in terms of higher log-likelihood values, when compared to maximum likelihood estimation methods.

The Wang-Landau algorithm is utilized to efficiently explore the vast configuration space of static granular systems within a fixed volume. By systematically altering the Boltzmann factor of individual grains, we transform the task of identifying stable structures into a problem of computing entropy. By updating the free-energy landscape, we can identify systems' equilibrium states and accurately calculate their associated entropies. Our approach enables the calculation of microstates with arches, leading to a deeper understanding of how these structures emerge from disordered states. Furthermore, this method allows us to analyze the properties of configurations that involve the destruction of arches and their transformation into more disordered states.

We investigate an intrinsically linked game of cat-and-mouse on graph structures, 
involving a coordinated effort between two players. The graph consists of a 
graph divided into distinct subsets, denoted as vertices V and sets A, B, with 
V partitioned into A and B respectively. The game's objective is to identify a 
common point within V, represented by a node that is simultaneously part of 
A and B, with the goal of achieving this result in the fewest number of steps 
possible, aligning with the concept of a well-documented 'h Hunter-victim' model 
of a graph game. The game's complexity is analyzed in relation to its graph 
topology, with the game being proven to be solvable within a limited timeframe 
for connected graphs with a limited number of vertices and a specific graph 
structure known as a tree. However, we also demonstrate the game's potential to 
be computationally challenging for certain types of graphs. Furthermore, we 
demonstrate that our results are not only applicable to the specific subset 
divisions of vertices but also to the subset divisions of edges.

This research examines the frequency-domain spectral distribution of Gaussian processes in a single realization, focusing on the correlations between frequencies. These single realizations deviate from the well-studied ensemble-averaged spectral behavior, which is characterized by a power-law frequency-frequency relationship. The origin of this distinct behavior is attributed to the natural fluctuations that occur when Gaussian processes are transformed from time-domain random walks to frequency-domain random walks through Fourier analysis.

This research examines the first-order corrections to the (1+1)-dimensional Broer-Kaup equation, incorporating higher-order terms to account for conservation laws, and then develops a Lax pair and bi-Hamiltonian structure for the modified equation. We utilize the resulting Floreanu-S Vinogradov linear compatibility matrix definition to determine conservation laws. By applying linearization techniques, we transform the modified Broer-Kaup equation into a linear form, enabling the derivation of its explicit solution. We also explore the relationship between gauge transformations and (weak) symmetries, and provide localized (weak) Lie point symmetries. Furthermore, we identify the (weak) engagement (Eng) criterion for the modified Broer-Kaup equation and its first-order corrections in terms of the Jacobian matrix of the linearized system. By applying this criterion, we derive engagement remedies for the original Broer-Kaup equation and its first-order corrections, and demonstrate that these remedies can be expressed in terms of Wronskian solutions.

We prove the existence of energy-conserving weak solutions for the incompressible Euler equations with the help of a concept called relative circulation. To achieve this, we first establish the existence of Euler flows with non-zero relative circulation, which enables us to demonstrate that these flows transport measure-preserving flows at the same relative circulation, leading to the existence of Euler trajectories with non-zero relative circulation, and ultimately allowing us to show that a flow with non-zero relative circulation is associated with a trajectory having the same relative circulation. This ultimately enables us to prove the strong convergence of an approximating sequence, leading to the existence of weak Euler solutions with preserved energy.

The Virtual Reality industry is rapidly expanding, marked by a significant surge in the adoption of Virtual, Mixed, and Augmented Reality technologies. This growth is driven by the increasing availability of affordable hardware and software, as well as a rising interest in the metaverse concept. This paper presents the VIRUP project, an innovative initiative that enables users to immerse themselves in a virtual environment where they can confront their avatars with fantastical, non-human entities. These virtual entities, designed to resemble human figures, are created using 3D scanning technology and brought to life through animation. The project's development offers opportunities for future research in the realm of Virtual Reality, focusing on the concept of illusion and the blurring of lines between reality and fantasy.

When adults encounter complex data, they often rely on user-friendly visualizations to make sense of it. Our research aimed to create similar tools for children to understand and interact with data, just like adults do. We developed a data visualization platform, Expedition, which utilizes a data-filled container to create an immersive experience, allowing kids to engage with data in a hands-on manner. Our study involved a pilot program with 19 kids aged 9 to 17, where they explored data visualizations in different formats, such as tables and graphs, and demonstrated their ability to identify patterns and connections. Our findings show that kids can develop an intuitive understanding of data visualizations by simply viewing them, without needing to read descriptions or explore the data points. Moreover, Expedition enabled kids to make connections between data across different formats, such as linking tables to graphs, and allowed them to engage in in-depth data analysis by examining multiple data visualizations simultaneously and identifying patterns that they could not previously see.

A data-path in a network allows data to be transmitted through a configured route. In traditional, non-programmable networks, these paths are set in stone by the manufacturer, with little room for change. In contrast, software-defined networks (SDNs) make data-paths programmable, enabling administrators to easily modify them. However, this flexibility comes with the risk of errors if paths aren't properly configured. This paper focuses on how SDN data-paths are designed and identifies the key design choices that affect their functionality. By examining these factors, we can identify areas where errors can occur and suggest improvements to help designers create more reliable paths.

We introduce a new generative model that combines strong and weak untangled
representations. Untangled representations are desirable as they facilitate
efficient learning and inference processes. Our proposed model, the Weakly
Untangled Factor Analyzer, leverages a factor analyzer with shared loadings
for each group of variables, resulting in separate encodings for each group.
This approach is motivated by the assumption that data from the same group
share similar patterns, while the remaining variables exhibit correlations
across the different groups. This framework is particularly useful in social
networking, where users from the same group (e.g., friends, followers) exhibit
similar patterns, while variables across the different groups exhibit
correlations (e.g., posts, comments across different groups of users). Our model
is applied to a real-world dataset of two graphs representing the friendship
and follower relationships of users in a social media network, resulting in
improved inference and classification performance.

The efficiency of energy collection from tandem oscillating blades in a wind turbine depends on several factors including the wake created by the first blade and its interaction with the second blade. To optimize performance, understanding these dynamics is essential. A study investigated the relationship between the wake created by the first blade and the performance of the second blade, particularly in terms of wake characteristics and energy transfer. The study focused on oscillating and fixed blades at various angles and compared their interactions using both direct and wake-based models. Results showed that oscillating blades performed better than fixed blades, particularly at higher angles. The energy collected by oscillating blades in tandem was higher than that from a combination of a fixed blade and an oscillating blade at similar conditions. The study's findings have significant implications for optimizing wind turbine performance.

To study particle physics via lattice QCD, researchers must determine the real part of correlation functions.  This task is particularly challenging as it involves identifying the contribution of physical particles amidst a backdrop of unobserved particle species, a problem akin to diagnosing the underlying dynamics of a system when the underlying process is unknown.  This paper presents a novel Bayesian approach that enables researchers to infer the real-time spectral function from lattice QCD simulations.  The proposed method is applied to the quark-gluon plasma's correlation function, yielding a solution that is both analytically and numerically feasible and can be validated experimentally.

A quantum point in a semiconductor can be used to probe the electronic environment of a superconducting material nearby. When a superconducting material is placed near a quantum point, the interaction between the two can result in the formation of quasiparticles that tunnel back and forth. The interaction between these quasiparticles and phonons can lead to the formation of quantum coherence, which in turn affects the superconducting material's ability to conduct electricity. This research focuses on the interaction between a quantum point and a superconducting material and demonstrates how to use a gate to investigate the mechanisms behind the charge tunneling between them. The findings of this research can be applied to the development of hybrid devices that combine superconductors with quantum dots or semiconductors.

In the field of drug discovery, reproducing the molecular structure of known drugs with similar properties is crucial. A key challenge is identifying drugs that share specific pharmacophore characteristics, which are crucial for a drug's effectiveness. A novel approach, Energy-driven Generative Models, is proposed to efficiently generate pharmacophore candidates based on molecular structure. This method uses a two-step process involving an autoencoder and an adversarial network to extract and generate pharmacophore characteristics. By leveraging a pre-trained autoencoder, the method achieves accurate reconstruction of the latent code and outperforms unsupervised models in reconstructing molecular properties.

A new approach called Energetic Geometry (EG) has been developed to analyze the complex interactions within web-based systems, such as The Engagement Machine. This system, driven by tokens, creates multiple interconnected networks among users. By modeling these networks as a directed graph, called Token-Directed Graph (TDG), our research aims to understand the geometric patterns that emerge from the energetic interactions among users. Our theoretical framework demonstrates that TDG can be represented as a transformation of EG, and that the unique topological features of these networks are consistent across different scenarios. Furthermore, we have identified that TDG networks exhibit clustering properties, both globally and locally, and that the distribution of nodes and links within these networks follows a power-law distribution. The findings of this research have significant implications for the design of web-based systems, such as social media platforms, and can also be applied to other areas where similar energetic networks exist.

The Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) is a critical target in understanding star formation and dynamics. The precise motion of its stars, particularly those on the outskirts, is vital for modeling the LMC's evolution. Our research involves analyzing the proper motion of stars in the LMC and surrounding environment, using data from the VMC survey. The data reveals that stars in the outer regions of the LMC exhibit a range of motions, with some aligning with the LMC's rotation and others showing no correlation. Notably, the motion of stars in the outer SMC exhibits a distinct pattern, suggesting a possible merger between the LMC and SMC. The stars in the SMC exhibit a similar motion to the LMC, indicating a possible merger between the two galaxies. The findings also suggest that the SMC had a lower mass than the LMC, possibly accounting for the influence of tidal interactions.

A significant concern in smart grid systems is the power theft problem, which involves malicious entities siphoning off electricity while concealing their actions from utility providers. Identifying and stopping power theft promptly is critical to prevent substantial financial losses and maintain grid reliability. Recent research has employed deep learning techniques, particularly neural networks, to detect power theft from smart grid systems. These methods, however, rely on optimizing hyper-parameters through a labor-intensive, manual process, which can be impractical for real-world applications due to the high computational cost. To overcome this limitation, this study introduces a novel approach using a recurrent neural network to detect power theft, and demonstrates that a well-trained network can function optimally after adjusting its hyper-parameters randomly. A detailed analysis of the proposed method is provided, along with experimental results showing its effectiveness in detecting power theft from smart grid systems.

A compact two-dimensional surface graph G is defined as the one-dimensional skeleton of a two-dimensional topological space formed by the vertices of G and its one-dimensional skeleton. A compact surface graph is topologically equivalent to a compact space X if and only if it can be embedded in a one-dimensional skeleton of X. It is demonstrated that for a compact surface graph G and a compact two-dimensional space X, there exists a homeomorphism from X to G if and only if G can be obtained from X through a sequence of specific transformations involving the addition of one hole to a compact graph. Additionally, a method of creating one-dimensional skeletons on a torus by gluing one-hole handles to compact graphs is also presented.

The lifetimes of two types of baryons, the omega-c and xi-c, which are quickly produced in high-energy collisions, have been measured using a specific technique that examines the decay patterns of these particles. This method involves comparing the decay rates of the omega-c and xi-c particles to those of another particle, the D0, which is used as a comparison standard. The study found that the omega-c and xi-c particles have lifetimes similar to each other and significantly different from that of the D0 particle. The study's results, which are based on a large data set, provide a more accurate measurement of the lifetimes of these particles, which are critical for understanding certain particle decays. The study found that the omega-c and xi-c particles have lifetimes of 280.9 with an uncertainty of 2.8 picoseconds and 3.083 with an uncertainty of 0.019 picoseconds, respectively, which are consistent with previous studies.

Hyperspectral images serve as a valuable resource for land use classification tasks, offering a wealth of information in multiple dimensions.  However, the high dimensionality of hyperspectral images poses a significant challenge for traditional land cover classification methods, which often rely on sparse and noisy data. To overcome this limitation, we propose a new approach that utilizes a two-stage method, incorporating a similarity-based subspace clustering technique and a high-dimensional spectral classification method. At the initial stage, the approach identifies key subspace clusters from the embedded hyperspectral image, which are then classified using a high-dimensional spectral classification method. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in efficiently and accurately categorizing both low and high-dimensional spectral data.

The shape and appearance of snow-covered Arctic sea ice serve as indicators for its condition, which is crucial for understanding its role in shaping Earth's climate.
